title: Introduction to Flight
description:
This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic
aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems,
and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts
that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight
mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.
Following are the scope and objective of this course:
a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four
forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion.
b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures,
propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions.
c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and
engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems.
d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in
flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes
Explain the principles of flight by describing the four fundamental forces (lift, weight, thrust, and drag) and their interactions during flight.
Analyse atmospheric effects on flight by interpreting how atmospheric properties influence aircraft performance and operations.
Apply basic aerodynamic concepts to evaluate the performance of airfoil, wings, and aircraft under various flight conditions.
Evaluate aircraft performance by estimating take-off, climb, cruise, descent, landing, range, and endurance characteristics using fundamental engineering principles.
Describe aircraft stability and control and explain how control surfaces affect aircraft motion and manoeuvrability.
Compare aircraft propulsion systems, including propeller- and jet-powered engines, and explain their operating principles and performance characteristics.
Learn Hypersonic flight, concepts of Newtonian theory and its application to Hypersonic vehicles.
Solve introductory flight-related engineering problems using mathematics, physics, and computational tools where appropriate.
Interpret the relationship between aircraft design and flight performance, recognizing how design choices affect efficiency, safety, and operational capability.
Communicate technical concepts related to flight through written reports, calculations, and engineering discussions
topics: M1: Introduction
M2: Standard Atmosphere

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
description:
Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes,
Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant
tissues and Cell cycle analysis.
The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies
to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of
practical biology.

title: Biological Chemistry
description:
This course is intended to offer an introduction to the world of Biological
Chemistry. The course deals with the structure, properties, and significance of the major groups of
biochemical compounds (amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids), the
bioenergetics, enzyme mechanisms and regulation of the central metabolic pathways. Efforts will
be made to include the recent advances and methodologies related to biochemistry. This would
help students going for higher level activities, appreciation of biochemical problems, evaluation
and problem solving.

title: CELL BIOLOGY
description:
A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural
and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic
and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by
providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the
working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure,
intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms
and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational
for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental
biology.

title: INTEGRATED BIOLOGY
description:
The course intends to bridge the gap and open new vistas to students taking up biology. The
course covers two tracks, essentially. The first track introduces the student to the ordering that helps biologists to
actually study the vast diversity of the living world. This track would encompass questions related to the origin and
evolutionary pathways followed in nature, as well as the methods followed by biologists to systematically categorize and
document them. The second track highlights the uses and applications of biology in everyday life – whether in the
economic or in the social realms. Together, the course projects the subject in a way from which the student can choose
and implement his biological knowledge vis-à-vis his/her interests.
Being the second course on General Biology, the course exposes the students
to the foundational aspects as described above. At the end of the course, the student will have developed a basic
understanding of the evolutionary processes, rationale for taxonomic arrangements and familiarity of selected,
representative members of the major kingdoms of living organisms. Further, the student will also become aware of how
knowledge of biology (both botany and zoology) is applied for benefit of mankind and other organisms.
learning_outcomes: To understand the scientific basis of evolution in populations
To apply the evolutionary knowledge in classification scheme of organisms

title: RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY
description:
The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation.
Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental
work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic
systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.
Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This
course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods
and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology.
topics: L1: Defining the scope and context of the course. Introduction to Recombinant DNA Techniques and workflow summary.
L2-5: Enzymes for manipulating DNA; Restriction mapping and analysis
L6-12: Understanding PCR; different types of PCR – inverse PCR, multiplex PCR, quantitative real time PCR, DD PCR Genomic, cDNA & specialized libraries

title: Animal Physiology
description:
Basic functional processes in animals; like homeostasis, membrane physiology, digestive, respiratory,
excretory, circulatory, reproductive, nervous, sensory, muscular, endocrine systems will be studied at
structural, functional, cellular and molecular level.
This course attempts to bring the awareness among students for major features of animal physiology and co-
relate that to the human physiology. Emphasis will be on structure and function relationship and importanc
of every organ. In addition, the course will also discuss about some of the diseases that are associated with
complication in different organs.
learning_outcomes: Integration of multiple organ systems to regulate and maintain homeostasis between the internal and external environments.
Explore the process of enzymatic digestion and its physiological outcomes within the digestive tract.
Functional mechanisms of the human kidneys in regulating fluid homeostasis and urine formation.
Overview of the cardiac cycle, electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, types of circulatory vessels, regulation of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the various cellular components of blood.
Anatomical and functional organization of nervous system, including its structural and spatial characteristics.
The role of hormones in regulating homeostasis and supporting essential physiological functions.
Understanding gas partial pressures, intrapleural pressure dynamics, lung volumes and capacities, respiratory disorders, and the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin.
Study of sarcomere structure, the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction, the physiological basis of rigor mortis, and the phenomenon of muscle twitching.
Exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing gametogenesis, fertilization, and progression of pregnancy.

title: Biomolecular Modeling
description:
Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding,
Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice
models, usage of modeling packages.
The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience
of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and
structural biology. It describes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard computing
strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to
carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling
to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data
in a research or industry laboratory environment.

Conformation and Variability in DNA and RNA structures

title: ENZYMOLOGY
description:
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation,
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology
and will create research interest among the students.
topics: L#1-2: Broad overview of the subject and field of Enzymology and Quick preview of the entire course contents.
L# 3-4: Brief history of Enzymology; EC system of classification; Main classes of enzymes, with examples.
L# 5-7: Enzyme structure and conformations; Types of enzyme specificity; Specificity Hypotheses.

L# 8-11: Introduction to catalysis and kinetics; Kinetics of single-substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions; Enzyme inhibition; Kinetics of multi- substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Mechanisms of catalysis with examples; Enzymes and metabolic regulation; Investigation of active site structure.
L# 12-19: Extraction of enzymes; Enzyme assay methods; Enzyme purification techniques.
L# 20-21: Various Instrumental techniques used in Enzymatic analysis
L# 22-23: Kinetic methods; Enzyme- immunoassays
L# 24-26: Methods of immobilization, Properties of immobilized enzymes and Applications

L# 27-35: Applications of enzymes and enzymatic analysis in clinical medicine, biotechnology, and pharmacology; Industrial Production of enzymes and applications (examples: in Food, Process industry).

L# 36-38: Enzyme & Co-factor engineering – Current trends and Future prospects in Pharmaceutical & Fermentation Industries. Enzymes & Biosensors; Latest advances in enzymes - Industrial and Research-applications will be discussed.

title: Molecular Mechanism of Gene Expression
description:
Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic genomes and their topology; DNA protein interaction, RNA transcription and
transcriptional control, Translation, RNA processing, Post transcriptional control and other mechanisms of
gene expression
This course is designed to impart knowledge of molecular genetics, which is one of the fundamental
requirements for the biotechnology. This course is designed to make the student understand the various
mechanisms, which regulate the biological processes at genetic level including transcriptional and post
transcriptional regulation of gene.
topics: L. 1-5. Genes are DNA, Different methods to map a gene in prokaryote and eukaryotes. Fine structure of Gene L 6-8. title: Molecular Immunology
description:
The course will deal extensively with topics like molecular basis of T and B
cell antigen recognition and activation. Immunity to microbes and diseases caused by humoral
and cell mediated immune responses will be covered and emphasis placed on congenital and
acquired immuno-deficiencies. Advanced topics like antibody engineering will be discussed with
the help of review articles.
The course intends to familiarize the students with modern concepts in
immunology. The endeavor will be to highlight concepts in immunology, which would have an
influence on understanding the fascinating entity which comprises the body’s immune system
and ancillary procedure of therapy.

title: Advanced & Applied Microbiology
description:
This course deals with an in-depth study of microbial taxonomy and evolution, as well as the
molecular aspects of microbe-host interactions. In addition, it includes applied aspects of
microorganisms being utilized in industry and human health. It also emphasizes on recent
development in microbial genomics, nanotechnology and biotechnology.
topics: L1: Introduction to the course
L 2- 4: Chemical and molecular methods for identification, species concept, molecular phylogeny, and typing of strains
L 5-9: Microbial ecology, ecosystem services, surface and microbial assemblages, Ecology of soil, and marine ecosystem. Host-associated microbiome (including human)

L 10 – 11: Methods in microbial ecology, Culture-dependent and independent analysis of microbial communities, metagenomics, stable isotope probing, Application of metagenomics in bioprospecting of drugs and enzymes.
textbooks: Madigan M.T., Martinko J.M., Bender K.S., Buckley D.H., Stahl D.A. (2017). Brock Biology of Microorganism, 14th Ed., Pearson International Education

title: Microbiology
description:
Introduction and classification of microbes; isolation, cultivation, physiological and biochemical
characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology;
host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical
microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.
This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as
their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry.
topics: L 1-3. The microbial world
L 4. Microscopy and Specimen preparation
L 5-6. Requirement for growth, obtaining pure cultures and maintenance
L 7-10. The morphology & fine structure of bacteria
L 11-13. Eukaryotic microorganisms
L 14-16. Characterization, classification and identification of microorganism
L 17-19. Virus, Viroids, Prions
L 20-22. Growth of Microbes and its measurement; Synchronous and continuous culture
L 23-25. Microbial metabolism
L 26-28. Physical and chemical methods of microbial control, Antimicrobial drugs
L 29-32. The genetics of microorganisms; Synthetic Microbiology
L 33-35. Principles of diseases and epidemiology, Microbial Mechanisms of Pathogenicity
L 36-38. Microbiology of soil, domestic and waste water
L 39-41. Microbiology of food and Industrial microbiology
textbooks: Tortora, G.J., Funke, B.R. and Case, C.L. 2020. Microbiology: An Introduction, 12th Ed., Pearson India Education Services Pvt. Ltd. India
references: Willey, J.M., Sherwood, L.M. and Woolverton, C.J. 2017. Prescott, Harley and Klein’s Microbiology, 7th Edition, The McGraw-Hill Companies Inc., New York.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND WASTE
description:
Application of biotechnology to the management of environmental problems. Biotechnology for
enhanced plant and animal production through biological insecticides, herbicides resistance, mineral
cycling, conservation of genetic resources and biological nitrogen fixation. Use of biotechnological
processes for pollution control, bioremediation of toxicants and treatment of domestic and industrial
wastes. Ethical issues related with the release of genetically modified organism.
The major objective of this course is to impart knowledge on application of biotechnological processes
for betterment of environment. This course is designed to make the student understand the various
biological phenomena, which can be exploited to save environment from eventual deterioration.
topics: Basic concept of environment and its components. Biotechnology for environment; definitions and facts
Sources of various pollutions and their environmental impact.

Methods for the measurement of pollution. Air, water and soil sampling; Analyses of samples; physical, chemical and biological methods. Nucleic acid based techniques for analyses of diversity, structure and dynamics of microbial
community in wastewater treatment, Concept of biomarkers. Metagenomics.
Basics of sewage treatment processes. Function of various treatment systems. Microbiology of sewage treatment
Fundamentals of clean technology. Integrated pest management and bio- control of plant diseases. Microbial polymer production and bio-plastic technology
Pros and cons of nano- biotechnology
Biotechnology for energy production; basic concept. Biological energy sources and bio- fuels. Biotechnology for enhanced oil recovery
Release of genetically modified organisms
Pressing environmental issues in India, Government's policies and programs
Nitrification and denitrification– microbial fundamentals and application. Biological phosphate removal

Microbial interaction with metallic elements. Metal Toxicity. Molecular mechanism of metal resistance. Biosorption and biotransformation of metals and radionuclides. Recent developments in metal bioremediation.

Aerobic and anaerobic degradation of organic pollutants. Principles, biochemical pathways and genetic regulation. Degradation of aliphatic, aromatic, polyaromatic and chlorinated compounds. Recent developments in waste treatment.
Use of plants for removal of organic and metallic pollutants
Concepts of bioleaching, microbial aspects, regulatory factors and process application
Sources, health hazards, treatment and disposal technologies
Principle, types and applications
textbooks: Environmental Biotechnology by Alan Scragg, Oxford University Press, UK.2015
references: Environmental Biotechnology: Basic concepts and applications by Indu Shekhar Thakur, Second edition. I.K. International Publishing House Pvt. Ltd. New Delhi 2011.

title: BIOSTATISTICS & BIOMODELING
description:
Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics
part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students
with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard
deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA
etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations.
Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling
biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function.
Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be
discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.
The student would learn how to collect data suitable for
statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical
inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of
significance.
topics: Introduction
Protein structure and conformation
textbooks: Biostatistics: A foundation for Analysis in the Health Sciences. Wayne Daniel, Ninth Edition, Wiley-India Edition, 2009.
Molecular modeling: Principles and Applications. Andrew R Leach, 2nd Edition, 2001, Pearson Education Lim.
references: Principles of Biostatistics, M. Pagano and K. Gauvereau, Thomson Learning Publ., Indian Ed., 2007.
Molecular Modeling and Simulation - An Interdisciplinary Guide. Tamar Schlick, Springer, New York, 2002.

title: Advanced Cell and Molecular Biology
description:
The course deals with in-depth aspects of molecular biology of eukaryotic cell. We will discuss about
molecules regulating and functional in Eukaryotic cell cycle: restriction point, G1 phase progression, role of
cyclin and CKIs, cell cycle & cancer, metastasis, molecular chaperones, apoptosis and necrosis, Extra cellular
matrix & adhesion, growth factors, cell signal transduction, stem cells and their potential in therapy,
transport in and out of nucleus.
This course will give insights to the students into some frontier areas in cell and molecular biology helping
students understand the overall functioning of a cell under different environmental conditions including
presence or absence of mitogens/ nutrition/ stress conditions, etc.. This will enable student draw concept
map about different cell functions and related proteins.
topics: Course Orientation, discussion on mode of conductance of various evaluation components, seminar topics, etc
Cell cycle Overview, different phases, cell cycle control and regulatory components, control of cell division and cell growth, Cyclin Kinase inhibitors
Mechanism of cell death with special reference to apoptosis and necrosis, cascade of apoptosis implications
Mechanism of protein folding in E.coli and mammalian systems, Molecular chaperones, Protein trafficking across cell and export, Proteolysis

Mechanisms of signal transduction by cell surface receptor proteins (G proteins, enzyme coupled receptors), growth factors and their interaction with receptors in cell proliferation and its regulation, JAK – STAT, Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, NF- B pathways.
Molecular basis of cancer, Cancer as micro-evolutionary process, cancer critical genes, molecular basis of cancer – cell behavior.
Mechanism for the transport of RNA and “Cargo” proteins into and out of nucleus
Cadherins, cell – cell adhesions, tight junctions and gap junctions, Role of CAMs in cell attachment, Basal Lamina, integrins, Components of ECM, role of ECM in bi-directional signaling.
Epidermis and its renewal by Stem cells, multipotent stem cells, stem cell engineering
Duration
90 minutes
variable
3 hrs.
textbooks: Molecular Biology of the Cell (7th/ 6th edition), Bruce Alberts, Alexander Johnson, Julian Lewis, David Morgan, Martin Raff, Keith Roberts and Peter Walter. Garland Publishing Inc., New York and London, 2022.
references: Molecular Cell Biology (Ninth Edition), Lodish, Berk, Krieger, Scott, Bretscher, Ploegh, Matsudaira. Freeman, 2022.

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES

Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant
tissues and Cell cycle analysis.
The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies
to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of
practical biology.

title: ENZYMOLOGY
description:
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation,
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology
and will create research interest among the students.
topics: L#1-2: Broad overview of the subject and field of Enzymology and Quick preview of the entire course contents.
L# 3-4: Brief history of Enzymology; EC system of classification; Main classes of enzymes, with examples.
L# 5-7: Enzyme structure and conformations; Types of enzyme specificity; Specificity Hypotheses.

L# 8-11: Introduction to catalysis and kinetics; Kinetics of single-substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions; Enzyme inhibition; Kinetics of multi- substrate enzyme-catalyzed reactions. Mechanisms of catalysis with examples; Enzymes and metabolic regulation; Investigation of active site structure.
L# 12-19: Extraction of enzymes; Enzyme assay methods; Enzyme purification techniques.
L# 20-21: Various Instrumental techniques used in Enzymatic analysis
L# 22-23: Kinetic methods; Enzyme- immunoassays
L# 24-26: Methods of immobilization, Properties of immobilized enzymes and Applications

L# 27-35: Applications of enzymes and enzymatic analysis in clinical medicine, biotechnology, and pharmacology; Industrial Production of enzymes and applications (examples: in Food, Process industry).

L# 36-38: Enzyme & Co-factor engineering – Current trends and Future prospects in Pharmaceutical & Fermentation Industries. Enzymes & Biosensors; Latest advances in enzymes - Industrial and Research-applications will be discussed.
L# 39: Pointers for R&D and industrial applications of enzymes

title: Food Biotechnology
description:
The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is
one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course,
a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their
processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future
biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the
production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically
modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste
management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food
Biotechnology will be discussed.
The aim of this course is providing the students with basic
knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors.
These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in
food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced
techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.
topics: Introduction to Food Science and Technology

Food spoilage: physical, chemical and biological agents, Factors influencing the growth and survival of microorganisms in foods, Food borne illness: Infection & intoxication; Detection of micro- organisms/ spoilage in food; Strategies for the control of spoilage agents.
Use of temperature (Heat Sterilization, refrigeration); Radiation etc. for food preservation
Nutraceuticals in health and disease management; Probiotics and prebiotics, Protein foods; Single Cell Proteins; Mycoproteins
Enzymes in food science: friend and/or enemy; Modification of enzymes involved in food processing
Bio fortification; CRISPR based gene editing; GMO crops
Microbial cultures used in food industries (LAB); Production of Cheese, Beer Brewing, Wine Making, Yoghurt
Food additives, food colors & sweeteners, emulsifiers; antioxidants etc.
Sensory evaluation of food quality; Ethics and safety of food biotechnology; Food Safety Rules and Regulations
Utilization of wastes for food production, fuel and fertilizers, Integrated processes & strategies in food production
Case studies of Successful Entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology

title: Social Conduct 1
description:
Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and
Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity &
Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety.
This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all
students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core
emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes
conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries
and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior
and building awareness against substance abuse.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to CLO1.Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. CLO2. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. CLO3. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. CLO4. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. CLO5. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. CLO6. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. CLO7. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. CLO8. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community.

title: Science, Technology and Modernity
description:
This course is designed to provide students with a
comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures,
economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to
foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a
basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the
examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such
as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and
final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to
consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and
outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of
scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.
topics: The Kuhnian revolution; Industrial Revolution; The Social Construction of Scientific and Technical Realities; Actor- Network Theory
Knowledge protection; Innovation process; Spatial dimensions of innovation; Technology diffusion; Policy debates in innovation
Stratification and Discrimination; Political economy of technology transfer; Role of power; Just Transition
textbooks: Sismondo, Sergio, An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies, UK: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010. Jacob, Margaret. 1997. Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West. New York: Oxford University Press. Friedman, Thomas L. 1999. The Lexus and the Olive Tree. New York: Anchor Books.
consultation_hours: 5-6 pm (Office: 6168L-by prior appointment).

title: General Mathematics III
description:
Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen
Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method,
Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming
(Unconstrained optimization).
The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear
programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear
algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of the most important practical concepts in mathematics.
Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose
requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various fields of
study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries
that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Apply the concepts of matrix algebra, systems of linear equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, and eigenvalues/eigenvectors to solve mathematical problems arising in science and engineering. CLO2. Formulate and solve linear programming problems using graphical and simplex-based methods, analyze duality and post-optimality, and apply optimization techniques to transportation and assignment problems. processes and equipment involved in extraction and filtration; mixing and granulation; size reduction

title: Environmental Studies
description:
Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the
impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity
and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact
assessment.
The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development
(UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the
people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be
ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC
to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India.
The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and
abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary
nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic
factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment,
different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and
economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also
provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of
environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested
students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other
electives/projects in these areas.

title: Introduction to Engineering Design
description:
This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific
advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and

Students will learn to create detailed designs of real-world products and systems by applying design thinking and

The scope and objectives of the course are as follows:

standards; and

title: GAME THEORY & ITS APPLICATIONS
description:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions
among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete
Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of
strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with
and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian
games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to
economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial
organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.
Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for
analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who
proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of
Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel
Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of
knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals
only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real
world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.
learning_outcomes: The course would aim to illustrate economic & other real-world concepts and to make students adept at approaching financial problems from a game-theoretic perspective. CLO1) Understand the Fundamentals of Game Theory, including game construction, analysis, and solutions. CLO2) Able to apply game theory tools to real-world contexts such as economic, political & environmental settings, trade negotiations, environmental agreements, cartels, oligopolistic competition, and in social choice contexts, among others. CLO3) Understand the collective decision-making mechanisms using game-theoretic tools. CLO4) Gain exposure to games with imperfect Information, including understanding the basic concepts of Bayesian games (types, beliefs, and strategies). CLO5) Develop problem-solving and strategic thinking skills.
topics: 1 [Introduction to Game Theory and Basic Concepts]
2 [Games with complete Information: Solution Concepts for Simultaneously Played finite games with Discrete Strategies, Non- cooperative, One- Time, Static Games]

title: Artificial Intelligence for Robotics
description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with
emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of
intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning
and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain
manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision
making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera
sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of
intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of
adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on
analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent
decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles.
Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and
biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive
reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how
intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory
generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation.
topics: Foundations for Terminology in AI and Robotics (M1) | Lectures 1 to 3 – Introduction to AI in Robotics, Evolution of robot intelligence, AI/ML vs Model-based vs adaptive vs learning algorithms, Basic robot terminology and nomenclature.

Adaptive Learning in Dynamical Systems (M2) | Lectures 4 to 12 – Biological inspiration, central pattern generators, Hebbian Learning (dynamic), Learning rhythmic motion, effect of perturbations, applications in walking robots, exoskeletons, and prosthetic systems. Hands-On Experiment/Practical Project: Apply dynamic Hebbian learning algorithm to real-life periodic signals generated from IMUs and/or Encoders.

Adaptive Statistical Learning for Robotics (M3) | Lectures 13 to 20 – Least square Error Wiener-Kolmogorov Filters, Derivation of Wiener Filter Equation, Autocorrelation of Input and Cross-Correlation of I/P and Desired signals, QR Decomposition, Interpretation of Wiener Filters as projections in vector space, Analysis of LMS Error Signal, Applications Hands-On Experiment/Practical Project: Apply statistical based learning on real-time IMU data and/or Case Study on Kalman Filtering with IMU.

Data-Driven Machine Learning approach in Kinematics and Trajectory Planning of Serial-Chain Manipulators (M4) | Lectures 21 to 35 – Forward/Inverse Kinematics and Trajectory Planning in SCM (Conventional way), Data-driven modeling using Neural Networks for inverse kinematics in SCM. Reinforcement Learning approach in Trajectory Planning

title: FUZZY LOGIC & APPLICATIONS
description:
Fuzzy sets, fuzzy binary relations, fuzzy logic, fuzzy reasoning, applications in decision making, control theory,
expert systems, artificial intelligence etc.
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts of fuzzy sets, fuzzy relations,
fuzzy logic, and fuzzy reasoning, along with their applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems,
artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical, computational,
and problem-solving skills through real-world applications. Each student is required to undertake a project involving
the application of fuzzy logic, which may be study-oriented, computer-oriented, simulation-based, or model-based, and
provides an opportunity to explore research articles and recent developments in fuzzy logic and its applications.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts and mathematical foundations of fuzzy sets, fuzzy numbers, fuzzy relations, and fuzzy logic. CLO2. Formulate and analyze problems involving fuzzy relations, fuzzy reasoning, fuzzy inference, and related logical structures. CLO3. Apply fuzzy logic techniques to real-world problems in decision making, control systems, expert systems, artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. CLO4. Develop and evaluate a fuzzy logic-based project using appropriate computational tools, with reference to relevant research literature and contemporary applications.

title: Human Computer Interaction
description:
Introduction to HCI in the AI era; Understanding People: Perception, Motor control,
Cognition, Needs, and Experience; User Research: Interviews, Field research, and Survey research;
Understanding Interaction: Usability Engineering, Information and control, Dialogue, Tool use, Automation,
and Rationality; User Interfaces: Input devices, Displays, Interaction techniques, and Reality-based
interaction; Design: Cognition, Practice, and Processes; Engineering: Systems, Design engineering, Safety
and risk, and Computational representations and models; Evaluation: Analytical methods, Think-aloud
studies, and Experiment.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Understand the concepts and theories of human-AI interaction. Furthermore, they will be able to
explain basic concepts from the relevant theories in cognitive and social sciences. (LO1)
• Illustrate and compare methods of “user-centered engineering (UCE)”, involving future users in
various stages of the design and development process of AI systems. (LO2)
• Apply “user-centered” methods appropriately, as a team; as part of design, development, and
evaluation of AI systems. (LO3)
• Apply ethics procedures for user studies (e.g., privacy, consent) and FATE principles in design of
prototype based AI systems. (LO4)
• Describe the perspectives and values of multiple stakeholders at different stages of the user-centered
engineering process (requirements, design, and evaluation). (LO5)

title: Introduction to Nano Science
description:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address
critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This
course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and
nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this
rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials,
their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent
physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials
in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will
be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to
nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and
future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview
of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis
of nanoparticles and nanostructures.
Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials
and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights
real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological
domains.
This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical
exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into
advanced study or research in the field.

title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment
description:
This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and
environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and
nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform
many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and
operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells,
fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials
for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving
solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course
further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation,
nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment,
and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit
society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and
skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular
emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3
modules as decribed below.
o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology
o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector
o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector.
The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).
learning_outcomes: o Introduce the importance and application of nanomaterials and the origin of their unique properties. o Summarize the fabrication methods, characterization techniques, and operating principles of solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and CNT-based energy storage systems. o Explain the merits and motivation in the renewable energy and environmental sectors. o Define toxic effect of nanomaterials on human and environment, relative remediation and precautions.

title: Flexible Manufacturing Systems
description:
Introduction of CAD/CAM systems, overview of FMS, system hardware and general
functions, material handling system, work holding systems, cutting tools and tool
management, physical planning of system, software structure functions and description,
cleaning and automated inspection, communications and computer networks for
manufacturing, quantification of flexibility, human factors in manufacturing, FMS and CIM
in action (case studies), justification of FMS, modelling for design, planning and operation
of FMS.
In recent years the manufacturing industries are facing problems of survival. They find it
difficult to maintain a long term competitive advantage due to uncertainty in environmental
conditions. The ideal production system for such environment is Flexible Manufacturing
Systems (FMS), which are considered to meet the demand for a variety of products with
improvement of productivity in mid-volume manufacturing. This course will highlight the
fundamentals of FMS and modelling for design, planning and control of FMS.

title: Pattern Recognition
description:
This is a first course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of
digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to
discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation
and description and finally the object recognition. During the course, a flavour of matlab programming
will also be given.
Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject
embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic
vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to verification of signatures, and from
analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of fingerprints and human blood cells. Currently,
pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces-
sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course
introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that
are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.

title: Cryptography
description:
This course is an introduction to the basic theory and practice of cryptographic techniques
used in information security. The course is intended to understand the mathematical concepts used for
designing cryptosystems. The focus would be on the mathematical concepts from Number Theory and
Abstract Algebra. We will delve into topics such as encryption (private-key and public-key), digital
signatures, user authentication, key management, cryptographic hashing, Network security protocols,
public-key infrastructure, digital rights management, and advancement in modern cryptology such as
Identity Based Encryption, Steganography and Watermarking, Post-Quantum Cryptography, and Zero-
Knowledge protocols.
Prerequisites: The course is self-contained, however a basic understanding of probability theory,
complexity theory, and modular arithmetic from number theory would be helpful. The course is
intended for advanced undergraduates and master students.
Lectures deal with mathematical cryptography and related mathematical concepts
required for modern cryptography and information security. The objective is to discuss and learn about
basic tools and applications used in modern cryptography and to learn about some cryptographic
protocols. On successful completion of the course students should be able to: understand basic principles
and results of the theory of secure communication; know principles and problems of basic cryptosystems
for encryption (both private and public key), digital signing and authentication; know methods to create
core cryptographic protocols primitives; analyze and practically use simple cryptosystems; be
understand basic principles of post-quantum cryptography and steganography.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. Understand the fundamental principles and security requirements of modern cryptography. CLO2. Utilize mathematical structures and ideas from Number Theory and Abstract Algebra to design and attack Cryptographic Protocols. CLO3. Construct and Analyse various symmetric-key and public-key Cryptosystems. CLO4. Reason and measure security of various Cryptosystems using computational and probabilistic techniques. CLO5. Design and Analyse common cryptanalytic attacks and tools. CLO6. Design secure communication mechanisms for the real-world using appropriate cryptographic primitives. CLO7. Implement and Evaluate cryptographic algorithms with respect to security and computational efficiency. CLO8. Understand modern developments in the area of Cryptography including zero-knowledge proofs and post-quantum cryptography.
topics: Objectives of Cryptography, Art of Cryptography, Security Overview (Goals, Attacks and Mechanisms), Classical Encryption Techniques - Historical Notes.

Basic Definitions (Encryption, Decryption, Keys, Cipher-Text, Plain- Text), Trade-off between Security and Speed (Standard Examples - Enigma Vs Lattice-based Cryptography), Motivation for Steganography and Watermarking.

Public Vs Private Key Cryptography, Motivating Examples - Shift Cipher, Substitution Cipher, Affine Cipher, Block Cipher, Stream Cipher, RSA (Only Key Exchange), How financial institutions ensure safety of our credit/debit cards?
Zero Knowledge Proofs (Introductory Concept). Poker and Secret Coin- Flipping Game.

Role of Mathematics in Cryptography, Connections between Probabilistic Algorithms and the art of secret sharing. Motivation for Complexity Theory - How do we know that a Cryptographic Protocol is safe? How we efficiently communicate through noise channels without loss of information? - Motivation towards Error Correcting Codes.

Machine Learning is an exciting sub-area of Artificial Intelligence which deals with designing machines which can learn and improve
their performance from examples/experience. This course introduces the student to the key algorithms and theory that forms the core of
machine learning. The course will cover all major approaches to learning namely, supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and

and our ability to produce and capture huge volumes of data. The topics covered in the course include regression, decision trees,
support vector machines, artificial neural networks, Bayesian techniques, Hidden Markov models etc. Some advanced topics like
active, deep, & topological learning will also be covered.

title: New Venture Creation
description:
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are
expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business
model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture.
In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases
of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3)
go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on
customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive
analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest-
lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running
Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide
them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be
invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the
completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.
NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence,
the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC
helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform
an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a
reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific
market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build
an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win
customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key
external partners?

title: Introduction to Large Language Models
description:
Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs); prompt engineering techniques (e.g., zero-shot, few-shot,
chain-of-thought), autonomous prompt optimization; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector
databases, multi-modal RAG methods; tool and function calling; multi-agent workflows (memory, planning,
action, reflection); safety, guardrails, reliability; LLM-based evaluation, human evaluation; life cycle of LLM
training, LLM architecture, fine-tuning LLMs using supervised learning or reinforcement learning; inference
optimization; Mechanistic Interpretability; real-world case-studies
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs.
b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge
bases.
c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models.
d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs.
e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks.
f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments.
g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning.
h. Evaluate the performance and accuracy of LLM-powered applications using appropriate metrics.
i. Understand the principles of inference for deploying LLM models efficiently at scale.
topics: Prerequisites [Basics of Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing]
Introduction to LLMs
Prompt Engineering
textbooks: The field of LLM Engineering is rapidly evolving and still in its early stages. Hence, in addition to using textbooks, we will also be directly covering the contents of this course from research papers published in top-tier CORE A* conferences and journals such as ICLR, NeurIPS, NAACL and ACL. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback by Nathan Lambert, Online.
Raschka, Sebastian. Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch). Manning, 2024. ISBN: 978-1633437166.

title: Creating and Leading Entrepreneurial Organization
description:
Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship; Elements of Leadership; Identifying
Business Opportunities; Market Study and Research; Business Plans; Finance, Issues in Raising
Finance, Venture Capitalist Evaluation of Business Plans, Technical Aspects for the Project;
Corporate Strategies for Growth; Legal Aspects to entrepreneurship; People Skills; Marketing and
Branding; Creativity and Communication.
This Course is about creating, managing, and leading an organization. This
course helps in creating an entrepreneurial mindset, developing entrepreneurial skills and
equipping students with the basic knowledge necessary for an entrepreneur.
learning_outcomes: The course shall enable the participants to acquire and equip themselves with requisite knowledge and skills to start and run a business successfully, which is divided into personal skills (entrepreneurial skills) and those to start a company (Start-up tools). The learning outcomes are
To understand about entrepreneurship and getting inspiration from successful entrepreneurs.
To learn about idea generation, opportunity assessment and evaluation and the process to create, build, and lead an entrepreneurial organization.
To learn about nitty gritty of preparation of Business Plan.
To know about different sources of funding and identify an appropriate source of funding for the venture.
To learn about launching a business venture and growing it to next level of growth. 1
topics: Understanding and appreciating the importance of Entrepreneurship: The roller coaster ride of entrepreneurship, Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship, Entrepreneurship vs Intrapreneurship, Risks, Challenges, Uncertainty

Entrepreneurial Leadership: Leader vs Manager, Principled Centered Leadership, Entrepreneurial Leadership, Case studies on some of the most successful business Leaders. To diagnose self in relation to business leaders and prepare Oneself with requisite skills, especially to identify and prepare a plan of action to overcome some of the critical weaknesses.
Assessing Business Potential of an Idea: Creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship, Sources of new ideas, Techniques for generating new ideas, Opportunity recognition and Assessment.
Managing Legal Aspects of a business: Forms of business entities and related Implications, winding up of accompany, Need for a lawyer. Intellectual Property Rights and Implications for Entrepreneur.

Developing the Business idea into a Business Plan: Business plan – what, when and for whom?, Business plan drivers, Pitching BP, Why plan fails? Various facets of BP - market, management team, financial requirements, risks involved, and exit strategy. Marketing Plan- Need and importance of marketing research, tools and techniques for undertaking market research. Operation and Production Plan – Product design & analysis, New product development, Product specifications and customer needs, Production, planning and control.

Incorporating Revenue model into Business: Basic financial modeling, Basic elements of finance, Understanding cash flow projection and budgeting, Balance sheets and income tax, Break-even analysis, ratio analysis.

Art of raising finance: Raising Finance, Assessing financial requirements, Issues in raising finance, Understanding the financers. Sources of finance - seed funding, angel funding, venture capitalist funding, raising money from banks, lease financing and financial institutions etc. Start up to Going Public: What is an IPO? When to go for IPO? Steps involved in issuing an IPO, Marketing strategies for IPO.

Art and science of Managing People: Venture team development, Building winning team, People management – key to success, organizational structure and systems, Designing an effective organizational structure.

Developing Business Strategy - Launching and Growth of Business: New Venture launch and Managing Early Growth, Steps involved in launching a business, Raising different resources, motivating and inspiring a team, Understanding technology trends, managing cash, Record keeping and due diligence, Implementation plan. Managing Growth - Venture development stages, Why entrepreneurs do not scale up?
Revival, Exit and End of a venture: Managing Change, Key strategies to turn around, liquidation, exit strategy for entrepreneur.
Final Pitch Presentations
Weightage

Entrepreneurship; Robert D Hisrich, Michael P Peters, and Dean A Shepherd, Tata McGraw Hill Publishing Company, New Delhi, 6th ed., 2006. III. title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
learning_outcomes: Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions.
Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines.
Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.
topics: Fundamental Approach to Environmental Impact Assessment
EIA Notifications (legal Aspects)
EIA Methodologies
Prediction and Assessments of impacts on soil and ground water environment
Prediction and Assessments of impacts on surface water, biological environment, air environment, noise environment
Prediction and Assessments of impacts of socio – economic and human health aspects
Environment Management Plan (EMP), Disaster Management Plan (DMP)
Environmental Auditing and Post Project Monitoring Case History
ISO, Environmental Clearance, LCA
Weightage
textbooks: Y. Anjaneyulu, V. Manickam, Environmental Impact Assessment Methodologies, BS Publications, Third Reprint, 2013.
Larry W. Canter, Environmental Impact Assessment, McGraw-Hill, Second Edition, 1996.
[Method of conduct of the course] PowerPoint presentation and black board when necessary
references: Kiely G., Environmental Engineering, Tata McGraw-Hill Indian Editions, 2007.
M. Anji Reddy, Environmental Impact Assessment: Theory and Practice, BS Publications, 2025.

title: Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation
description:
This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles
of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision,
calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments
across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using
modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and
experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems,
documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration
to ethical practices in experimentation.
The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of
measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement
concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable
data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to:
(i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali-
bration, and uncertainty.
(ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif-
ferent domains.
(iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational
tools.
(iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation,
experimental design, and validation.
(v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering
principles.
(vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen-
tation and technical reporting.
1
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: CO1: Understand and apply fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, calibration, and uncertainty. CO2: Use appropriate measuring instruments/sensors to solve a problem and acquire experimental data across different disciplines. CO3: Analyze experimental data using graphical and statistical methods, including error estimation and uncertainty propagation. CO4: Formulating hypotheses and their validation through design and conducting experiments. CO5: Interpret experimental observations using fundamental scientific and engineering principles. CO6: Document and communicate experimental findings effectively through structured reports and presentations.
topics: Overview of the Course

Accuracy, precision, resolution, calibration, and uncertainty, use of appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across different domains, data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools.
Conduct the experiments pertaining to the given departments, interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering principles, and validation. (8 Experiments)
textbooks: There is no textbook for this course. Lab manuals will be distributed to the students.

Bevington and D. K. Robinson, McGraw-Hill, 2003, 3rd Ed. (iii) An Introduction to Error Analysis, John R Taylor, 2nd Ed, University Science Books, 1997. (iv) The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, Edward R. Tufte, Graphics Pr., 2001.

title: SURVEYING
description:
The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for
Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been
included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a
road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes,
which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these
areas have also been included.
The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane
table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced
surveying techniques.
learning_outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to
Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses.
Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination.
Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction.
Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. 1
Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations.
Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods.
Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks.
Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications.
Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data.
Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software.

title: Civil Engineering Materials
description:
Different types of cements, chemical composition, properties and tests, coarse and fine aggregate for concrete,
tests on aggregates, grading of aggregates and its effect on concrete properties, chemical and mineral
admixtures, properties and tests on fresh and hardened concrete; transportation and placing of concrete, non-
destructive testing of concrete, durability of concrete, quality control and acceptance criteria of concrete,
Factors in the choice of mix proportions, Proportioning of concrete mixes by various methods – BIS method
of mix design; Introduction to special concretes. Manufacturing/sources, classification, applications,
properties and testing of bricks, blocks, tiles, aggregates, lime, timber, paints, glass, bitumen, cutback,
emulsion, modified bitumen, steel, non-ferrous metals, polymeric materials, geo-synthetics, etc. Low cost and
waste material in construction. Latest, BIS, IRC & ASTM specifications and guidelines of all above-
mentioned material, and construction equipment.
The course deals with properties, characterization, testing, selection and quality control of construction
material. For economical, durable and high performance of structure, it is imperative to have knowledge on
construction materials and their wider applications. This course provides a basic and enhanced overview of
