title: Fluid Mechanics
description:
Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics,
especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing
laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following
topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics,
buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential
analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis
of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and
similitude.
The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide
a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further
advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.
• Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications
• Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques
• Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces
• Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies
• Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow,
control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions
• Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier
Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems
• Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches
• Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction
• Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for
flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in
series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles
• Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude
learning_outcomes: On completion of this course, the students will be able to,
Demonstrate the difference between solid and fluid, its properties and properties in static and dynamic conditions
Estimate pressure exerted by fluids and experiment with pressure measurement devices 1
Apply conservation laws applicable to fluids and its applications through fluid kinematics and dynamics
Perceive and formulate relationship among the parameters involved in the given fluid phenomenon and apply concepts of similitude in analyzing models and prototypes
Estimate the losses in pipelines for both laminar and turbulent conditions and analysis of pipes connected in series and parallel.

title: Hydraulic Engineering
description:
This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing
on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of
closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in
pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non-
uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to
fluid machinery.
learning_outcomes: Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following: 1 CLO1. Explain the behaviour of real fluids, including boundary layer development and turbulent flow through conduits, and apply these concepts to practical hydraulic engineering problems. CLO2. Analyze closed-conduit hydraulic systems by evaluating head losses, pipe flow characteristics, pumps, valves, fittings, and the effects of water hammer in pressurized pipelines. CLO3. Analyze and solve pipe network problems using the Hardy Cross Method for the design and operation of water distribution systems. CLO4. Analyze uniform and non-uniform flow in open channels using fundamental hydraulic principles and empirical equations for engineering design and performance assessment. CLO5. Evaluate fluid forces on immersed bodies, including drag, lift, and the impact of jets on stationary and moving surfaces, for engineering applications. CLO6. Explain the classification, operating principles, and applications of fluid machinery, particularly hydraulic turbines and pumps, and relate them to hydraulic engineering systems.
topics: L1: Introduction to Hydraulic Engineering; Behaviour of real fluids. L2: Laminar and turbulent flow; Reynolds number. L3: Pipe flow equations and friction losses. Major and minor losses in pipes.
L4: Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) and Total Energy Line (TEL). L5: Velocity profiles in turbulent flow. L6: Turbulent flow through conduits and engineering applications.
L7: Boundary layer theory, formation and thickness.

title: Foundation Engineering
description:
General requirement for satisfactory performance of shallow foundations, general, local and punching
shear failures, bearing capacity, settlement, tilt and rotation of foundations, proportioning of Shallow Foundations, footings on
layered soils and slopes, Deep foundations, capacity of single and group Piles, laterally loaded pile, Earth Pressure theories,

earthquake engineering and liquefaction of soils, computer applications in foundation design
The main goal of this course is to provide an in-depth understanding regarding
different types of foundations. Analysis of foundations and retaining structures (Shallow foundations, pile foundations, machine
foundations, retaining walls, slope stability etc.) considering all geotechnical aspects. Emphasis will be given on complete coverage
of code of practices for various types of foundations and retaining structures. Geotechnical earthquake engineering, ground

title: DESIGN OF REINFORCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description:
Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy,
Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams;
Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams
and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability;
Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending;
Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases.
In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of
Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The
course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently,
the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced
rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond,
and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to
axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different
types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this
course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.
topics: Introduction
Concepts and Principles of Limit state Design
Analysis of beams and one-way slab for Flexure
Design of beams and one-way slab for Flexure
Design of Flexural members for Shear
Design of Flexural Members for Bond
Design of Flexural members for Limit State of Serviceability
Design of two-way Slabs
Design of Staircases
Design of Compression Members

title: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering
description:
In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to
various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results,
including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone
penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface
waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test.
Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will
be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil
property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and
liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing
engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering.
Introduction to in-situ testing, drilling, and sampling, advantages and disadvantages
of in-situ testing, and scope of using the test results for direct and indirect design of geotechnical structures.
• Learn about SPT, test procedure, SPT corrections, and frequently used correlations to estimate
different geomaterial properties.
• Become familiar with some of the frequently used methods for the design of foundations using SPT
data.
• Learn about CPT, test procedure, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial
properties.
• Design of foundations based on CPT results.
• Assess liquefaction potential for a site based on SPT and CPT results.
• Estimate seismic wave velocities and interpret subsurface profiles based on seismic reflection and
refraction tests, and SASW test.
• Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs
based on exploration findings will be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Remember different in-situ testing methods related to geotechnical engineering. 1
Understanding of different widely used in-situ testing procedures and principles pertaining to geotechnical engineering.
Knowledge of appropriate correlation equations available to interpret different geomaterial properties using in-situ test results.
Apply different direct design methods for designing foundations.
Analyze and compare different in-situ test results for tests conducted at the same site and decide suitability of different test methods.

Evaluate the suitability of different test methods based on site details and purpose of testing, select suitable method for foundation design using in-situ test results and assess potential for liquefaction.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Civil Engineering
description:
Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and soft computing; Neural networks: Introduction, models, and its application in civil
engineering, fuzzy logic and its application in decision making, Clustering; Genetic algorithms; Expert systems; Introduction to machine learning
(Support Vector Machine), case studies.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) may be considered a field of computer science that attempts to build technology to inculcate human
cognition in computer systems, but applications are not limited to. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities. This course is structured to give
an overview of the area, as well as some important soft computing techniques which are essential to solve the complex problems in terms of the
fundamentals. The attributes of human intelligence such as reasoning, planning, learning etc. will be attempted to be understood to incorporate in
problemsolving.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, the students should have a. Out of various techniques, emphasis will be on Genetic algorithm, Artificial Neural Network, and Fuzzy Systems
General knowledge of the field of AI
They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve civil engineering problems.
The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter.
Students will take up a group project/ term paper to study in detail the theoretical details of an intelligent system and implement that during the semester.
topics: Overview of AI
Artificial Neural Network
Fuzzy System
Genetic Algorithm
KBS
Hybrid System

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.

Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines.
Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.

title: Fundamentals of Systems Engineering
description:
Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on
the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems
across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation,
maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical,
organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic,
systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of
systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them
to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.
The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems
engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure
planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems
architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks
relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern
tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support
informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop
technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world
infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and
evidence-based planning.
learning_outcomes: Understand systems engineering principles and their application to infrastructure life-cycle management.
Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex infrastructure systems.
Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure planning and operations.
Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment analysis methods.
Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into infrastructure systems design and management.
topics: 1. Introduction to basics of System Engineering and related approaches
2. Solving System Engineering problems using Linear Programming, Queuing theory, and
Inventory control techniques
4. Network scheduling, resource planning and financial management
5. Application of AI, IoT, Robotics in Civil Engineering systems
Weightage
textbooks: Blanchard, B. S., & Fabrycky, W. J. (2010). Systems Engineering and Analysis (5th Edition). Pearson.
Systems Engineering Fundamentals, Defense Acquisition University Press, 2001 (available on line as pdf, Link: www.dau.mil/pubs/pdf/SEFGuide 01-01.pdf)

[Method of conduct of the course]: The course will be conducted through lectures, case discussions, simulation exercises, and group projects. Students will engage with real-world infrastructure problems using analytical tools and modern technologies like AI and IoT. Emphasis will be placed on both conceptual understanding and practical application, with evaluation based on assignments, project work, and exams.

title: Transportation Systems Planning and Management
description:
System and environment; sequential transportation systems planning:
trip generation, trip distribution, modal split and traffic assignment, Transportation surveys,
Land-use models, Travel demand forecasting, Urban structure and its influence of travel
intensity, Urban goods movement. Transportation Systems Management (TSM) actions: traffic
management techniques for improving vehicular flow, preferential treatment for high
occupancy modes, demand management technique for reduced traffic demand, staggered hours,
vehicle restrictions; planning for pedestrians.
The course aims at imparting knowledge on
understanding of urban transportation problems in planners’ perspective, definition of the
problem, setting clear goals and objectives to serve as guiding factors in the planning process,
identification of the causal factors influencing the demand for urban travel and development of
relationship between the factors and the travel demand.
topics: 5 lectures on transportation planning process and basic concepts of travel demand.
9 lectures on travel surveys and data collection, and travel demand estimation; this will include trip generation and trip distribution
6 lectures on modal share estimation using Utility Theory and Multinomial logit model
8 lectures on traffic assignment techniques using various shortest path algorithms
4 lectures on regional as well as long-term transportation planning
4 lectures on transportation systems management

title: Water Resources Planning and Management
description:
The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive
understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning
and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water
systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed
management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application
of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective
programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic
considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools
such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory
experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems.
The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible
water resource development and policy-making.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to
Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems.
Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project evaluation.
Analyze point and non-point source pollution using water quality modeling techniques.
Assess groundwater resources and apply methods for sustainable groundwater management.
Perform statistical and uncertainty analyses related to streamflow and water availability.
Formulate and solve water resource problems using linear, non-linear, and multi-objective optimization techniques.
Plan and manage reservoir operations under both deterministic and stochastic environments.
Utilize modern tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence in water resource management.
Evaluate real-world case studies and apply integrated approaches to address complex water management challenges.

title: CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT
description:
The course deals with planning techniques, engineering economy, valuation including
estimation & costing, system design, construction methodologies ranging from small buildings to large
infrastructure projects, construction technologies including recent advancements. Relevant Indian Standard
codes of practices will be given emphasis.
2 (a): Scope of the Course:
The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of construction planning and management right from
the knowledge of various activities till the estimation, costing, valuation, tendering etc., Though this course
covers wider infrastructure projects, the primary focus will be on building and road infrastructure.
2(b): Objectives of the course:
➢ To understand the different construction projects and basic objective of project management [Module
- I]
➢ To understand the project management techniques (CPM and PERT) [Module - II]
➢ To analyze the various requirements of manpower and other resources [ Module-III]
➢ To analyze the various control methodologies keeping in line with project requirements [Module-IV]
➢ To get exposed to construction contracts and tenders [Module-V]
➢ To estimate the quantity and rate of different building components (including materials) [Module VI]
➢ To discuss the various aspects of valuation of properties [Module VII]
➢ To highlights various aspects of construction quality and safety with case studies [Module VIII]
➢ To understand the best practices of construction management [Module IX]
topics: • Construction Industry • Project categories • Project classification • Project Life cycle • Project participants • Project Management and Functional Management
• Real time project networking of big infrastructure projects. • Construction of a network
• Planning construction manpower • Planning construction materials • Project construction equipment including selection of equipment

K.K. Chitkara Construction Project Management, Tata McGraw Hill publications.

Albert Lester, Project Management, Planning and Control, 7th edition, BH (Elsevier) publications

title: Pavement Material Characterization
description:
[as per the Bulletin]
This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil,
aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil
characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification,
compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production,
mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed.
Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application,
chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of
bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties,
mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would
be covered along with design example.
The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical
in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for
effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the
guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used
in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide
research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different
lectures.
learning_outcomes: . To characterize pavement materials
. To perform bituminous mix design
. To perform mix design of concrete

Aggregates – Geological sources & rock types, production and storage, sampling,

title: AIRPORT PLANNING & DESIGN
description:
The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis
on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other
connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and
pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc.,
The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of airport
planning and design. This course is expected to provide a broad overview on various topics as mentioned
below.
➢ To understand briefly air transport and aviation industry [Module I]
➢ To understand the need to forecast air transport demand [Module II]
➢ To get the overall idea about aircraft and its influence on entire planning [Module III]
➢ To get a comprehensive overview about airport system and master planning [Module IV]
➢ To get an overview about the factors affecting the airport capacity [Module V]
➢ To comprehensively analyze the airside configuration and geometric design [Module VI]
➢ To understand the structural pavement design and airport drainage [Module VII]
➢ To get a quick overview about different visual aids in airport and in airspace [Module VIII]
➢ To acknowledge the importance of maintenance and rehabilitation of pavement [Module IX]
➢ To know the parameters influencing the airport performance including benchmarking [Module X]
learning_outcomes: o Complete comprehensive understanding of airport planning process o Structural pavements, maintenance and failures o Detailed insights into various guidelines and standards
topics: • Need for air transport • Advantages and disadvantages of air transport • Types of air transport • Governmental and Non-governmental organizations related to aviation industry • Functions of AAI • Revenues and expenditures at Airports
• Factors related to air transport demand • Conventional airport forecast methods • Demand forecast framework and models • Overview of components of airside and landside infrastructure
• Characteristics of aircraft • Influence of aircraft on airports and runway length • Other airport layout factors • Airport capacity factors
• Aviation system planning • Airport system planning • Hierarchy of planning • Airport Layout Design • Airport Site Selection
• Level of service • Airside capacity and runway capacity • Taxiway capacity • Gate capacity • Capacity-Delay analysis • Passenger Terminal – Functions, Terminal Design

title: Pavement Failure Evaluation and Rehabilitation
description:
This course covers topics related to pavement failure, evaluation and rehabilitation such as pavement
deterioration, distress and different types of failures, methods of measurement and treatment, use of modern
equipment for pavement surface condition measurements, analysis of data, interpretation, Structural
deterioration of pavements: causes, effects, methods of treatment, structural evaluation of flexible pavements
by rebound deflection method, analysis of data, design of overlay, use of FWD and other methods for
evaluation of flexible and rigid pavements and their application, pavement testing under controlled conditions,
test track studies, Instrumentation for pavement testing.
The course includes the determination of causes of failure in flexible and concrete pavement. The different
techniques for evaluation and rehabilitation of different types of distresses will be taught to the students. The
use of modern equipment’s for structural evaluation of pavement, and design of overlay with the help of data
collected by using the equipment will be covered in this course. The accelerated test facilities constructed
worldwide and instrumentation used in these test facilities for pavement evaluation will be taught to the
students.

title: Rural Road Technology
description:
Network planning, accessibility and mobility; road alignment and survey; geometric design: cross
sectional elements, sight distance, horizontal and vertical alignments; road materials and use of
marginal materials; pavement design, drainage, culverts and small bridges; construction and
specifications; quality control in construction; pavement failures; maintenance; preparation of
detailed project report (DPR); community participation in planning, design, construction and
management.
Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide
connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the
various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of
technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various
aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the
recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states.
Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various
technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.
learning_outcomes: . To perform the geometric design of rural roads
. To design the flexible and rigid pavement
. To prepare the detailed project report
topics: Planning of Rural Roads – Introduction to rural road technology; classification of roads; road development plans; Low connectivity
Planning of Rural Roads – network planning Models, accessibility and mobility; PMGSY history, salient features, NRRDA; Introduction to Detailed Project Report (DPR)
Geometric Design of Rural Roads – Road alignment and survey; geometric design : cross section elements, Sight distances
Geometric Design of Rural Roads – Horizontal alignment, Vertical alignment, safety aspects, Incorporation of geometric design in DPR preparation
textbooks: IRC:SP 20 Rural Roads Manual.
references: Quality Assurance Handbook for Rural Roads - published by NRRDA, Volume I & II
IRC:SP 72 -2015, Guidelines for the design of flexible pavements for low volume roads
IRC: SP 62 – 2014, Guidelines for design and construction of cement concrete pavements for Low volume roads

Guide on Managing Maintenance of Rural Roads in India, NRRDA publication
Specifications for rural roads, First Revision, Ministry of Rural Development, 2014
Other relevant IRC, BIS codes and peer reviewed journal articles

title: DYNAMICS OF STRUCTURES
description:
Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures;
origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s
principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot,
mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion;
Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free
vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution
of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced
vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces
(time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited
vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response
of SDOF system; time domain analysis; direct integration techniques; finite
difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average
and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution
for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems;
frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes;
Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer
method; Stodola’s method; Rayleigh’s method; Rayleigh-Ritz method; Inverse
iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient iteration method;
Matrix iteration method; Generation of damping matrix for MDOF; dynamic
properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and
Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal
combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method.
Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on
various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures
subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on
this scope, the following objectives have been listed:
 To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/
industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall
chimneys etc.
 To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure
which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced
vibration force etc.
learning_outcomes: Development of software for the analysis of framed/skeleton structures.
Capability development for the use of structural dynamics concept and its applications for framed structural analysis and design under dynamic loading.
Determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure, which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.
topics: Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures
Elements of a structural system
Free vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system
Forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system
Forced vibration under various dynamic loadings
Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response of SDOF system
Two-degree-of-freedom systems
Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems
Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes
Generation of damping matrix for MDOF
Weightage
textbooks: Anil K. Chopra, “Dynamics of Structures: Theory and applications to earthquake engineering”, Prentice Hall India Ltd., 2007.
Mukhopadhyay,M., “Structural Dynamics: Vibrations & Systems” Ane Books Pvt. Ltd., 2006.
[Method of conduct of the course] The course will be conducted primarily through Chalkboard with ppt as well online medias such as Google class and/or Nalanda.
references: R.W. Clough and J. Penzien, “Dynamics of Structures”, McGraw Hill International edition, 1993.
Paz,M., “Structural Dynamics: Theory & Computation” CBS Publishers & Distributors, 2001.

title: Transportation Planning
description:
Basic concepts in transportation planning, accessibility and mobility, land use
interaction, government role in transportation planning, characteristics of travel and transport problems;
transportation survey and data collection: planning, design and implementation, travel analysis zone (TAZ)
development, traditional four-step modelling process; analysis of travel behaviour and demand: studying
travel behaviour, analysing urban travel markets; innovations in transportation modelling: travel behaviour
model, activity-based models, econometric modelling using r-studio, modelling travel demand with cube,
transportation demand management (TDM), transportation system management (TSM), smart city
transportation planning: transit-oriented development (TOD),pedestrian-oriented development, liveable street
planning, multimodal transportation planning, shared mobility concepts, integrated transportation
management and planning, transportation and energy, climate change, fuel choice and green mobility.
The course aims at imparting knowledge on understanding of urban
transportation problems from planners’ perspective, definition of the problem, setting clear goals and
objectives to serve as guiding factors in the planning process, identification of the causal factors influencing
the demand for urban travel and development of relationship between the factors and the travel demand.
learning_outcomes: The candidates will understand the process of planning transportation infrastructures,
. The candidates will learn to model and analyze demand of transportation infrastructures.
topics: 5 lectures on transportation planning process and basic concepts of travel demand.
9 lectures on travel surveys and data collection, and travel demand estimation; this will include trip generation and trip distribution
6 lectures on modal share estimation using Utility Theory and Multinomial logit model
8 lectures on traffic assignment techniques using various shortest path algorithms
4 lectures on regional as well as long-term transportation planning
4 lectures on transportation systems management
textbooks: Sarkar, P.K., Maitri, V., and Joshi, G.J. Transportation Planning, Principles, Practices and Policies, PHI Pvt. Ltd., latest edition.
Chakroborty, P. and Das, A. Principles of Transportation Engineering, PHI Pvt. Ltd., latest edition.
[Method of conduct of the course]: By using both slides (using Power Point) and, chalk and board. 1
references: Papacosta, C.S., and Prevedouros Transportation Engineering and Planning, PHI Pvt. Ltd., latest edition.
Kadiyali, L. R. Traffic Engineering and Transport Planning, Khanna Publishers, latest edition.

title: Highway Design
description:
Highway functional classification; route layout and selection, design controls and criteria: turning paths, driver
performance, traffic characteristics; highway capacity; access control; safety; environment; Elements of
design: sight distance, horizontal alignment, transition curves, super elevation and side friction; vertical
alignment: - grades, crest and sag curves; highway cross-sectional elements and their design; at-grade Inter-
sections - sight distance consideration and principles of design, canalization, mini roundabouts, layout of
roundabouts, inter-changes: major and minor interchanges, entrance and exit ramps, acceleration and
deceleration lanes, bicycle and pedestrian facility design; parking layout and design; terminal layout and
design.
The highway vehicle and individual users are integral parts of transportation safety and efficiency. The
objective of the course is to expose the students to the various components of the geometric design of
highways.
topics: Highway functional classification, functional system characteristics
Design vehicles, minimum turning path, driver performance
Volume, directional distribution, traffic composition, speed, highway capacity, levels of service
Walking speed, walkway capacity and bicycle facilities
Stopping Sight distance, decision sight distance, passing sight distance
Superelevation and its design consideration, transition curve, methods of attaining super- elevation, off-tracking and widening of roads
Critical length of grades, climbing lanes, de- sign controls of vertical curves: crest and sag, climbing and emergency escape lane

title: ADVANCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description:
The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design
of various elements and exposure to different code provisions.
Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and
anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip
method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall
buildings, detailing in concrete structures
The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise
and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind &
earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as
construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins,
nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to
technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete.
Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction
still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally
unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important
reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but
different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and
economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of
structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures
such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under
earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding.

➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II]

➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI]
➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII]
➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII]

title: PRESTRESSED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
description:
Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in
prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders.
The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due
to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete
is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a
structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service
period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications.
The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural
elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of
practicing structural design engineers.
The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and
structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in
solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members.
This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction
industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed
concrete structures.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental concepts of prestressing and the different systems used in prestressed concrete construction. They will gain the ability to –
Understand the basic principles of prestressing and identify various prestressing systems including pre-tensioning and post-tensioning methods. 1
Analyze the behaviour of prestressed concrete members under axial loads and bending, including the use of pressure/thrust lines and load balancing concepts.
Calculate different types of prestress losses and understand their causes and effects on structural performance.
Evaluate the flexural and shear strength of prestressed concrete members and design appropriate reinforcements.
Analyze the transfer of prestress in pre-tensioned members and anchorage zone stresses in post- tensioned members.
Design prestressed concrete sections for flexure using limit state concepts and apply methods such as Magnel’s approach.
Compute short- and long-term deflections in prestressed concrete members and assess crack width control under service loads.
Analyze statically indeterminate prestressed concrete structures, including secondary moments and concordant cable profiles.
Understand and design composite structures involving prestressed and in-situ cast concrete under different support conditions.
Apply engineering knowledge and analytical skills to solve real-world structural design problems involving prestressed concrete.
topics: Introduction and Prestressing systems; Materials used – High Strength Concrete, High strength steel etc.; Prestressing systems –
pre-tensioning systems, post tensioning systems
Basic assumptions and analysis of prestress; Pressure line or thrust line and internal resisting couple; Concept of load balancing; Stresses in tendons; Numerical examples.
Nature of loses of prestress; Reasons for losses of prestress; Numerical examples.

Types of failure in flexure; Methods of determining flexural strength for prestressed concrete sections; Numerical examples; Shear resistance of prestressed concrete members; Design of shear reinforcements; Numerical examples.

Transfer of prestress in pre- tensioned members – estimation of the transfer bond stresses, estimation of transverse tensile stresses; Numerical examples; Anchorage zone stresses in post- tensioned members – investigation on anchorage zone stresses; Numerical examples.
Design for flexure; Numerical examples; Limitations of Prestress in long span; Limiting zone for the prestressing force; Magnel’s method; Numerical examples.
Factors influencing deflections; Deflection of prestressed
concrete members – uncracked and cracked; Numerical examples; Philosophy of limit state design; Crack widths in prestressed members

Statically indeterminate (continuous) prestresses concrete structures; Secondary moments; Equivalent load method; Concordant cable profile and concordant beam; Ultimate strength behavior; Numerical examples.

Types of composite constructions commonly used; Propped and unpropped constructions; Differential shrinkage; Deflection of composite members; Flexural strength of composite sections; Numerical examples.
references: N. Rajagopalan, “Prestressed Concrete”, Alpha Science International Ltd., 2nd edition, 2005.
Singh S. B., “Analysis and Design of Prestressed Concrete Structures”, Wiley India Pvt Ltd.
IS 1343:2012, Indian Standard Code of Practice for Prestressed Concrete, BIS, 2012.
Lin T.Y., Design of Prestressed Concrete Structures”, Third Edition. John Wiley & Sons. New York, USA
Collins M. P. and Mitchel D., “Prestressed Concrete Structures”, Prentice Hall New Delhi.
Naaman A. E., “Prestressed Concrete Analysis & Design Fundamentals”, Mc-Graw-Hill.

title: BRIDGE ENGINEERING
description:
Purpose of bridge; Classification of bridges; Characteristics of different types of bridges; Loads stresses
and their combinations; Design of RCC Slab culverts, Box-culverts, T-beam bridges; composite bridges;
continuous bridges; design of bearings; design of piers and abutments and their foundations.
Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways
and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges.
This course will mainly focus on the design of three types of bridge superstructures namely Slab
culverts/bridges, T-beam bridges, and Composite bridges. The design of the bridge substructure will include
the design of elastomeric bearings and the design of abutments and piers. Moreover, the course will include
the design aspects of continuous bridges. At the end of this course, the students would be equipped with the
complete analysis and design of slab, T-beam and composite bridges, along with the design of substructures
for them.
topics: Purpose of bridges, components of bridges, selection of optimum span of bridge
Dead loads on bridge superstructure, types of IRC vehicular Live loads, impact factors

Dispersions of IRC Class 70R tracked vehicular loads on slabs, Maximum bending moment and shear due to IRC Class 70R tracked vehicle considering dispersion of loads, critical position of IRC Class 70R wheeled and Class-A loading for moment and shear treating the loads as concentrated loads, determination of design moment and design shear force under different IRC Class-70R and Class- A loading, design of slab culvert/bridge using the limit state method.
Loads considered in design of box-culverts, Design of Box- culverts for highways

Components of T-beam bridges, Design of slabs spanning in two directions for flexure (Pigeaud’s Method) and shear, Design of cantilever slab panels, Live-Load distribution in longitudinal girders using Courbon’s method, Guyon & Massonet method, Hendry-Jaegar method, Design of Transverse Girders
General aspects and components of composite bridges, design of laterally restrained steel girders, types and design of shear connectors, analysis and design of composite bridges for highways
Necessity of bearings, Loads acting on bearings, Types of bearings, Design of Elastomeric Bearings, Necessity and types of expansion joints
Loads and Forces considered for designing Abutment and Pier, Determination of Design Moment and forces in abutment and pier, Limit state Design of Abutment and Pier
Necessity of continuous bridges, analysis and design aspects of continuous bridges
textbooks: Krishna Raju, N. (2018), Design of Bridges, 5th Edition, Oxford & IBH Publishing Co. Pvt. Ltd., New Delhi.
Standard Specifications and code of Practice for Bridges
references: Johnson Victor, D. (2010), Essentials of Bridge Engineering, 6th Edition, Oxford & IBH Publishing Co. Pvt. Ltd., New Delhi.
Ponnuswamy, S., ‘Bridge Engineering’, 2nd Ed., 2009, McGraw-Hill, New Delhi.

title: Advance Structural Analysis
description:
[as per the Bulletin]
Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three
dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive
software development for analysis of structures.
Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools
for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning
advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using
computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the
fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation
in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures.
By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural
analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility
method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized
learning_outcomes: Development of softwares for analysis of framed/skeleton structures.
Capability development for the use Matrix based structural analysis principles and formulations for framed structure.
Development of capability to analyze curved members and non-prismatic members using stiffness matrices derived from flexibility matrices.
topics: Introduction to Advance Structural Analysis
Selection of Methods of Structural Analysis and Concept of Equivalent Joint Loads
Fundamentals of Stiffness method
Formalization of stiffness method and solutions of relevant problems
Computer Oriented Direct Stiffness method
Formulation of member and joint stiffness matrices for beams and Plane Truss structures
Formulation of member and joint stiffness matrices for Plane frames
Formulation of member and joint stiffness matrices for Grillage structures
Formulation of member and joint stiffness matrices for space truss and frame structures
Fundamentals of Flexibility Methods
Use of basic flexibility methods to analyze the truss and plane frame structures
Use of basic flexibility methods to analyze the grillage structures
Effect of Temperature changes, prestrains, support displacements and formalized version of flexibility method
Additional Topics on Stiffness method of structural analysis
Weightage

title: Advance Structural Analysis
description:
[as per the Bulletin]
Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three
dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive
software development for analysis of structures.
Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools
for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning
advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using
computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the
fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation
in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures.
By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural
analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility
method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized
learning_outcomes: Development of softwares for analysis of framed/skeleton structures.
Capability development for the use Matrix based structural analysis principles and formulations for framed structure.
Development of capability to analyze curved members and non-prismatic members using stiffness matrices derived from flexibility matrices.

title: Finite Element Analysis
description:
Fundamentals of the finite element method (FEM); basic formulations of FEM; steps in FEM; 1-D, 2-
D and 3-D elements; axi-symmetric elements, isoparametric formulations; programming aspects in
FEM; plate bending elements; shell elements; material and geometric nonlinearity; Buckling and
Vibration problems, application of FEM to civil engineering problems.
Finite element method is the most powerful numerical method widely used for solving problems in
different branches of engineering especially Civil Engineering. This method is usually used to solve
complex problems with regard to complexity in material, geometry, boundary, and loading
conditions, such as non-homogeneous material, irregular geometry, boundary conditions, and static
& dynamic loading conditions. The finite element formulation from the weak form of the governing
differential equations is also covered. The course is aimed to enable students to understand the
advanced concept of finite element method and its application to Civil Engineering.
topics: L1.1. Basic overall introduction in structural mechanics, Problems not under structural mechanics(fluid flow, heat transfer etc.)
L1.2. Need of FEM in solids and structures, basic concept of FEM, advantages of FEM, Steps in FEM, Concepts of compatibility and completeness
L1.3. Functionals and Governing Differential Equation, Strong and Weak form of Differential Equations,
L1.4. Essential and Natural Boundary Conditions. Finite element formulations(Differential equation based and Non differential equation based).
L2. 1-5 General introduction, Some mathematical concept and Formulae, Elements of calculus of variation, Integral formulations, Variational methods.
L3. 1-2 Interpolation function for basic and higher order elements, criterion for selecting the interpolation function.
L4. 1-2 Principle of virtual work, Derivation of generalized Force- displacement relationship using principal of virtual work, expressions for stiffness matrix and load vectors.

L5. 1-4 Development of interpolation function for one- dimensional elements, Development of stiffness matrix for Bar Element (from weak form of DE and from other forms), Assembly of Elements, properties of structural stiffness matrix, application of boundary conditions, development of load vector, solution of equations, determination of strains, stresses and reactions, analysis of truss structures, Higher order 1-D elements, development of stiffness matrix and load vector for Higher order one-dimensional. Use of this element in other physical problem.

L6. 1-5 Displacement functions for 2-D elements, Stress-strain relation for plane stress and plane strain problems, stiffness matrix for linear triangular element(in structural mechanics-CST) and quadratic triangular (in structural mechanics- LST) element, interpolation function for higher order Triangular elements, Lagrangian and Serendipity shape functions for linear quadrilateral elements and quadratic quadrilateral elements, stiffness matrix of these elements(from weak form of DE and other forms), defects in quadrilateral elements, Comparison of triangular and quadrilateral elements, Use of these element in other physical problem.
L7. 1-2 Formulation of axi- symmetric elements and its application.
L8 1-3 Stiffness matrix for beam elements(from weak form of DE and other forms), in 2-D and 3-D, shear deformation in beams, analysis of 2-D and 3-D framed structures.
L9 1-2 Review of various 3-D elements, Lagrangian and Serendipity Shape functions for 3-D elements, constitutive matrix for 3- D elasticity

L10 1-4 Introduction to isoparametric formulation of different elements, linear quadrilateral elements, Quadratic quadrilateral elements, Hexahedral elements, Incompatible modes, static condensation, choice of numerical integration, consideration to various types of loads, stress calculation, effect of element geometry, validity of elements with iso-parametric formulations, Patch Test, Iso- parametric formulations of Triangular and tetrahedral elements.
L11 1-4 Plate Behaviour, Kirchhoff Plate Elements(from weak form of DE and other forms), Mindlin Plate Elements(from weak form of DE and other forms), shear locking,
L12 1-4 Shell theory, Arch Elements, Shells of revolution, general three and four node shell elements, curved isoparametric shell elements, shear and membrane locking.
textbooks: R. D. Cook, D. Malkus, M. E. Plesha, and R. J. Witt, Concepts and Applications of Finite Element Analysis, Wiley India, Fourth Edition, 2003.
references: O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor and J. Z. Zhu, The Finite Element Method: Its Basis & Fundamentals, Butterworth-Heinemann, 6th edition, Elsevier India, New Delhi, 2005.
Huebner and Thornton, The Finite Element Methods for Engineers, 2nd Edition, Mc-Graw-Hill.
Chandrupatla and Belegundu, Introduction to Finite Elements in Engineering, 2nd Edition, Prentice-Hall

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
description:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
learning_outcomes: Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including physical and social dimensions.
Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using modeling tools and legal guidelines.
Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and international frameworks, including ISO.
topics: Fundamental Approach to Environmental Impact Assessment
EIA Notifications (legal Aspects)
EIA Methodologies
Prediction and Assessments of impacts on soil and ground water environment
Prediction and Assessments of impacts on surface water, biological environment, air environment, noise environment
Prediction and Assessments of impacts of socio – economic and human health aspects
Environment Management Plan (EMP), Disaster Management Plan (DMP)
Environmental Auditing and Post Project Monitoring Case History
ISO, Environmental Clearance, LCA
Weightage

title: Chemical Process Calculations
description:
Historical overview of Chemical Engineering, Principles of balancing with examples to illustrate differential and
integral balances lumped and distributed balances, Material balances in simple systems involving physical
changes and chemical reactions, Systems involving recycle, purge and bypass, Properties of substances: single
component & multicomponent, single and multiphase systems. Ideal liquid and gaseous mixtures, Energy balance
calculations in simple systems, Introduction to Computer aided calculations-steady state material and energy
balances for chemical plants
This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations,
which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual
knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and
energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical
process plants. Fundamentals of this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process
Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. At the end of this course, the students must be able to apply important definitions and conventions in chemical processes. CLO2. They can solve material and energy balances for single and multiple units with or without chemical reaction and feedback/bypass.
topics: L1-L3: Introduction to Chemical Engineering; Importance of CPC; Units & Dimensions; Conversion of Units; Dimensional consistency; Mole, Density, Specific Gravity, Flow Rates, Concentration
L4-L6: Open vs Closed Systems; Steady vs Unsteady State; Multi- component Systems; Chemical Reactions; Problem Solving Strategy
L7–L9: Material Balance Problems without Reaction
L10–L12: Stoichiometry & Reaction Terminology; Material Balances with Reaction (Species, Elemental, Combustion)
L13–L15: Sequential Multi-Unit Systems; Recycle, Bypass & Purge
L16–L18: Industrial Applications of Material Balances
L19–L21: Ideal Gas Law; Ideal Gas Mixtures; Real Gas Compressibility; Real Gas Equations of State
L22–L24: Phase Diagram, Vapor Pressure, Phase Rule; Vaporization, Saturation, Condensation
L25–L27: Humidity Concepts; Humidity Chart
L28–L30: Energy Balance Terminology; Types of Energy; Enthalpy Balances (Closed & Open Systems)
L31–L33: Heats of Formation, Reaction, and Combustion
L34–L36: Degrees of Freedom; Simultaneous Material & Energy Balances
L37–L39: Heats of Solution and Mixing; Gases & Liquids in Equilibrium with Solids
L40–L42: Unsteady-State Material and Energy Balances

title: Fluid Mechanics
description:
Fundamental Concepts, Fluid Statics, Integral and Differential Analysis for Fluid Motion,
Dimensional Analysis, Internal and External Fluid Flow, Fluid Machinery, Flow through Packed Bed,
Agitation, Introduction to Compressible Flow.
This course is an introduction to the field of fluid mechanics. It mainly covers the basic principles of
fluid mechanics. It introduces the student to the fundamental and practical aspects of fluid flow
operations that a practising chemical engineer encounters regularly. The physical concepts of fluid
mechanics and analysis methods, beginning from basic principles, shall be dealt with in this course.
learning_outcomes: Recognize and define key fluid properties (such as pressure, density, temperature, viscosity, and velocity fields), calculate shear stresses and viscous forces, and apply fundamental fluid laws including the ideal gas law, surface tension, and speed of sound.
Evaluate pressure distributions in hydrostatic fluids and submerged surfaces across various geometries, and predict buoyancy forces on floating bodies.
Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to establish conservation laws and solve problems involving the Conservation of mass and momentum using integral and differential analysis.
Apply Bernoulli and Euler equations to solve incompressible inviscid flow problems, and develop key dimensionless groups using principles like the Buckingham Pi Theorem.
Analyze fully developed laminar and turbulent pipe flows, calculate pipe losses using the Moody chart, and evaluate pressure drops across fittings, valves, and sudden expansions or contractions.

Apply boundary-layer concepts (including calculating thickness and pressure gradients), evaluate Drag on immersed bodies, analyze fluid flow through solid beds, and determine minimum fluidization velocities.
Understand the characteristics and operations of pipes, fittings, and valves, and select and design pumps based on specific process requirements.
topics: L 1-2 Definition of a fluid, Basic equations, Dimensions and units, Dimensionless equations and Consistent units, Dimensional equations, Method of analysis.
L 3-5 Concept of fluid, continuum, Velocity and stress field, Viscosity, Viscosity of gases and liquids, Surface tension, Description and classification of fluid motions.
L 6-8 Basic equations of fluid statics, Pressure variation in static fluids, Hydrostatic Equilibrium in a centrifugal field, Buoyancy and stability.
L 9-12 Basic laws for a system, Conservation of mass and momentum equations for integral control volumes,
L 13-16 Conservation of mass and momentum equations
L 17-19 Euler's equations, Bernoulli's equation,
L 20-22 Nondimensionalization, Buckingham Pi Theorem,
L 23-29 Fully developed laminar flow, Flow in pipes and ducts, Flow measurements

L 30-35 Boundary Layers, Fluid flow about immersed bodies, Boundary layer concept, Boundary layer thickness, Pressure gradient in the boundary layer, Drag & flow through beds of solids, fluidized beds, Sedimentation.
L 36-42 Pipe, Fittings, and Valves; Pumps: Classification & selection, Performance Characteristics

title: Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics
description:
Applications of first and second laws; relations between state properties; chemical equilibria in reacting and
non-reacting systems; statistical concepts, and brief exposure to irreversible thermodynamics; extensive
problem assignments throughout. [Review of work, heat, reversible and irreversible processes, First Law
applications to closed and open systems, Second Law, Entropy, Heat effects, Equations of state and
generalized correlations for PVT behavior, Maxwell relations and fluid properties estimation; Residual and
excess properties, Partial molar quantities; Gibbs-Duhem Equation, Fugacity and Activity Coefficient
models, Vapor-Liquid equilibria, chemical reaction equilibrium.
 Understanding laws of thermodynamics and applying the concept for heat, work and energy
calculations.
 Analyze essential conditions (temperature, pressure, composition, etc.) for simple physical and chemical
changes.
 Thermodynamic properties calculation for ideal and real fluids.
 Apply thermodynamic principles in estimation/calculation of thermodynamic efficiency
 Application of thermodynamic principals for understanding the criterion (G, equilibria constant, etc.)
of simple chemical reaction at equilibria, degree of conversion, composition and effect of P, inert gas
addition, excess reactants, products on conversion, etc.

title: Engineering Chemistry
description:
Introduction to basic principles of various branches of chemistry and their applications in chemical
Industries. Organic chemistry (Important functional groups and their reactions, Some important name
reactions commonly used in the chemical industry); Physical chemistry (Thermodynamic processes,
Thermochemistry, Electrochemistry, Adsorption, Catalysis), Chemical methods of analysis (volumetric
analysis: neutralization, redox, complexometric titrations), Instrumental methods of analysis ( IR, UV-
vis spectroscopy, Chromatography), Engineering materials (cementing materials, refractories, polymers),
Metals and alloys (Iron and steel), Corrosion (types of corrosion and corrosion control methods), Water
treatment (Hardness of water, water analysis and water treatment), Fuels and combustion (Classification
of fuels, Analysis of coal, Combustion, Calorific value and its determination).
The course aims to introduce various aspects of chemistry as applied to
engineering. The course also aims to bridge the theoretical concepts and their practical engineering
applications, thus highlighting the role of chemistry in the field of chemical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to
Identify and illustrate key functional groups and industrially important organic reactions used in chemical synthesis.
Explain the principles of thermodynamics and apply them to evaluate energy changes in chemical processes.
Analyze electrochemical systems and interpret electrode potentials, electrochemical cell behavior, and battery performance.
Describe adsorption processes and interpret isotherms and breakthrough curves relevant to industrial separations.
Perform and evaluate chemical and instrumental analytical techniques such as titrations, spectroscopy (IR, UV-Vis), and chromatography.
Classify polymers and engineering materials and assess their structure-property relationships for industrial use.
Distinguish between various metals and alloys, especially steel, and justify their use based on physical and chemical properties.
Assess the types and characteristics of fuels and calculate their calorific values using standard methods.
Identify different types of corrosion and propose suitable prevention and control methods.
Analyze water samples for impurities, determine hardness, and recommend appropriate water treatment techniques.
Integrate chemical concepts to solve practical problems in industrial and environmental engineering contexts.
Demonstrate scientific thinking, analytical reasoning, and technical communication skills through tests, quizzes, and project work.

title: Separation Processes II
description:
Special equilibrium-based separations like humidification and water cooling, drying of wet solids, adsorption,
crystallization etc., Mechanical separations like filtration, centrifugation, froth floatation etc., Solid
separations based on size reduction including sieving operations and related equipment like crushers, mills,
pulverizers etc., special separation processes like ion-exchange, membranes, chromatography etc.
This course gives the basic understanding of Mechanical Operations, which involves size reduction, size
separation, filtration, etc. and certain Mass Transfer Operations like humidification, drying, adsorption,
membrane separation, and crystallization. It covers the fundamentals, application of each of these unit
operations and the equipment used is discussed in detail. The objective of the course is to orient the students

title: Process Design Principles I
description:
Process invention using heuristics and analysis (The Design process, Process creation and heuristics for process
synthesis, Role of process simulators like Aspen Plus in process creation), Strategic designs in process synthesis and
analysis, Detailed process synthesis using algorithmic methods with emphasis on reactor networks, separation trains,
batch processes, heat and mass integration, energy integration analysis; pinch technology.
This course introduces the student to process engineering and provides an insight into various aspects of process design.
This course mainly deals with the process synthesis part of process design. It covers in detail the preliminary process

title: Environmental Pollution Control
description:
Air & water pollutants; sampling and analysis; control methods for air & water pollutants;
modeling of different control techniques; advanced wastewater treatment processes; solid
waste management, noise pollution; case studies; associated laboratory.
1. Students will learn significance of environmental engineering course, effect of
greenhouse effect on climate change, river pollution etc.
2. They will know theoretically how to do air pollutants sampling & Analysis of Air
Pollutants
3. They understand basic modelling techniques of the dispersion of the pollutant in air.
4. They will learn basic designing aspects of different methods and equipment for air
pollution control.
5. Students will gather idea on sources & classification of water pollutants: Origin of
wastewater, their effects, Dissolved oxygen estimation, etc.
6. They learn how to collect wastewater samples and analyse: Understanding and analysis of
concepts of DO, BOD, COD, TOC, Water Quality Standards, etc.
7. They comprehend the basics of wastewater treatment methods, biological treatments,
Tertiary treatments, Zone settling process & technology
8. Students will learn Sources and Classification of solid wastes, Methods of Collection, Disposal
methods , different Hazardous Wastes, treatment and managements, etc.
9. In Module 9 they will explore sources of noise, effects, measurement of noise, control
techniques, etc.

Air borne pollutants.
Water borne pollutants.
Solid waste pollutants.
Noise pollution.
Hazardous pollutants. CLO 2: At the end of this course student should have the preliminary understanding/skill set required to work on designing and/or capacity enhancement of
Air pollution control equipment. 1
Water treatment processes.

Solid waste disposal and control processes. CLO 3: At the end of this course student should have the preliminary understanding/skill set required to apply Laws and regulation related to pollution control in general.

2.Air pollution sampling & measurement

5.Sources & classification of water pollutants

title: MOLECULAR AND STATISTICAL THERMODYNAMICS
description:
Fundamental of Statistical Mechanics, Postulates, Concept of Ensembles, statistical interpretation of entropy.
Intermolecular Potential Energy functions; Distribution functions: Radial Distribution Function (RDF);
Applications of Statistical Mechanics: Thermo-physical property calculations in ensembles; Cooperative
Phenomenon: Phase Equilibria: Ising model, Gibbs Ensemble (VLE), Thermodynamic Integration, Gibbs-
Duhem Integration, Free Energy calculation; Virial EOS: second virial coefficient; Special Applications:
From Surface Adsorption: Adsorption Isotherm. Molecular Simulation Techniques: Molecular Dynamics and
Monte Carlo Simulation, Monte Carlo Simulation in various Ensemble.
The objective of the course is to introduce the students with the microscopic description of the
thermodynamics system and how macroscopic properties can be derived from microscopic description using
statistical mechanics or statistical thermodynamics. In this course the statistical ensembles in classical
mechanics, the concept of ensemble and phase space will help in understanding equilibrium statistical
mechanics. Beyond this, this course will introduce the coding in either MATLAB or Python to do statistical
analysis to find the thermodynamic or dynamic properties of the system. Several simulation techniques such
as Monte Carlo Simulations and Molecular Dynamics using GROMACS will be introduced to study
applications of statistical thermodynamics to calculate various properties at nanoscale.
• Course learning outcomes:
a. Learning the fundamental concept of Statistical Thermodynamics
b. Learning the concept of molecular dynamics simulation and Monte Carlo Simulation
c. Learning the GROMACS and LAMMPS software to perform
1

L.4.4. Langmuir isotherms of adsorption of gas on lattice structure. BET isotherms of adsorption of gas on lattice structure.
