title: Atomic and Molecular Simulations
description:
This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the
atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods
e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy
algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for
simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages
such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on
programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case
studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.
This course aims to give an overall introduction to various types of particle-based simulation
techniques in the sub-micro level phenomena with hands-on training. Currently, with the advances in
computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to
study material properties for various applications. The course will include computational multi-scale
methods, from first principle ab initio calculations to molecular mechanics, offering potential pathways for
studying advanced materials for several applications such as molecular electronics, energy
storage/generation, separation, and purification, to name a few. After successful completion of the course,
the students will be equipped with the theoretical basis and algorithms of several atomic and molecular
simulations techniques (DFT, MD, MC) with their typical application areas and will be able to solve real-
world problems by choosing the right simulation techniques.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply fundamental atomic and molecular simulation techniques, including DFT, MD, MC, and multiscale methods.
Select and apply appropriate simulation approaches to solve real world problems by understanding the phenomena in atomic and molecular scale .

Analyze and evaluate simulation data to extract meaningful physical and chemical insights for advanced materials applications. Course Pre/Co- requisite (if any) & Catalogue / Bulletin Description: No prerequisite (Given in the Bulletin) 1
topics: L1-L5: Overview of Atomic and Molecular Simulation Methods Fundamental of Statistical Mechanics, Quantum Mechanics, Review of Probability, Micro State, Macro State, Thermodynamic Ensembles

L6-L11: Born-Oppenheimer Approximation, Hydrogen and Multielectron Atoms, Hartree-Fock Theory and Basis Sets, Density Functional Theory, Geometry Optimization, Electronic Structure of Atoms and Molecules, Ab Initio MD, Application, A Case Study
L12-L14: Hands on simulations using DFT package, e.g., Gaussian, Quantum Espresso
L15-L17: Making Model Structure, Viewing Simulation Structures and Movies, Making Movies from
Simulation Trajectories

L18-L22: Basics of Molecular Dynamics, Integrators for Newton’s Equations, Time step and Timescale Considerations, Thermostat, Barostat, Constant Temperature and Pressure MD, Practical Aspects of Simulations: Simulation of Bulk Phases, Periodic Boundaries, Initialization, Force Computation, Long-Range Interactions, Potential Energy Truncation, Minimum Image Convention
L23-L25 : Classical Force Field, Bonded and Nonbonded Interactions, Implicit Solvation, Output and Analysis, Application, A Case Study
L26-L33: Hands on simulations using MD simulation package, e.g., LAMMPS, GROMACS

L34-L37: Introduction to Monte Carlo Simulation, Markov Chains, The Metropolis Method, Random Number Generator, MC Simulation in Various Ensembles: Canonical Ensemble MC, Isobaric-Isothermal Ensemble, Grand Canonical Ensemble, Rigid Molecules and Orientation Moves, Equilibration, Hybrid MC/MD, Application, A Case Study
L37-L40: Kinds of Simplified Models, Advantages of Coarse Graining, Development and
Parameterization of Coarse- Grained Models

title: Advanced Transport Phenomena | ATP
description:
Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity, Shell momentum and energy
balance, equations of change for isothermal and non-isothermal systems, Concentration distribution in
solids and laminar flows, momentum, thermal and concentration boundary layers near walls, origin of
turbulence, length scales in turbulent flows, Reynolds (RANS) equations, estimates of Reynolds stress
(k-epsilon and k-omega type models), turbulent shear flow near a wall, turbulent flow in pipes and
channels, turbulent heat transfer, Introduction to large eddy simulations models, rheology and material
functions, non-Newtonian viscosity and generalized Newtonian models, Linear and non-linear
visco-elasticity, radiation heat transfer, multi-component systems, Coupled heat and mass transfer,
evaporation, boiling and condensation, chemical reactions, Special topics: Flow through porous media,
compressible flows, multiphase flow, Transport phenomena in biochemical systems.
Transport phenomena is one of the basic subjects of chemical engineering and
includes study of fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer. The governing equations for the aforementioned
transport processes are analogous in nature as the underlying molecular mechanisms are very closely
related. The objective of this course is to cover advance topics in this area like the transport of momentum,
heat and mass in turbulent flow, creeping flows, flow through porous media, flow over flat plates and
curved surfaces, interphase transport, etc. A balanced overview and fundamental equations for transport
processes would be provided along with illustrations regarding solving relevant problems. Further, some
special cases which are frequently encountered would also be covered.
topics: Scope, Objectives, Methodology, Importance, Preliminary assumptions, Foundations and concepts related to transport phenomena, Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity
Shell Momentum Balances and Boundary Conditions, The Equations of Change in terms of the Substantial Derivative, Use of the Equations of Change to Solve Flow Problems
Shell Energy Balances and boundary conditions, Free and forced convection, Use of the Equations of Change to Solve Steady-State Problems

Shell mass balances, Boundary conditions, Diffusion through a stagnant gas film, with a chemical reaction, Diffusion and chemical reaction inside a porous catalyst, Multicomponent equations of change, multicomponent fluxes, use of the equations of change for mixtures
Laminar hydrodynamic, thermal and mass transfer boundary layers, flow over cylinders, spheres; flow in tubes

Basic features of turbulence, Time-Smoothed Equations of Change for Incompressible Fluids, The Time-Smoothed Velocity Profile near a Wall, Empirical Expressions for the Turbulent Momentum Flux, Turbulent flow in pipes and channels, Eddy diffusivity models
Time-Smoothed Equations of Change for Incompressible Non-isothermal Flow, The Time-Smoothed Temperature Profile near a Wall, Empirical Expressions for the Turbulent Heat Flux, Temperature
Distribution for Turbulent Flow in Tubes and jets
Time-smoothing of the equation of continuity, Enhancement of mass transfer by a first-order reaction in turbulent flow, Turbulent mixing and turbulent flow with second-order reaction

Heat Transfer Coefficients for Forced Convection, Free and Mixed Convection, Heat Transfer Coefficients for Condensation of Pure Vapors on Solid Surfaces, Definition of transfer coefficients in two phases, Effects of interfacial forces on heat and mass transfer
Coupled diffusion and reaction, coupled heat and momentum transport
Absorption and emission at solid surfaces, Planck's distribution law, Wien's displacement law, and the Stefan-Boltzmann law, Radiation between non-black bodies at different temperatures
Fundamentals of rheology, types of complex fluids, origins of Non-Newtonian behavior
Non-Newtonian viscosity and generalized Newtonian models, elasticity and linear viscoelastic models, un-entangled and entangled polymer melts
Heat and mass transfer using extended surfaces, diffusion and reaction in catalyst pellets Multidimensional effects, potential functions and fields

title: COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS
description:
Philosophy of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD); governing equations of fluid
dynamics; mathematical behaviour of partial differential equations and their impact on CFD; finite volume and
finite difference discretization, the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Iterative methods, simulation
procedures for sample chemical engineering problems using FLUENT.
This course aims to apply numerical methods and transport phenomena to understand and
use CFD as a scientific tool. The course is research-oriented. A student is expected to do an extensive guided
reading of CFD applications and practice with building CFD models using ANSYS and COMSOL. The students
will review and present research papers using CFD as investigative tools in class.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to
Explain the philosophy, scope, and applications of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in research and engineering design contexts.
Derive and interpret the governing equations of fluid dynamics and explain their physical significance in various flow conditions.
Classify and analyze partial differential equations relevant to CFD and evaluate their physical and computational implications.
Apply finite difference and finite volume methods for the discretization of governing equations and assess stability, accuracy, and convergence of numerical schemes.
Demonstrate the concepts of grid generation, transformation, and meshing techniques for CFD simulations.

title: Chemical Process Optimization
description:
Introduction to Process Modelling and simulation, Fundamentals of analytical optimization. Survey of one dimensional
line-search methods, and multidimensional unconstrained and constrained numerical optimization algorithms.
Applications of linear programming, nonlinear programming, mixed integer linear/ nonlinear programming, and
parameter estimation in chemical engineering. Feasible-path and infeasible path techniques for chemical process
flowsheet optimization, Evolutionary computation in Chemical Engineering.
The chemical industry has undergone significant changes during the past 25 years due to the increased cost of energy,
increasingly stringent environmental regulations, and global competition in product pricing and quality. One of the most
important engineering tools for addressing these issues is optimization. Optimization as the name suggests, deals with
finding the optimum design parameters for maximizing the profit or minimizing the total investment on a process plant. The
criteria for analysis of the economic objective function involve fulfilling a process criteria restrictions, conditions, design
equations, and respecting the limits of the variables. Most problems in chemical engineering processes have many
solutions, in some cases becoming endless. The optimization is related to the selection of an option that is best in a
variety of efficient options but being the only one that comes closest to an economic optimum performance and
operation. This course, as a subject, deals with the concepts of modeling & simulation, various methods of optimization,
objective functions, constraints, theoretical & computational basis for optimization techniques, various chemical
engineering examples, etc.
The objective of the course is to apply the optimization techniques in chemical engineering processes for reducing the
operating cost and maximizing the profit. After completing this course the students will be able to apply the principle of
optimization in solving engineering problems and understand the scope of optimization in solving Chemical Engineering
problems.
topics: 1.The Nature and Organization of Optimization Problems
2.Developing Models for Optimization (4)
3.Formulation of Objective Functions (5)
4.Basic Concepts and Types of Optimization (6-8)

6.Unconstrained Multivariable Optimization (12-13)
7.Linear Programming (LP) and Applications (14-16)
8.Nonlinear Programming with Constraints (17-20)
9.Mixed-Integer Programming (21-24)
10.Global Optimization for Problems withContinuous and Discrete Variables (25-29)
11.Applications of Optimization (30-35)
12.Evolutionary computation in Chemical Engineering (36-40)

references: Kalyanmoy Deb, “Optimization for Engineering Design: Algorithms and Examples”, Second Edition, PHI Learning Private Limited, New Delhi, 2012.

title: Inorganic Chemistry I
description:
Structure of molecules: VSEPR model; ionic crystal structure, structure of complex solids; concepts
of inorganic chemistry: electronegativity, acid-base chemistry, chemistry of aqueous and non aqueous
solvents; descriptive chemistry of some elements: periodicity, chemistry of transition metals,
halogens and noble gases; inorganic chains, rings, cages and clusters.
The course is designed in consideration to growing the basic level knowledge and understanding in
inorganic chemistry. It includes electronegativity, detailed study of acid-base chemistry, non-aqueous
solution chemistry, concept of redox chemistry, shape and structure of inorganic covalent molecules
using VSEPR model and bonding of ionic compounds in solid state. It includes the chemistry of
halogen and noble gases and main group elements. There will have thorough discussion of chemistry
of macromolecules containing inorganic chains, rings and cages.This course will attempt to provide
the students with sufficient basic knowledge of the structure and reactivity of inorganic systems to
ensure a more comprehensive understanding.
By the end of semester, you will be able to learn –
➢ Different scales to define electronegativity; rationalization of unusual reactivity
➢ Shape and structure of different covalent molecules and ionic compounds
➢ Measures of acid-base strength in gas and solution phase; Relation between hardness and
softness, Symbiosis
➢ Chemistry of protonic and aprotic solvents; Redox stability; Diagrammatic presentation of
potential data
➢ Use (or not) of d orbitals by nonmetals; Reactivity and d orbital participation
➢ Positively charged halogens; Pseudohalogens
➢ Numerous examples in nature of inorganic chains, rings and cages – their structures and
chemistry

title: Physical Chemistry IV
description:
Weak forces; surface chemistry: interphase region, thermodynamics, surface films on liquids, adsorption of gases
on solids, colloids, micelles, and reverse micellar structures; transport processes: kinetics, thermal conductivity,
viscosity, diffusion, sedimentation; electrical conductivity in metals and in solutions; reaction kinetics, measurement
of rates; integrated rate laws; rate laws and equilibrium constants for elementary reactions; reaction mechanisms;
temperature dependence of rate constants; rate constants and equilibrium constants; rate law in non-ideal systems;
uni, bi and tri molecular reactions, chain reactions, free-radical polymerizations; fast reactions; reactions in
solutions; heterogeneous and enzyme catalysis; introduction to statistical mechanics; theories of reaction rates;
molecular reaction dynamics.
This is the last one of the four Physical Chemistry courses named for M.Sc. (Hons.) Chemistry Programme. The
course mainly covers chemical changes in terms of chemical kinetics, surface and interfacial phenomena, and the
associated theories. The objective is to understand the chemical changes and also to be able to connect these changes
to structure and equilibrium properties learnt in the previous courses.

title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
description:
Principles and practice of modern instrumental methods of chemical analysis.
Emphasis on spectroscopic techniques such as UV Visible, infrared, NMR (1H, 13C and other elements,
NOE, correlation spectroscopies), ESR, atomic absorption and emission, photoelectron, Mössbauer, and
fluorescence. Other topics will include mass spectrometry, separation techniques, light scattering,
electroanalytical methods, thermal analysis, and diffraction methods.
Chemists extensively use modern sophisticated electronic
instruments in various areas such as chemical analysis, structure determination, identification of reaction
pathways and rates etc. This course aims to introduce the basic theory and experimental details of such
chemical instrumentation. Some of the popular absorption spectroscopic techniques such as UV-visible,
IR, NMR, mass spectrometry etc. will be discussed in detail.

molecules using open source and proprietary software; specific computational experiments will be in the areas of
potential energy surfaces, geometry optimization, molecular geometry from symmetry and trigonometric relations
without visualization software, molecular orbitals and bonding patterns, Hartree-Fock calculations, correlation energy
and size-consistency, DFT based calculations, computing excited states using CIS, EOM-CCSD jobs for computing
energies of excited, ionized and electron-attached states; methods to estimate activation energy, solvent effects etc.;
molecular dynamics simulation, molecular mechanics will also be explored; the actual experiments may vary and can
have more specific learning outcomes so as to enhance the course with the latest developments in electronic structure
theories of chemistry.
This is an elective laboratory course to gain introductory exposure to practical
computational chemistry with major focus on computation of electronic structure of atoms and molecules. Other
branches of computational chemistry such as molecular dynamics simulation, molecular mechanics will also be
explored briefly.
learning_outcomes: CLO1: Defining the computational problem and identifying the computational method to study the same
CLO2: Preparing the input files and setting up the computational jobs
CLO3: Analyzing the output file and the generated data and interpreting to understand the phenomena

title: Photophysical Chemistry
description:
Absorption of the electromagnetic radiation; photophysical processes such as fluorescence,
phosphorescence, non-radiative transitions, and delayed luminescence, excimer and exciplex
formation; triplet state: radiative and non-radiative transitions; energy transfer, fluorescence
resonance energy transfer (FRET), quenching of fluorescence; fluorescence decay; protein and
DNA fluorescence; time-resolved emission spectra (TRES); time-dependent anisotropy decays;
application of photophysics for the characterization of biological and bio-mimicking systems. In
addition to the theory, through simple experiments, laboratory training will be imparted.
The main objective of this course is to introduce the
students to basic concept of physical processes induced by absorption of light, pathways for loss
of electronic excitation such as fluorescence, quenching, and energy transfer.
learning_outcomes: Key concepts of photophysical processes, analysis of Jablonski diagrams and excited state dynamics Interpretation and applications of spectroscopic techniques Calculation of photophysical parameters Evaluation of mechanisms of energy and electron transfer Application of photophysical principles to real-world applications Design and critique experiments in photophysical chemistry

title: Chemistry of Materials
description:
Solid state structure : unit cells, metallic crystal structures, polymorphism and allotropy, crystallographic
direction and planes, closed packed crystal structures, polycrystalline materials, anisotropy; meso and micro
porous materials: zeolites, composites, synthesis, characterization (XRD, SEM, TEM, AFM, FTIR, NMR,
TGA, and DTA) and applications; ceramics and glass materials: crystalline and non-crystalline nature, glass-
ceramics, processing; polymers: synthesis, structure, properties, inorganic polymers; mechanical properties:
stress and strain, elastic and tensile properties, hardness, phase transformations, microstructure, alteration of
mechanical properties; magnetic properties: atomic magnetism in solids, the exchange interaction,
classification of magnetic materials, diamagnetism, pauli paramagnetism, ferromagnetism,
antiferromagnetism, ferrimagnetism, superparamagnetism, ferromagnetic domains, hysteresis loop, hard and
soft ferrites, applications; electrical properties: conductivity, band theory, types of semiconductors, time
dependence of conductivity, mobility of charge carriers, metal-metal junction, metal–semiconductor junction,
n-type and p-type semiconductors; optical properties: refraction, reflection, absorption, transmission,
luminescence, photoconductivity, opacity and translucency in insulators, optical fibers; thermal properties:
heat capacity, thermal expansion, conductivity, thermal stresses; corrosion: electrochemistry of corrosion of
metals, different forms, environmental effects, prevention.
• To provide a comprehensive understanding of crystalline structures, crystal systems, unit
cells, crystallographic directions and planes, defects, and structure determination techniques.
• To develop knowledge of diffusion mechanisms, phase diagrams, phase equilibria, phase
transformations, and their influence on microstructural evolution in materials.
• To establish the relationship between processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties
of metals, including stress–strain behavior, elasticity, tensile properties, hardness, and
deformation mechanisms.
• To introduce the structure and properties of ceramics, polymers, and other engineering
materials, along with concepts of degradation, corrosion, electrical, and magnetic behavior.
• To enable students to analyze material structures, interpret phase and microstructural
information, and correlate structure–property relationships for engineering material design
and applications.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe different crystal structures, unit cells, metallic crystal arrangements, and crystal systems.
Calculate basic crystal parameters, including density, lattice parameters, and atomic packing characteristics.
Represent atomic positions using point coordinates and determine crystallographic directions and planes.
Explain the concepts of polymorphism and allotropy and their influence on material structures and properties.
Analyze the relationship between crystal structure and the physical properties of crystalline materials.

title: Organic Chemistry and Drug Design
description:
An introduction to organic chemistry principles and reactivities vital to drug design,
drug development and drug action; the role of molecular size, shape, and charge, and in drug action; proteins
and nucleic acids as drug targets; bioisosterism; ADME, QSAR and drug design; applied molecular modeling
and combinatorial synthesis; Synthesis of some selected chemotherapeutic agents (antibacterial, antiviral
agents, antimalarial, anticancer etc.)
To familiarize the students with basic aspects of drug discovery and more
importantly, the applications of organic chemistry in drug design, important drug targets, marketed drugs,
synthesis of drugs; the overall objective is to have a reflective teaching and learning environment
learning_outcomes: The student should be able to accomplish the following: CL01. Understanding about structure & function of receptors, enzymes, and nucleic acids CL02. Able to identify and list at least five biological targets for drugs CL03. For the above targets be able to identify ten important available drugs with molecular mechanism CL04. Be able to use computational software/tools to determine given properties of the drug target of his choice CL05. At the end, be able to rationally design and propose simple synthesis of a drug for a disease.
topics: Drugs and Drug targets; Intermolecular bonding forces. Structure and function of protein, enzyme, receptors and nucleic acids

Enzyme inhibitors; Receptor role and action; affinity, efficacy, and potency. Basic idea of PK; its applications to drug discovery; elementary idea of Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination, and Toxicity (ADMET)
Drug discovery, design, and development choosing a disease, target, and bioassay; finding leads from natural drugs, libraries, existing drugs, optimizing target interactions & access to the target
textbooks: An Introduction to Medicinal Chemistry by Graham L. Patrick, Oxford University Press 5th Ed.
references: The organic chemistry of drug design and drug action 2nd edition by Richard B Silverman.

title: Green Chemistry and Catalysis
description:
Definition and overview of the twelve principles of Green Chemistry, alternative starting materials; alternative
synthesis and reagents; E-factor and the concept of atom economy; the role of catalysis, alternate energy
sources (microwave & ultrasound), catalysis by solid acids and bases, bio-catalysis, catalytic reduction,
catalytic oxidation, catalytic C–C bond formation, cascade catalysis, enantioselective catalysis, alternative
reaction media, renewable raw materials, industrial applications of catalysis.
The objectives of this course are to provide the students with a fundamental understanding of Green Chemistry
with an emphasis on the design, prepare and use of chemicals and protocols that have little or no pollution
potential or environmental risk. Catalysis being considered as the prime tool to efficiently inculcate the ‘green’
aspects, will be discussed at length including its types, guiding principles and milestone applications. The
students will get exposed to the latest development trends to obtain a comprehensive understanding.
learning_outcomes: (i) Describe principles of Green chemistry, (ii) Define basic terminologies associated in Green chemistry, (iii) Delineate importance of green chemistry aspects and catalysis phenomena 1 Factors for Green Process
5.1- 3-4 Evaluating effects of: chemistry, feedstock, reaction type, methods to design
5 safer chemicals
topics: Introduction and Tools of Green Chemistry Definition and overview of the twelve principles of Green Chemistry, E factor and the concept of atom economy, Alternative feedstock/ starting materials, reagents, solvents, product/ target molecule and catalysts
Factors for Green Process Evaluating effects of: chemistry, feedstock, reaction type, methods to design safer chemicals

Alternative modes for chemical activation Alternate (Efficient/ cheaper) modes for heating/ activation of molecules in chemical reactions, Applications of microwave & ultrasound radiation in green synthesis

Case studies: Green chemistry Polysaccharide polymers, chemical from glucose, halide free synthesis of aromatic amines, alternative to Strecker synthesis, non-phosgene isocyanate synthesis, Haas Sea –Nine insecticide.

Basics of Catalysis Basic terminologies, Energetics in Catalysis, Catalysis types, Tools in Catalysis, Kinetics in Catalysis, Catalyst Stability and Deactivation - Sintering and Thermal Degradation; Catalyst Inhibition and Poisoning
Homogeneous Catalysis - Principles Elementary steps in homogeneous catalysis, Structure-Activity Relationships (SAR) and their contributing factors, Asymmetric homogeneous catalysis principles

Homogeneous Catalysis – Discussions and Case Studies Major milestone processes in development of homogeneous catalysis in industry with high impacts, Catalytic cycles e.g. SHOP, Wacker oxidation (WO) process, Dupont Adiponitrile process, Ciba-Giegy Metolachlor process, Terephthalic acid process etc. Homogeneous catalysis in Hydrogenation, Hydroformylation, Carbonylation, Oxidation, C-C couplings etc.

Homogeneous Catalysis – Emerging trends Metal-free Catalysts: Acid-base catalysts, Organocatalysts, Catalysis in Click Chemistry, Cascade, and Combinatorial Catalysis, Homogeneous Catalysis - pros and cons

Heterogeneous Catalysts – Principles, Synthesis and Characterizations General understanding, Classification, Catalyst preparation principles, Porous matrices, Catalyst Formation, Characterization techniques employed – Surface analyses, microscopy and spectroscopy, Diffraction techniques, NMR techniques

Heterogeneous Catalysts – Illustrations and Case Studies Catalyst systems – L-S, L-L, Phase transfer catalysis (PTC), Case studies – BP AVADA process, ABB AlkyClean process, IFP, Yellowdiesel process, UOP Smart process etc.
Heterogeneous Catalysts – Emerging Trends Nanomaterials as catalysts, Novel reaction media in catalysis- Supercritical fluids, Ionic liquids, Xerothermic media in catalysis
Biocatalysis: Basics Common terminologies, Concepts of Active sites and intermediates, Mechanisms, Applications of enzymatic catalysis, Combining Bio- and
Conventional catalysis, Non-enzymatic biocatalysts – Abzymes etc., Industrial case studies

title: Environmental Chemistry
description:
Energy-flows and supplies, fossil fuels, nuclear energy, nuclear waste disposal, renewable energy, industrial
ecology, green chemistry, ozone chemistry, effect of SOx, NOx as pollutants, reformulated gasoline, water
pollution and treatment, organochlorine and organophosphate pesticides, eco-system effects, Toxic
chemicals – Effect of dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and species of metals such as lead,
mercury, cadmium etc.
This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the scientific principles
underlying environmental issues and the strategies needed to achieve sustainable development. It introduces
the relationship between human activities, industrial growth, energy consumption, and environmental
quality, enabling students to understand both the causes of environmental degradation and the methods
available to prevent or reduce it.
learning_outcomes: CLO 1: Explain the principles of energy flow and evaluate conventional and renewable energy resources, including fossil fuels, nuclear energy, and their environmental impacts. CLO 2: Analyze the concepts of industrial ecology and green chemistry for sustainable resource utilization and pollution prevention. CLO 3: Describe ozone chemistry and assess the environmental and health effects of air pollutants such as SOₓ, NOₓ, and reformulated gasoline. CLO 4: Evaluate the sources, effects, and treatment methods of water pollution for effective water quality management. CLO 5: Compare the characteristics, environmental fate, and ecological impacts of organochlorine and organophosphate pesticides. CLO 6: Assess the toxicity and environmental impacts of hazardous chemicals, including dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and heavy metals such as lead, mercury, and cadmium, and recommend appropriate pollution control measures.

title: Advanced Organic Chemistry
description:
The latest development in the area of organic chemistry will be taught in this course.
The course aims to cover topics in advanced areas of organic chemistry. The
focus will be on the application of structure and theory to the study of organic reactions: nucleophilic aromatic
substitution, organometallic reagents in organic synthesis, reaction dynamics, isotope effects, and molecular orbital
theory applied to pericyclic and photochemical reactions; reactive intermediates including carbenes, carbanions, and
benzyne; and asymmetric synthesis and multistep synthesis using the disconnection approach. Starting with fundamental
principles and their application, the ultimate purpose of this course will be to understand the recent developments in
organic chemistry.
topics: Some aspects of basic physical organic chemistry
Determining reaction mechanisms
Enol, enolates, and nucleophilic acyl substitution; Controlling reactivity, regioselectivity, and stereoselectivity
Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group and Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution, including the benzyne mechanism
Synthesis and reaction of nitrenes and carbenes as reactive intermediates

Using organometallic reagents to make C-C bonds: Lithium and Magnesium reagents, other organometallic reagents (Si, Sn, B, Cu), and Transition metal- catalyzed reactions - Stille, Suzuki, Negishi, Heck, and other couplings
Rearrangement reactions in organic chemistry
Pericyclic reactions: The effects of orbital symmetry, Diels-Alder reactions, cycloadditions, Sigmatropic rearrangements, and Electrocyclic reactions.
Asymmetric synthesis: chiral reagents, chiral catalysts, chiral auxiliary, chiral pool, and resolution
Natural products: multi-step synthesis involving protection, deprotection, and retrosynthetic analysis
textbooks: "Organic Chemistry," J. Clayden, N. Greeves, S. Warren, P. Wothers, Oxford University Press, New York (2001).
references: "Advanced Organic Chemistry: Reaction Mechanism and Structure," J. March, 4th Edition, Wiley-Interscience, New York (1992)
"Organic Chemistry," R. T. Morrison, R. N. Boyd, S. K. Bhattacharjee, 7th Edition, Pearson, India (2011)

title: Computational Thinking & Programming
description:
Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition,
abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic
thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of
efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive
and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and
structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design,
functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive
problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative
approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers,
dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output
operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools
for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and
verification of generated code.
Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals,
iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory;
file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted
code.
This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes
programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail,
express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to
realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular
design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is
anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and
program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures,
operating systems, computer architecture, and networks.
This subject aims to achieve the following goals:
● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express
solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language.
● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control
constructs, and modular function design.
● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through
recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management.
● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data,
and in persisting data through file operations.
● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and
to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1: Express computational problems using abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and structured representations including flowcharts and pseudocode. CLO2: Implement programs using fundamental constructs including variables, data types, conditionals, iteration, and modular function design. CLO3: Apply recursion and dynamic memory management to solve problems involving structured and linked data representations. CLO4: Implement file handling operations for sequential data processing and structured input/output.
topics: Basic model of computation, input, processing, output and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition. Introduction to Programming Languages.
Algorithms: efficiency, stepwise refinement, algorithm tracing, verification; Pseudocode, Flowcharts using Mermaid

Program structure, compilation and execution model, Numbering system, variables, data types, expressions, type conversion, operator precedence, formatted input and output. The programming toolchain, including AI code generation assistants, prompt formulation, and critical evaluation and verification of generated code.
Conditional statements, nested conditions, else-if chains, switch construct, conditional operator

title: Object Oriented Programming
description:
Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects,
methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of
classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded
programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification,
analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some
object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and
Creational.
a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object-
oriented analysis and design, and design patterns.
b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on
tools like Eclipse.
c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.
learning_outcomes: On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development. CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces, collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading. CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles. CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable. CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability. 1

title: Discrete Structures for Computer Science
description:
This course aims in providing mathematical foundations for many other computer science courses
including data structures and algorithms, automata, compiler theory, databases, operating system etc.
This course encompasses topics including sets & operation on sets; relations & equivalence relations;
number theory; weak & strong form of mathematical induction; principle of inclusion & exclusion,
pigeonhole principle; recurrence relations; digraphs & graphs, graph isomorphism & sub-graphs,
spanning trees, Euler & Hamiltonian graphs, planar graphs, chromatic numbers & graph coloring;

To develop logical and mathematical concepts necessary to appreciate computational systems. &

encountered in design and analysis of algorithms. To provide mathematical foundations for courses
in computer science that rely upon the comprehension of formal abstract concepts. To study
recursion and to write recursive definitions for certain sequences and collections of objects.
Graphs, directed graphs, planar graphs & their relevance to circuit design & map coloring
problems. Trees and their applications. Basic algebraic structures and their applications.

title: Principles of Programming Languages
description:
The course covers features of programming languages and introduces the main programming paradigms. It
covers, in detail, the semantics of the features of programming languages – Control Abstraction, Data Types,
and Data Abstraction, Scope and Parameter passing, inheritance, polymorphism and Concurrency related
features. It covers various aspects of runtime environments like global and local data, code, function call
stacks, dynamically allocated data, runtime features for exceptions and threads. Different programming
paradigms, namely imperative, functional, object oriented and logic programming will be discussed in detail.
Students will be introduced to the significance of a construct and how different languages implement that. The
Lambda calculus will follow an introduction to functional programming languages. Formal elements of logic
programming and programming tasks that explore the logic paradigm will be discussed.
• Develop familiarity with the different paradigms of languages (imperative, functional, object oriented
and logic) in programming and understanding the features of programming languages like abstraction,
data types, etc.
• Understand the aspects of run-time environments like global and local data, function call stacks, and
static and dynamic allocation of data.
• Introduction to the syntax and semantics of common functional programming languages.
• Students will be encouraged to learn the design aspects of languages belonging to different paradigms
rather than learning a new language.
• Understand the basis of logic programming and basic elements of prolog.
• Understand synchronization features in concurrent programming.
topics: Introduction and Motivation, Language Paradigms, Imperative vs. Declarative Styles of Programming; Programming Languages that support these styles, Compilers. Language evaluation criteria.
Lexical patterns in a program, language recognizers, formal methods of describing syntax, parse trees, attribute grammar, static and dynamic semantics.
Names, variables, bindings, scope and lifetime, referencing environment, static and dynamic type binding, storage binding and lifetime, categorization of static variables based on their lifetime.
Statements, control abstraction, Structured programming, syntax directed control flow, conditional statements, Loops and jumps, Case statements
Data Representation, Primitive and Structured Data types, ADTs; data type descriptor or type expression, enumerated data type, subrange data type, static layout decisions

Array types, design issues, indices, array bounds, subscript binding and array categories, array layout, relative addresses and efficient address computations, array initializations and operations, jagged and associative arrays, static and dynamic array bounds.
Records Structures, Variants and union, component selection, operations on records, static layout, design issues, layout of variant records.
Sets, pointers, dynamic structures. Type checking vs. Type Inferencing, Type Equivalence and Subtyping.

Introduction to procedures, Recursion, Parameter Passing Methods, Call-by-Value, Call-by- Reference, Call by Value Result. Scope rules for names, static and dynamic scope rules, nested scope, Activation Records, Lexical Scope, Dangling Pointers

title: Reinforcement Learning
description:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is based on the idea where we learn by interacting with
our environment. It is a collection of machine learning techniques where agent(s) learn how to behave in an
environment by performing actions and assessing the results. RL approach is building programs that learn
how to predict and act in stochastic environment, based on experience. This course will provide an overview
to students on some of the fundamental ideas on which modern RL is built including Markov decision
processes, Mult-armed bandits value functions, Monte Carlo estimation, dynamic programming, TD methods,
approximation methods, Actor-Critic methods, etc. This course will help students to understand and apply RL
in several systems including video distribution systems, game development, IOT devices, robotics, clinical
decision making, industrial process control, finance portfolio balancing, etc.
This course aims to achieve the following goals:
• To provide students with the knowledge to structure a reinforcement learning problem.
• To introduce students to learn and apply basic RL algorithms for simple sequential decision-making problems in
uncertain conditions
• To introduce students research and development work in reinforcement learning by interpreting state-of-the-art RL
research and communicating their results.
• To provide knowledge to students to build a RL system that knows how to make automated decisions.
• To give students opportunities to understand the space of RL algorithms including Temporal Difference Learning,
Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, approximation solution methods, A2C, A3C, etc.
topics: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning. A brief summary of the pre- requisites, mathematical and programming tools required.
Bandit problems
Finite Markov Decision Processes

Solution Methods: Temporal- Difference Learning
Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
Function approximation for generalization
Multi-agent reinforcement learning

title: COMPUTER ARCHITECTURE
description:
This course develops a comprehensive understanding of computer architecture and organization, from
quantifying processor performance to designing a working processor and its supporting memory system. It
begins with performance measurement and comparison using key metrics, benchmarking tools, and Amdahl's
law. Building on this, it covers the MIPS architecture and instruction set. The course then examines the design
of single-cycle and multi-cycle processor. It further explores pipelined processor design, the handling of
structural, data, and control hazards through forwarding, stalling, reordering, and branch prediction techniques.
The memory hierarchy is studied to exploit locality of reference, covering memory technologies, cache
mapping functions, cache controller design, cache performance metrics, and multi-level caches. Finally, the
course introduces advanced techniques for increasing instruction-level parallelism, including multiple issue,
loop unrolling, speculation, and dynamic scheduling.

MIPS Architecture and Instruction Set
Data-path and Control Design: Single Cycle and Multi-cycle processor Architectures

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that seeks to build systems that emulate human cognition.
A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities that mimic human intelligence, such as problem-solving,
reasoning, planning, uncertainty handling, and learning. The course introduces students to a large collection of
algorithms and techniques for building these intelligent entities. By the end of the course, the students should have
a general knowledge of the field of AI. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to
solve problems. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter.
This course covers the issues and techniques involved in creating computer systems that exhibit intelligent
behavior. The following are among the topics that we will cover: AI search techniques, Game Playing, Planning,
Knowledge Representation, Reasoning under Uncertainty, and Reinforcement Learning.

title: Data Mining
description:
Introduction to Data Mining, fundamental concepts; motivation and applications; role of
data warehousing in data mining; challenges and issues in data mining; Knowledge Discovery in Databases
(KDD); role of data mining in KDD; algorithms for data mining; tasks like decision-tree construction, finding
association rules, sequencing, classification, and clustering; applications of neural networks and machine learning
for tasks of classification and clustering.
The course explores the concepts and techniques of data mining, a promising and flourishing frontier in
database systems. Data Mining is automated extraction of patterns representing knowledge implicitly stored in
large databases, data warehouses, and other massive information repositories. It is a decision support tool that
addresses unique decision support problems that cannot be solved by other data analysis tools such as Online
Analytical Processing (OLAP). The course covers data mining tasks like constructing decision trees, finding
association rules, classification, and clustering. The course is designed to provide students with a broad
understanding in the design and use of data mining algorithms. The course also aims at providing a holistic
view of data mining. It will have database, statistical, algorithmic and application perspectives of data mining.
topics: Introduction to Data Mining • Motivation • What is Data Mining? • Data Mining Tasks • Issues in Data Mining • Applications
Data Preprocessing • Types of data • Data Quality • Data preprocessing
• Similarity and Dissimilarity Measures
Data Exploration • Data Set & its Statistics • Visualization • OLAP & Multidimensional Data Analysis
Classification • Introduction • Applications • Decision Tree based Algorithms • Model Over-fitting • Performance Evaluation of a Classifier • Comparing Classifiers

Classification: Alternative Techniques • Rule Based Classifier • Nearest Neighbor Classifier • Bayesian Classification • Support Vector Machine • Ensemble Classifiers • Class Imbalance Problem • Multiclass Problem
Association Rule Mining • Introduction • Applications • Market-Basket Analysis • Frequent Itemsets • Apriori Algorithm • Alternative Methods

Advanced Association Rule Mining • Generalized Association Rules • Multilevel Association Rules • Multidimensional Association Rules • Temporal Association Rules • Infrequent Patterns • Constrained Based Association Rules
Clustering • Introduction • Applications • Partitioning Algorithms • Hierarchical Algorithms • Density based Algorithms • Cluster Evaluation
Clustering: Additional Issues and Algorithms • Characteristics of Data, Clusters and clustering Algorithms • Graph Based Clustering • Scalable Clustering Algorithms
Anomaly Detection • Preliminaries • Statistical Approaches • Proximity based Outlier Detection • Density based Outlier Detection
• Clustering Based Techniques
Advanced Topics • Web Mining • Incremental Algorithms for Data Mining • Stream Data Mining
textbooks: Tan P. N., Steinbach M & Kumar V. “Introduction to Data Mining” Pearson Education, 2016.
references: Han J & Kamber M, “Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques”, Morgan Kaufmann Publishers, Third Edition, 2012 ii) Zaki MJ & Wagner M JR, “Data Mining and Analysis-Fundamental Concepts and Algorithms” Cameridge Univ Press, 2014.

title: Deep Learning
description:
In the last decade, due to the availability of cheap computational power and relevant software tools,
several neural networks are explored to advance state-of-the-art of many hard AI problems. These
architectures have successfully advanced various areas such as image searching, natural language
understanding, medical applications, autonomous vehicles etc. All these problems rely on efficient,
accurate and robust solutions for basic vision tasks like image classification, localization and detection.
In this course students will be given an exposure to the details of neural networks as well as deep
learning architectures and to develop end-to-end models for such tasks. Students will learn to
implement, train and debug their own neural networks. This is a project oriented practical course in
which every student has to develop a complete working model to solve some real world problem.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able
To understand importance of learning when sufficient data and processing power is available.
To understand the importance of general purpose solution with end-to-end learning.
To understand the hierarchical training and learning of features.
To apply deep learning for basic computer vision tasks such as image classification, localization and detection.
To apply deep learning for generating interesting and new patterns using GAN.
To understand how to apply deep learning in sequence discovery problems such as text, voice, video etc.
topics: Introduction to machine learning, end to end learning, optimization, linear model of regression and its convergence, loss function, function approximation, evaluation parameters
Perceptron, multi-layer perceptron, activation functions, neuron, computational models of neurons, artificial neural networks (ANN), multilayer feedforward neural networks (MLFFNNs)
Training feedforward neural networks, gradient descent, backpropagation learning, Regularization methods (L1, L2, dropout, batch normalization), loss landscape, parameter initialization.
Deep neural networks (DNNs), difficulty of training DNNs, Greedy layer wise training, Optimization for training DNNs, optimization methods for neural networks (SGD, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam).

Convolution neural networks (CNNs), convolution, pooling and its variations, striding, CNN training and fine-tuning: weights initialization, hyper-parameter tuning. Different deep CNN architectures - LeNet, AlexNet, VGGnet.
Understanding and visualizing CNNs. Image classification with CNNs. Applications in Computer Vision.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs): Sequence modeling using RNNs, Back propagation through time, Vanishing and exploding gradients, Long short term memory (LSTM), Bidirectional LSTMs/RNNs, GRU
Generative models, Autoencoders, Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative adversarial networks (GAN), encoder decoder architecture
Advanced Topics in Deep Learning: Interpretability, Explainability, Attention, Transformers, Large Language Models (LLMs)
Applications: Applications in vision, speech and natural language processing.
textbooks: Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville, Deep learning, In preparation for MIT Press, Available online: http://www.deeplearningbook.org, 2016
Aston Zhang and Zachary C. Lipton and Mu Li and Alexander J. Smola, Dive into Deep Learning, https://d2l.ai/index.html 2021
references: Satish Kumar, Neural Networks - A Class Room Approach, Second Edition, Tata McGraw-Hill, 2013
S. Haykin, Neural Networks and Learning Machines, Prentice Hall of India, 2010
Kevin Murphy, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press, 2012 Online Link https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/machine-learning-0
Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer, 2006.

title: Natural Language Processing
description:
The intent of the course is to present a broad undergraduate/post-graduate level introduction to Natural
Language Processing (NLP, a.k.a. computational linguistics), the study of computing systems that can process,
understand, or communicate in human language. The primary focus of the course will be on understanding
various NLP tasks as listed on the course syllabus, algorithms for effectively solving these problems, and methods
for evaluating their performance.
This subject aims to achieve the following goals:
• To introduce students, the challenges of empirical methods for natural language processing (NLP)
applications.
• To introduce basic mathematical models and methods used in NLP applications to formulate computational
solutions.
• To provide students with the knowledge on designing procedures for natural language resource annotation
and the use of related tools for text analysis and hands-on experience of using such tools.
• To introduce students research and development work in information retrieval, information extraction, and
knowledge discovery using different natural language resources.
• To give students opportunities to sharpen their programming skills in neural networks (and deep learning)
for computational linguistics applications.
topics: Introduction to NLP, Text Preprocessing, Standardization
N-Gram Language Models, Evaluation, Smoothing Interpolation, etc.
Text classification, Traditional sentiment analysis, Naïve Bayes
Logistic Regression, Sigmoid, Softmax, Cross entropy loss function and Stochastic Gradient Decent algorithm
Word embeddings- co-occurrence matrix based, wor2vec (Skip gram and CBOW) Glove, Vector semantics
Neural Networks and Neural language models
Sequence Labeling- Part-of- Speech Tagging and Named Entity Analysis, hand crafted features
RNNs and LSTMs
LLM Introduction
Conditional Text Generation, Prompting, sampling, decoding
Self-supervised pretraining, finetuning, evaluation
Transformers
Post-training: Instruction Tuning, Alignment, and Test-Time Compute
Masked Language Models

title: Information Retrieval
description:
This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information
Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs
and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language
modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental
evaluation. The software architecture components include design and implementation of high-capacity text and
multimedia retrieval and filtering systems.
The course is designed to provide students with a broad understanding in the design and use of information retrieval
techniques. The course also aims at providing a holistic view of information retrieval, which includes several retrieval
concepts and techniques such as representation and indexing of data, text mining, websearch: basics and advances,
multimedia retrieval, etc.

title: Advanced Computer Networks
description:
This is a graduate level course on computer networking and assumes a
student has a basic understanding of computer network concepts. This course is a topic-based
course which primarily covers topics from Internet Architecture, Internet Congestion Control,
Software Defined Networking, Delay Tolerant Networks, Wireless Networking, Quality of
Service & Traffic Engineering, Network Performance & Management, Overlay Networks and
Network Applications. Several research papers/articles/case studies will be discussed on
different aspects of computer networking. This course will introduce students to the basic design
principles on which today's Internet is based upon along with the current and emerging research
topics in the computer networking area. In addition, this course will cover some recent proposals
to improve network performance, functionality and scalability. This course will provide plenty
of opportunity for learning by doing through projects, assignments and laboratory exercises.
a. To understand the state of the art in network protocols, network architectures, and
networked systems.
b. To develop a strong understanding of the core concepts of computer networks.
c. To get practice of reading the research papers and critically understanding the research
of others.
d. To engage ourselves in networking research.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Analyze the design principles, architectures, protocols, and performance trade-offs of modern computer networks. CLO2. Critically evaluate networking research by identifying key contributions, assumptions, limitations, and alternative design choices. CLO3. Design, implement, and experimentally evaluate solutions to networking problems using appropriate tools and methodologies.
topics: M1

Software Defined Networking (SDNs): ✔ To learn about centralized control vs. SDN Architecture and Components, SDN distributed control of the network. Controller, Network Programmability, ✔ To understand about network functions, M2 Network Function Virtualization (NFV), virtualization, and architectural SDN Frameworks, Use cases for traffic principles of SDNs monitoring & management, bandwidth ✔ To understand technical challenges and scheduling and monitoring. potential issues arising in SDN deployment.
M3

Wireless & Mobile Networks: Wireless ✔ To understand wireless networks and node M4 Networks fundamentals, Wi-Fi Protocol, mobility issues in IP networks and Mobile IP and Micro Mobility Protocols, their solutions. TCP protocol Performance Issues in ✔ To understand TCP performance Wireless Networks, Modified TCP for challenges in wireless networks. Wireless Networks. ✔ To learn about solutions for improving TCP performance in wireless networks.
M5

title: Cloud Computing
description:
The primary objective of the course is to introduce the student to cloud computing from architectural and design
perspectives. As such, the emphasis of the course would be on the underlying infrastructure and architecture of
clouds, techniques for enabling services and the quality of such services, as well as issues in designing clouds.
Select research issues in performance, security, and management would also be addressed. Programming on the
cloud would be encouraged but not taught in class. Students are expected to learn and understand tools and
techniques for using, designing, and implementing clouds and services via assignments and a term project.

title: Reconfigurable Computing
description:
Overview of Programmable Logics. FPGA fabric architectures. Logic Elements and
Switch Networks. Design and Synthesis of Combinational and Sequential Elements. Placement and Routing.
Pipelining and other Design Methodologies. Fine-grained and Coarse-Grained FPGAs. Static and Dynamic
Reconfiguration. Partitioning. Hardware/Software Partitioning and Partial Evaluation; Systolic Architectures.
Users perspective of reconfigurability – implementation and use cases on modern FPGAs.
Reconfigurable (adaptive) computing is a novel yet important research field investigating
the capability of hardware to adapt to changing computational requirements such as emerging standards, late
design changes, and even to changing processing requirements arising at run-time. Reconfigurable computing thus
benefits from a) the programmability of software similar to the Von Neumann computer and b) the speed and
efficiency of parallel hardware execution.The purpose of the course reconfigurable computing is to instruct
students about the possibilities and rapidly growing interest in adaptive hardware and corresponding design
techniques by providing them the necessary knowledge for understanding and designing reconfigurable hardware
systems and studying applications benefiting from dynamic hardware reconfiguration.
learning_outcomes: CO1: Identify the role and advantages of reconfigurable computing compared to other computing paradigms. CO2: Understand FPGA design flow, placement, routing, and configuration aspects in reconfigurable systems. CO3: Understand reconfiguration techniques such as partial and run-time reconfiguration in adaptive hardware systems. CO4: Apply Verilog to model and implement digital designs on FPGA platforms.

Fine - Grained and Course - Grained Reconfigurable Architecture, Case Studies.
Logic Design Process ● Design ● Integration ● FGA Design Flow Implementation Approaches ● Run Time Reconfiguration (RTR) ● Partial Reconfiguration (PR)
Logic Implementation for FPGAs, Syntax- Directed Translation Logic Synthesis ● Two-Level Logic Synthesis ● Multi-Level Logic Synthesis LUT- Based Technology Mapping
Modeling ● DFG, CFG Introduction to Binding, Scheduling and Allocation, Temporal Partitioning Temporal Partitioning Algorithms ● ASAP ● ALAP
Offline and Online Temporal Placement Routing Cost, Routing- Conscious Placement

title: Agentic AI
description:
Introduction to Transformers; advanced architectures beyond Transformers (state space mod-
els/Mamba, mixture-of-experts, diffusion-based language models); Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning
(PEFT) Basics (LoRA), advanced PEFT (QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA, quantization-aware
adapters); inference and decoding (top-k, top-p, beam, contrastive; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAt-
tention, AWQ); Model quantization, pruning, distillation, on-device edge optimization; test-time
compute (self-consistency, Tree, Graph-of-Thought); post-training & alignment (Reinforcement
Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline, PPO, REINFORCE, GRPO; direct alignment:
DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO; rejection sampling, instruction tuning, distillation, tool & function calling,
Model Context Protocol (MCP)); Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Basics, Advanced RAG
(IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy); Agent Security (threat models, attack mecha-
nisms and defense strategies, red teaming, blue teaming);evolutionary/genetic methods (prompt
& agent evolution); multimodal LLMs & agents (Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA; MM-ReAct, ViperGPT).
• Compare and justify LLM/agent architecture choices for long-context, latency, and reasoning.
• Implement and evaluate PEFT methods under memory/compute constraints.
• Design decoding and test-time compute strategies within fixed latency/cost budgets.
• Build and align models/agents using RLHF and direct-alignment methods; diagnose reward
hacking and length bias.
• Construct robust, programmable RAG agent pipelines with provenance and corrective feed-
back.
• Analyze and mitigate AI agent security threats, conduct red & blue teaming.
• Apply evolutionary search to improve prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies.
• Fine-tune and evaluate multimodal LLMs/agents; integrate perception with tool-use plans
safely.
1
learning_outcomes: At the end of the course, the students will be able to
Explain and compare advanced LLM/agent architectures (Transformers, SSMs, Mamba, MoE, diffusion etc.).
Apply parameter–efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, ReLoRA) under memory and compute constraints.
Configure decoding and serving (top-k, top-p, beam; vLLM, KV-cache, PagedAttention) to meet latency and cost targets.
Implement test-time compute strategies (self-consistency, Tree/Graph-of-Thought) and eval- uate accuracy–cost trade-offs.
Build post-training model/agent pipelines (SFT → reward modeling → RLHF or direct align- ment) and mitigate reward hacking/length bias.
Use direct-alignment methods (DPO, SimPO, KTO, IPO) and rejection sampling to improve helpfulness and safety.
Design robust RAG agentic systems (IR foundations, HyDE, RAPTOR, CRAG, DSPy) with provenance and corrective feedback.
Evaluate and defend AI agents against adversarial threats (prompt injection, data poisoning, tool misuse); perform red & blue teaming.
Employ evolutionary methods to optimize prompts, tools, MCP usage and agent policies against defined fitness metrics.
Fine-tune and assess multimodal LLMs/agents (e.g., LLaVA, MM-ReAct) with appropriate safety guardrails.
textbooks: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Nathan Lambert, First Edition, On- line, 2025 [Online Link]
Introduction to Large Language Models, Tanmoy Chakraborty, First Edition, Wiley, 2024 [Online Link] Reference Textbooks
references: Generative Deep Learning (2nd Ed.), David Foster, O’Reilly, 2023 [Online Link]
Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd Ed.), Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto, MIT Press, 2018 [Online Link]
Research Papers published in Top CS venues (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, ACL, EMNLP, NAACL etc.) 2

title: Introduction to Python
description:
Introduction to Python, analysis of the problem, design, implementation, and testing, Python pro-
gramming fundamentals: program structure, data types, variables, expressions, assignment; Pro-
gram control statements: if, else, logical operators, assignment operators, conditional operators,
blocks. Program repetition statements: while, for; Data Structures: Lists, tuples, sets and dictio-
naries; Using functions: writing functions enhance program modularity; String handling, File han-
dling, Exception handling, Object-oriented fundamentals: classes, objects, methods, abstraction,
predefined classes; Writing classes: programmer-defined classes, instance data and methods,
parameters, overloading, encapsulation.
Python programming is an essential skill that is increasingly relevant in today’s technology- driven
world. This course is designed to introduce students to the core concepts of Python programming,
guiding them through essential topics such as problem analysis, design, implementation, and
testing. Students will gain hands-on experience with Python programming fundamentals, including
program structure, data types, variables, and expressions.
The course will cover key programming concepts such as control statements (if, else, logi-
cal and conditional operators), repetition statements (while, for loops), and data structures (lists,
tuples, sets, and dictionaries). By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and
skills to write Python programs from scratch, design custom classes, and apply core programming
techniques to real-world problems.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain Python fundamentals including variables, data types, operators, and control structures. CLO2. Develop Python programs using conditional statements, loops, functions, and built-in data structures CLO3. Apply Python to solve basic business problems through calculations, decision logic, and simple automation. 1 CLO4. Analyze and debug Python programs to identify errors and improve code efficiency and readability.
topics: Introduction to Programming & Business Applications of Python; Installing Python, IDEs (Anaconda / VS Code), Running First Program; Python Syntax, Keywords, Comments, Indentation
Variables and Assignment Statements; Data Types: int, float, string, Boolean; Type Conversion and Input/Output Functions
Operators: Arithmetic, Relational, Logical; Expressions and Operator Precedence; Decision Making: if, if-else statements
Nested if and elif ladder; Return Values and Scope of Variables; Looping Concepts: for loop

title: Computational Thinking & Programming
description:
Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition,
abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic
thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of
efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive
and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and
structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design,
functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive
problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative
approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers,
dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output
operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools
for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and
verification of generated code.
Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals,
iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory;
file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted
code.
This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes
programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail,
express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to
realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular
design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is
anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and
program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures,
operating systems, computer architecture, and networks.
This subject aims to achieve the following goals:
● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express
solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language.
● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control
constructs, and modular function design.
● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through
recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management.
● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data,
and in persisting data through file operations.
● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and
to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1: Express computational problems using abstraction, algorithmic thinking, and structured representations including flowcharts and pseudocode. CLO2: Implement programs using fundamental constructs including variables, data types, conditionals, iteration, and modular function design. CLO3: Apply recursion and dynamic memory management to solve problems involving structured and linked data representations. CLO4: Implement file handling operations for sequential data processing and structured input/output.
topics: Basic model of computation, input, processing, output and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition. Introduction to Programming Languages.
Algorithms: efficiency, stepwise refinement, algorithm tracing, verification; Pseudocode, Flowcharts using Mermaid

Program structure, compilation and execution model, Numbering system, variables, data types, expressions, type conversion, operator precedence, formatted input and output. description:

their performance from examples/experience. This course introduces the student to the key algorithms and theory that forms the core of
machine learning. The course will cover all major approaches to learning namely, supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and

support vector machines, artificial neural networks, Bayesian techniques, Hidden Markov models etc. Some advanced topics like
active, deep, & topological learning will also be covered.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that seeks to build systems that emulate human cognition.
A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities that mimic human intelligence, such as problem-solving,
reasoning, planning, uncertainty handling, and learning. The course introduces students to a large collection of
algorithms and techniques for building these intelligent entities. By the end of the course, the students should have
a general knowledge of the field of AI. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to
solve problems. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter.
This course covers the issues and techniques involved in creating computer systems that exhibit intelligent
behavior. The following are among the topics that we will cover: AI search techniques, Game Playing, Planning,
Knowledge Representation, Reasoning under Uncertainty, and Reinforcement Learning.

title: Deep Learning
description:
In the last decade, due to the availability of cheap computational power and relevant software tools,
several neural networks are explored to advance state-of-the-art of many hard AI problems. These
architectures have successfully advanced various areas such as image searching, natural language
understanding, medical applications, autonomous vehicles etc. All these problems rely on efficient,
accurate and robust solutions for basic vision tasks like image classification, localization and detection.
In this course students will be given an exposure to the details of neural networks as well as deep
learning architectures and to develop end-to-end models for such tasks. Students will learn to
implement, train and debug their own neural networks. This is a project oriented practical course in
which every student has to develop a complete working model to solve some real world problem.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able
To understand importance of learning when sufficient data and processing power is available.
To understand the importance of general purpose solution with end-to-end learning.
To understand the hierarchical training and learning of features.
To apply deep learning for basic computer vision tasks such as image classification, localization and detection.
To apply deep learning for generating interesting and new patterns using GAN.
To understand how to apply deep learning in sequence discovery problems such as text, voice, video etc.
topics: Introduction to machine learning, end to end learning, optimization, linear model of regression and its convergence, loss function, function approximation, evaluation parameters
Perceptron, multi-layer perceptron, activation functions, neuron, computational models of neurons, artificial neural networks (ANN), multilayer feedforward neural networks (MLFFNNs)
Training feedforward neural networks, gradient descent, backpropagation learning, Regularization methods (L1, L2, dropout, batch normalization), loss landscape, parameter initialization.
Deep neural networks (DNNs), difficulty of training DNNs, Greedy layer wise training, Optimization for training DNNs, optimization methods for neural networks (SGD, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam).

Convolution neural networks (CNNs), convolution, pooling and its variations, striding, CNN training and fine-tuning: weights initialization, hyper-parameter tuning. Different deep CNN architectures - LeNet, AlexNet, VGGnet.
Understanding and visualizing CNNs. Image classification with CNNs. Applications in Computer Vision.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs): Sequence modeling using RNNs, Back propagation through time, Vanishing and exploding gradients, Long short term memory (LSTM), Bidirectional LSTMs/RNNs, GRU
Generative models, Autoencoders, Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Generative adversarial networks (GAN), encoder decoder architecture
Advanced Topics in Deep Learning: Interpretability, Explainability, Attention, Transformers, Large Language Models (LLMs)
Applications: Applications in vision, speech and natural language processing.
