title: Natural Language Processing
description:
The intent of the course is to present a broad undergraduate/post-graduate level introduction to Natural
Language Processing (NLP, a.k.a. computational linguistics), the study of computing systems that can process,
understand, or communicate in human language. The primary focus of the course will be on understanding
various NLP tasks as listed on the course syllabus, algorithms for effectively solving these problems, and methods
for evaluating their performance.
This subject aims to achieve the following goals:
• To introduce students, the challenges of empirical methods for natural language processing (NLP)
applications.
• To introduce basic mathematical models and methods used in NLP applications to formulate computational
solutions.
• To provide students with the knowledge on designing procedures for natural language resource annotation
and the use of related tools for text analysis and hands-on experience of using such tools.
• To introduce students research and development work in information retrieval, information extraction, and
knowledge discovery using different natural language resources.
• To give students opportunities to sharpen their programming skills in neural networks (and deep learning)
for computational linguistics applications.
topics: Introduction to NLP, Text Preprocessing, Standardization
N-Gram Language Models, Evaluation, Smoothing Interpolation, etc.
Text classification, Traditional sentiment analysis, Naïve Bayes
Logistic Regression, Sigmoid, Softmax, Cross entropy loss function and Stochastic Gradient Decent algorithm
Word embeddings- co-occurrence matrix based, wor2vec (Skip gram and CBOW) Glove, Vector semantics
Neural Networks and Neural language models
Sequence Labeling- Part-of- Speech Tagging and Named Entity Analysis, hand crafted features
RNNs and LSTMs
LLM Introduction
Conditional Text Generation, Prompting, sampling, decoding
Self-supervised pretraining, finetuning, evaluation
Transformers
Post-training: Instruction Tuning, Alignment, and Test-Time Compute
Masked Language Models

title: Information Retrieval
description:
This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information
Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs
and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language
modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental
evaluation. The software architecture components include design and implementation of high-capacity text and
multimedia retrieval and filtering systems.
The course is designed to provide students with a broad understanding in the design and use of information retrieval
techniques. The course also aims at providing a holistic view of information retrieval, which includes several retrieval
concepts and techniques such as representation and indexing of data, text mining, websearch: basics and advances,
multimedia retrieval, etc.

title: Product Design
description:
The course covers various approaches to designing and developing a successful product. User research,
requirements analysis, problem-specific creative solution-finding, costing, synthesis and analysis of design are
included. Modularization necessary for administering large design exercises and design decision-making
processes, is deliberated. Concepts of value engineering, Engineering ethics, and Design for X, along with
case studies, are also incorporated.
This course is designed to impart the knowledge required to develop a new product – understand the
opportunity, develop a concept, and implement a concept. After the successful completion of this course,
students shall be able to understand and use the various processes, tools and techniques required for designing
a product: product specification development; concept generation, concept selection, concept testing and
embodiment; product architecture; industrial design; design for X; analytical and numerical models; physical
prototypes, models and experimentation; environmental, economic and social issues in product development;
patents and intellectual properties.

title: DYNAMICS & VIBRATION
description:
Steady and transient Vibration of single and multi degree freedom systems. Systems with distributed
mass and elasticity. Non-linear and self-excited vibrations, structural damping, Random vibrations,
vibration analysis, vibration control - reduction, isolation and vibration absorbers.
No Course Objectives

is an efficient way of deriving equations of motion. This also is a prerequisite for later content of
the course.
CO2 Present a matrix approach to the vibration of multi degree of freedom systems, placing emphasis on
modal analysis. To cover methods suited for automatic computation for obtaining the system
response.
CO3 Setting-up initial-boundary value problems for some important and fundamental structural
members viz. Bars, strings, rods and beams. Analytical and approximate solutions to these
problems for various loading and boundary conditions are discussed and analyzed.
CO4 Learn to use finite element methods for the analysis of the vibrations of structures.

title: Electrical Machines
description:
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion;
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations,
classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors;
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation.
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer,
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better
understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description:
Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics
(Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge
carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions,
forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors
(JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor
devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of
semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its
application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later
like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic
diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to
CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.
CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.
CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.
CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.

CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.

title: Communication Systems
description:
Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency
conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital
systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital
communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation
techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization
This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication
system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block
diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which
are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital
communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise.
The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of
random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR
and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon
theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication
systems using MATLAB and Python software.
The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog
and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced
level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on
communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of
Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

title: Electromagnetic Fields and Microwave Engineering
description:
Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission
Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric
Waveguides; Cavity resonator, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices
(Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; Microwave
Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types.
This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and
microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission
line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric
structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching
techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators,
amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip
students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply
high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications.
learning_outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to analyze electromagnetic wave propagation using Maxwell’s equations, understand wave behavior at interfaces, and design transmission lines with impedance matching using the Smith Chart. They will gain proficiency in characterizing waveguides, cavity resonators, and microwave devices, as well as interpreting S- parameters for network analysis. Students will also learn measurement techniques, explore microwave sources and amplifiers, and evaluate various antenna types and their radiation characteristics for practical applications.

title: PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
description:
This course is a foundation course for the students entering into the discipline of Economics & Finance.
This introductory course teaches the basic concepts related to the economic system that are listed as
follows: Introduction to Economics (Microeconomics) & Economic Problems; Demand, Supply, &
Elasticity; Household Behavior and Consumer choice; The Production Process; Costs and Output
Decisions; Demand for Production Inputs; Market Imperfections: Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic
Competition; Introduction to Macroeconomics and the Problems; Measurement of National Income &
Output; Money Supply and the Banking System
The main objective is to introduce the fundamental concepts and tools necessary to acquire an
understanding of economic decision making of market participants such as Individual households, firms,
and the government. The course covers two major areas of economics namely Microeconomics and

title: Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting
description:
Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not
only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also
communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize
transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails
two important and interrelated aspects, i.e.,
a. Recording transactions, and
b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc.
Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing
financial statements.
The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules
of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial
balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership,
credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the
statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold,
recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets.
This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students
and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from
Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and
financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced
courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent
semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance.
Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the
field of finance.
The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by
businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This
reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course
accomplishes enables participants in learning:
a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical
to day-to-day functioning of the company.
b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into
meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement
of income etc.
c. the key components that form part of these financial statements.
d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey
about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able to
Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions.
Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement.
Identify the financial position and performance of the companies.
Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS
description:
The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for
decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into
two parts: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and
describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data
describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regression analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses,
and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical
Inference: Introduction to Probability and its distributions, sampling distributions, theory of estimation, Tests of
Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non-Parametric); and Mathematical Methods include Concepts from Linear
Algebra & their Applications (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory); Concepts from Calculus and their
applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications.
The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of
the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these
fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic
system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve
graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course
uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for
students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Apply appropriate methods for data collection, sampling, organization, and descriptive analysis, using graphical and numerical techniques to summarize and interpret statistical data. CLO2. Analyze relationships among economic and business variables using correlation and regression techniques, and construct and interpret index numbers for relevant applications. CLO3. Analyze time-series data by identifying its components, understanding the underlying data-generating process, and assessing stationarity. CLO4. Apply probability concepts and statistical inference techniques, including probability and sampling distributions, estimation, and parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, to draw valid conclusions from data. CLO5. Apply mathematical methods to economic problems, using concepts from linear algebra, input-output analysis, game theory, calculus, and optimization to formulate and solve economic decision problems.

title: ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS
description:
Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its
population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does
not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business
within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions,
and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business
enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The
economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So,
the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with
its environment would generally determine its success or failure.
The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators,
economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate
changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business
decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of
this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of
individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context.

title: INTERNATIONAL ECONOMICS
description:
This course develops a systematic exposition of both classical and modern theories of international trade in
goods and services that try to explain the composition, direction, and consequences of international trade, and
the determinants and effects of trade policy. The course will look critically at the welfare and profit
implications of trade policy deviations from free trade. It then builds on the models of open economy
macroeconomics.
 To understand the effects of international trade on individuals and businesses
 To understand the effects of changes in trade policies on trade
 To apply macroeconomic models to understand the international economy.
 To focus on the interrelationships among aggregate economic variables such as GDP,
unemployment rates, inflation rates, trade balances, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.
 To focus on the significance of trade imbalances, the determinants of exchange rates, and the
aggregate effects of government monetary and fiscal policies.

title: ISSUES IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
description:
This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy
debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world
applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass
structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental
sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories
and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long-
run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis
on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including
poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education,
health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental
degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies,
students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and
evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.
The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical,
and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate
contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional,
technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It
emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty
reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability.
Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of
development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and
sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse,
including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender
equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing
students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators,
evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real-
world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies
and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts.

Explain and critically evaluate the major theories, concepts, and contemporary issues in development economics, including economic growth, structural transformation, poverty, inequality, employment, human development, institutional change, globalization, environmental sustainability, and emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and digital transformation. CLO2. Apply appropriate analytical, quantitative, and empirical tools to interpret development indicators, assess the effectiveness of development policies and programmes, and evaluate alternative strategies for promoting sustainable, inclusive, and equitable economic development at national and international levels. CLO3. Critically analyze contemporary development challenges using theoretical and empirical evidence, formulate evidence-based policy recommendations, and undertake independent research on key issues affecting developing economies, with particular reference to India and other emerging economies.

title: Financial Management
description:
Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as
a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial
decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate
level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic
experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of
Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by
the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm.
In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements,
the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of
firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other
are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available
to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with
uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of
fault lines in the financial markets.
To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress
suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More
importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite
managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm
must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment,
investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing
policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy.
The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital,
investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and
sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.
1
This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance
concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to:
a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations,
b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and
c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices.
Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing,
investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants
to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability.
Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong
foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities,
statistics, and MS-Excel.

title: Derivatives & Risk Management
description:
The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type
of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course
provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most
common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the
course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative
instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk.
No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp
over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value
of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield
and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and
convexity in mitigating interest rate risks.
The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about
common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure
by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to
creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level
courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course
concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as
forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist
students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk
Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA).

title: BUSINESS ANALYSIS AND VALUATION
description:
This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through
financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along
with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior
knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements,
assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment
banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking
in business valuation and decision-making.
The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis.
Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing
the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive
impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external
to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence,
asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal
objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and
analytical framework to answer this question.
The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall
enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation
approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types
of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the
financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality.
Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking,
corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to
be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing
their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their
investors.

earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom
discussions.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
description:
Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold.
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental,
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy,
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation
forms a major component of this course.
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes:
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.
The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to:
• Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics.
• Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance
management.
• Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation.
• Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques.
• Technical analysis.
• Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio.

Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests.
Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return.
Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance.
Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed.
Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change.

title: FINANCIAL ENGINEERING
description:
The Financial Engineering Concentration encompasses the design, analysis, and construction of financial
contracts to meet the needs of enterprises. It involves developing and creatively applying financial theory and
financial instruments to structure solutions to complex financial problems and exploit financial opportunities.
The objective of the course is to provide a preliminary understanding of financial engineering tools and
techniques in the present market environment, such as applications of futures and options for hedging, asset
price dynamics, and the use of simulation in decision-making. Financial Engineering is a multidisciplinary
field involving financial theory, the methods of engineering, the tools of mathematics, and the practice of
programming. The course on financial engineering would enable students to respond to the professional
requirements particularly related to investment banking, financial management, treasury operations, asset
management, risk management, consulting and capital markets, etc.

title: New Venture Creation
description:
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are
expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business
model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture.
In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases
of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3)
go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on
customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive
analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest-
lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running
Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide
them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be
invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the
completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.
NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence,
the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC
helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform
an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a
reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific
market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build
an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win
customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key
external partners?

title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INSURANCE
description:
Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention,
risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging;
life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation

 Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.
 Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization

description:
Principles of sample collection and data analysis/interpretation, Gravimetric methods,
titrimetric methods, electrochemical methods, Spectrometric method of analysis, Chromatographic method of
analysis, sampling techniques for air and water pollution, Biological methods of analysis, Interpretation of
data in environmental monitoring.
The course introduces methodology of sample collection (sampling

conventional (for example gravimetric, titrimetric) and advanced methods (for example electrochemical,
spectrophotometric, chromatographic). The course will also guide students, to apply concepts for
environmental monitoring.

title: Urban Water Management
description:
Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the
planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing
pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the
complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and
environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban
development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory
challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary
topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water
quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater
modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory
and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset
management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of
urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares
students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors
concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.
The course aims to equip students with comprehensive
knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and
sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and
urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban
design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning,
and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding
emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for
decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure,
the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its
components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure
assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems;
(4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5)
To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and
climate adaptation strategies.
learning_outcomes: Understand and assess the urban water cycle and system interactions under climate change and urbanization.
Demonstrate practical knowledge in water quality, stormwater, and sanitation system design and management.
Use hydroinformatics and modeling tools for flood forecasting and system performance evaluation.
Integrate water-sensitive urban design principles and sustainability indicators in planning.
topics: Module 1: Introduction to Urban Water Systems
Module 2: Urban Water Supply and Sanitation
Module 3: Stormwater and Groundwater Management
Module 4: Sustainable Design and Decision Tools
textbooks: Water Supply Engineering, S. K. Garg (18th ed.), Khanna Publishers.
Water Supply and Sanitary Engineering, G. S. Birdie & J. S. Birdie (8th ed.), Dhanpat Rai Publishing Company, New Delhi.

[Method of conduct of the course]: The course will be conducted through a combination of interactive lectures, software-based tutorials, case study discussions, and hands-on modeling sessions. Emphasis will be placed on blending theoretical foundations with practical applications to address real-world urban water challenges. Students will engage in
Lectures using multimedia tools to explain concepts related to the urban water cycle, supply, drainage, and quality management
Software training modules on stormwater modeling, urban flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics using tools such as SWMM, EPANET, HEC-RAS, and QGIS.
Group assignments involving real-world problem-solving, such as urban flood mitigation planning or rainwater harvesting assessment.
Guest lectures or webinars by industry/academia/government experts and municipal engineers to expose students to professional practices.
If possible, field visits (where feasible) to treatment plants, stormwater systems, or urban recharge zones for experiential learning.
Project-based evaluations including presentations, technical reports, and modeling outputs aligned with industry standards.
references: STORMWATER DRAINAGE MANUAL Planning, Design and Management, Drainage services department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Peavy, H. S., Rowe, D. R., & Tchobanoglous, G. (1985). Environmental Engineering. McGraw Hill Education (India Edition, 2013).
Garg, S. K. (2010). Sewage Disposal and Air Pollution Engineering: Environmental Engineering (Vol. 2). Khanna Publishers, Delhi.

title: ELECTRICAL SCIENCES
description:
Course covers basic passive circuit elements, dependent and
independent sources, network theorems, circuit analysis techniques, and
response of first and second order circuits. Introduction to three - phase circuits,
magnetic circuits, transformers, basics of rotating machines. Semiconductors -
operation of diodes, zener diodes, bipolar junction transistors and field effect
transistors. Biasing techniques and applications of diodes and transistors.
Introduction to operational amplifiers and applications. Introduction to Digital
Electronics
The primary objective of this course is to teach the principles
of three different aspects of electrical sciences: (1) Circuits Analysis (2) Electronic
Devices and (3) Electromagnetics, to the students of mixed disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Students will learn the circuit analysis (voltage, current and power calculation) techniques for DC and AC (1-pahse and 3-phase) circuits using Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL), Kirchhoff’s voltage, law (KVL), Ohms law, Nodal analysis, Mesh analysis, Network theorems (Thevenin’s theorem, Norton’s theorem, Maximum power transfer theorem, Superposition theorem) etc.
Students will able to perform circuit analysis on electronic circuit consisting of elements such as diode, transistor (BJT, JFET, MOSFET), OPAMP and digital logic.
Students will learn construction and operation electromagnetic devices such as transformer and machines
topics: Voltage and current sources, basic circuit components, Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL), Kirchhoff’s voltage, law (KVL), Instantaneous power, Inductors, Capacitors
Independent and dependent sources, Source transformation
Nodal analysis, Mesh analysis
Network theorems (Thevenin’s theorem, Norton’s theorem, Maximum power transfer theorem, Superposition theorem)
Transient response of first and second order circuits (natural and forced response)
Time-domain analysis, Phasor representation of alternating quantities, j operator and Phasor algebra, Frequency-domain analysis
AC power, Average power, apparent power and complex power, Power factor corrections
Three phase circuits (Y and Δ connections)
Filters - Low Pass, High Pass and Band Pass), Resonance and Quality factor
Basics of PN junction, Junction diode, Ideal diode, Applications in rectifier and clipper
textbooks: Leonard S. Bobrow and Navneet Gupta, Foundations of Electrical Engineering, Oxford University Press, Asian Edition, 2015
references: Allan R Hambley, Electrical Engineering: Principles and Applications; 7th Edition (global edition), Pearson education limited, 2019.

title: Electrical Machines
description:
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion;
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations,
classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors;
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation.
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer,
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better
understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description:
Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics
(Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge
carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions,
forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors
(JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor
devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of
semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its
application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later
like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic
diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to
CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.
CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.
CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.
CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.

CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.
topics: Brief history, recent trends and crystal lattices
Semiconductor models Charge carriers, effective mass.
Statistics of donors and acceptors, Space charge neutrality.
Conductivity and mobility, Hall effect
Optical absorption, excess carrier, Quasi- Fermi level
Diffusion of carriers, built-in field, continuity equation
Equilibrium conditions, Fermi levels, Poisson’s Equation, Depletion layer model.
Carrier injection, diode equation, and I-V characteristics, biasing, Reverse-bias breakdown
Capacitance of p-n junctions, Transient Analysis, non-ideal behavior.
Band-diagram of MS junction, Schottky diodes, & Ohmic contacts
Junction Field Effect Transistors (JFETs), MESFET, HEMT & MISFET
MOS structure, MOS Transistors, I-V characteristics and secondary effects
BJT operations, terminal current, Gummel plot, small-signal model, charge control model
Photodiodes, Solar cells, and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and their advanced version

sequential behavior

title: Communication Systems
description:
Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency
conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital
systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital
communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation
techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization
This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication
system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block
diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which
are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital
communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise.
The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of
random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR
and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon
theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication
systems using MATLAB and Python software.
The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog
and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced
level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on
communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of
Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

channel models; signal transmission over

distortion; random variables and random

and power spectral density; Gaussian processes;

figure.

title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
description:
This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using
CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level
building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area-
efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and
fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including
logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.
⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design
of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic.
⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design.
⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential.
⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference
Circuit.
⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs.
⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout.
⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments.
⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels
of design abstraction.
1
topics: Introduction to VLSI Design Methodologies
MOS Fabrication Process & technology, Circuit Layout & Design Rules, Layout, scaling techniques
MOS inverter- D.C and switching characteristics

title: FPGA BASED SYSTEM DESIGN
description:
Digital system design options and trade-offs, design methodology and technology overview,
Programmable Logic Devices, SPLDs, CPLDs, and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs); FPGA
architectural options, granularity of function and wiring resources, coarse vs. fine-grained, vendor-specific
issues (emphasis on Xilinx and Altera), Logic fabric, Look-up tables, block BRAMs, DSP slices etc.,
timing models, power dissipation, Input and Output cell characteristics, clock input, Timing, Power
dissipation, Programmable interconnect, Hardware Description Languages, FPGA system design tools,
synthesis, and implementation, design verification and debugging, FPGA based design studies, interfacing
with input-output devices and data converters.
This course aims to upskill the students with the following topics:
 Build a strong foundation in FPGA architecture, technologies, and design methodologies.
 Develop proficiency in HDL-based design for creating complex digital systems.
 Explore the full FPGA design flow—from concept to implementation and debugging.
 Integrate embedded processors, IP cores, and DSP functions into FPGA-based designs.
 Apply knowledge through hands-on labs and projects using modern FPGA platforms.
learning_outcomes: Students will gain a comprehensive understanding of FPGA architecture and design flow, develop proficiency in HDL-based digital design, and learn to integrate digital system, embedded processors, and IP cores. They will also acquire hands-on experience with modern FPGA tools and platforms to implement, debug, and optimize complex digital systems.
topics: Digital System design options and trade-offs
SPLDs, CPLDs and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)
Coarse vs fine-grained architectures, SRAM Based- FPGAs, Permanently Programmable FPGAs, Programmable I/O, Look-up tables, block BRAMs, DSP slices etc. SoC FPGAs,
Case Studies (Xilinx, Altera, Microsemi, etc.)
FPGA-based system design methodology - Simulation, synthesis and design implementation - Debugging and verification
Area, speed and power-aware design, Timing models, power analysis and clocking
Signal or image processing applications, interfacing with input-output devices and data converters.

title: Data Communications and Networks
description:
Communication Concepts; Data and Voice Communications; Hardware Systems and
Configurations; Network Topologies and Design Aspects; Protocols; Networking Local Area Networks;
Network Security and Management; Emerging Trends in Communications.
A communication network is one of the fastest-growing areas
today. The course introduces the concepts and mechanisms underlying the modern telecommunication
systems and networks. The course is designed in such a way that the course is accessible to students without
any special technical background in this area. The OSI model is used as a framework to introduce different
protocols and standards. The course will prepare the student for advanced courses in the areas of
telecommunication switching systems, computer networks, internetworking, etc.

title: Internet of Things
description:
Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points,
Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies.
This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE),
B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL).
This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things
(IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor
technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor
networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to
enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions.
Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and
networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand
the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to
how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart
farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT
systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this
course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world
problems.
topics: Introduction to IoT & Cyber-Physical Systems, IoT applications - an overview, Different Levels of IoT Applications: Level 1 - 6 with examples, IoT Design Methodology & Life Cycle, Introduction to IoT Physical End Points & Platforms, IoT System Design Examples (for applications like fitness tracker, smart parking etc.). Learning these concepts to understand how end to end IoT applications work.

Introduction to sensors for IoT application development, Data Acquisition, Signal Conditioning and Processing, Multi Sensor fusion for IoT, Advanced sensing techniques (e.g. BCI/HCI), Actuators and Controllers for IoT. Understand their working and how to apply them to develop novel technology solutions

Introduction to Arduino microcontroller & NodeMCU for IoT applications, Programming with Arduino & NodeMCU and prototype development (e.g. for smart farming, smart city applications etc.), Introduction to Raspberry Pi, Programming Raspberry Pi (Python), Rest API based hands on. Getting a hands on experience in these tools to enhance skill set.

Understanding wireless sensor networks: Introduction, Deployment, Localization, Routing, MAC, Time synchronization and Multi-sensor-fusion for WSN. Blockchain fundamentals and it’s applications in IoT
Get an overview of Ad Hoc networks (MANET, VANET, FANET), Industrial IoT Networks, Common network standards (Bluetooth, NFC, LORA) etc, COAP and MQTT (including lab/ hands-on)

Understanding data management for IoT, Advanced optimization for processing sensor data, Machine learning for IoT data analytics, Introduction to IoT Cloud Services, Case studies of Cloud services for IoT and learning how to use them.
Get an overview of cyber-attacks on IoT- Case study and understand security solutions for IoT: hardware/software

(R2) "The Internet of Things: Enabling Technologies, Platforms, and Use Cases", by Pethuru Raj and Anupama C. Raman (CRC Press), 2017. (R3) "Internet of Things: A Hands-on Approach", by Arshdeep Bahga and Vijay Madisetti (Universities Press), 2014. (R4) “Internet of Things” by Raj Kamal (Mc Graw Hill), 2017. 1

title: Modern Control Systems
description:
Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even
some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so-
called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course
on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state
variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of
nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and
also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments
drawn from various engineering domains.
topics: L1: Overview of the course and how it takes the previous course forward
L2-3: Review of state space modelling; State space and transfer function inter-conversion
L4-6: Similarity transformation; Controllable, observable, diagonal and Jordan canonical forms (graphical and analytical methods)
L7-8: Solution of state equation; Computation of state transition matrix by Laplace transform and Cayley-Hamilton methods
L9: Discretization of continuous time state space model by step and impulse invariance methods
L10-11: BIBO versus asymptotic stability; Controllability, observability, stabilizability, detectability
L12-13: Introduction to model order reduction techniques: state space/modal/balanced truncation/residualization
L14-15: Introduction to nonlinear systems: representations, examples; Hard nonlinearities
L16-17: Jacobian linearization; Peculiarities of nonlinear systems; Introduction to bifurcation and chaos
L18-19: Analysis of nonlinear systems: describing function method
L20: Analysis of nonlinear systems: phase plane method
L21-22: Stability analysis of nonlinear systems: Lyapunov’s indirect and direct methods and LaSalle’s invariance principle
L23-24: Linear state feedback control and its properties; State feedback with integral action
L25-26: Nonlinear state feedback control: sliding mode control algorithm
L27-29: Basics of calculus of variations
L30-32: Optimal linear state feedback: Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) and its properties
L33-34: Full order state observer; Disturbance observer
L35: Observer based state feedback control; Separation principle
L36: Nonlinear state observer; sliding mode observer
L37: Stochastic processes; Stationarity and ergodicity; White noise
L38-40: Stochastic state estimation – discrete time Kalman filter
L41: Kalman-Bucy filter; Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control
L42: Nonlinear stochastic state observer -Extended Kalman Filter; Concluding comments on the course

title: Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics
description:
Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and
applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and
coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave
systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul
communications; fiber optic networks.
In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These
developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information
technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging
technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers,
sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for
communication applications.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to
CLO1: Basic configuration of a fiber-optic system, Merits of Fiber Optic system, Ray propagation through different types of optical fibers and Estimation of different parameters of optical fibers.

CLO2: Familiarization with the background for learning of electromagnetic wave propagation in medium, Modal analysis of planar optical wave guides, Modal analysis of cylindrical optical waveguide and characterization of optical fibers.
CLO3: Concept of semi-conductor p-n junction towards design LED, LED designs characterization and ILD condition for laser action, Optical transmitter design and applications
CLO4: Basic principle of opto-electronic detection, Types of photodiodes, Structures of photodetectors and optical receivers, Operation of Optical Amplifiers, Optical modulators and demodulators.

CLO5: Optical Communication system design for single wavelength and multi wavelength systems. Design of fiber optic sensors, Extrinsic and Intrinsic Sensors Distinct Types of Sensors and their Industrial Applications
topics: A generalized configuration of a fiber optic system, Advantages, Role of fiber optic systems, optical spectrum.

Review of fundamental laws of optics, Ray propagation in step index fibers, Ray propagation in graded index fibers, Effect of material dispersion, Effect of multipath- dispersion and combined effect, Numerical problems

Maxwell's equations, Solution in an inhomogeneous medium, Planar optical waveguide, TE modes of a symmetric step index planar waveguide, Power distribution and confinement factor, Wave propagation in an ideal SI fiber, Modal power distribution in SI fibers, Wave propagation in GI fiber

Propagation through Single mode fibers, Single mode fibers, Fabrication of low loss optical fibers, Design aspects of optical fiber cables and connections, Evaluating the performance of optical fibers

Fundamental aspects of optoelectronic sources, Principle of operation of light emitting diodes(LED), Design aspects of LED, Principles of injection laser diode (ILD), Design aspects of ILD and source fiber coupling.
textbooks: Khare, R.P.: “Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics” Oxford University Press (2004)
references: Keiser, G., "Optical Fiber Communications", 5/e, McGraw Hill, 2013

title: Digital Image Processing
description:
This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an
introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations,
which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image
processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition.
Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer
algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information,
or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for
better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage
and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and
object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote
sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday
technology.

title: Semiconductor Fabrication Technology
description:
The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor
fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC),
i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such
as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and
lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be
discussed in detail.
This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to
discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical
engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges
across various disciplines.

Semiconductor Fabrication: Complete Process Flow
Crystal structures, defects, directions, planes
Bulk single crystal growth to Wafer preparation, dopant distribution
Semiconductor Manufacturing
Oxidation and Si/SiO interface 2

Thin Film Deposition

title: Satellite Communications
description:
Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO,
MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like
INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog
and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple
access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of
INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and
future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.
This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or-
bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link-
budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through
in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed-
assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access
schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the
course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite
links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine
satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.
learning_outcomes: Some of the key learning outcomes are stated below. CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts, historical evolution, segments, and subsystems of satellite communication systems. CLO2. Analyze radio-wave propagation effects and orbital mechanics (LEO/MEO/GEO) and their influence on system and link design. CLO3. Design and evaluate satellite RF uplink/downlink link budgets, including noise and intermodulation considerations, using hand calculations and simulation tools. 1 CLO4. Apply and compare digital modulation, coding, and multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) for satellite systems. CLO5. Identify and evaluate VSAT, mobile satellite links, understand GPS/GNSS system ar- chitectures and their performance limitations CLO6. To understand, appreciate and analyze recent trends in satellite communications such as next generation non-terrestrial network/space-air-ground integrated network.

title: Embedded System Design
description:
Introduction to Embedded System Design, Embedded System Design Example,
Modelling an embedded System, Design using ARM Processors - Core v7 , Cortex M, Buses, I/O interface -
Basic, Communication and Advance, Embedded Software Design, Embedded Software: Tasks, Task
Management RTS, Advanced Embedded System Design Concepts such as Power management, Fault Tolerant
System Design, Basics of H/W - S/W codesign, SoC based design etc, Memory Types, Cache, MMU/MPU
basics, On-chip/off-chip bus architectures, Hardware Accelerators.
The course intends to introduce the various components of an embedded system and embedded system design
considerations. The course also deals with processor architectures, on-chip & off- chip protocols,
programming techniques, performance analysis, and optimization techniques used in embedded system
development. This course introduces the students to standard Embedded System Development tools and gives
hands-on experience in developing various embedded applications.
