title: Machine Learning for Electronics Engineers
description:
The rise of machine learning (ML) has introduced many opportunities in the design of
electronic systems. This course provides a requisite conceptual foundation of ML and
contextual application of ML techniques for improving the performance of electronic systems.
The course introduces the major approaches to ML such as supervised, unsupervised, semi-
supervised, and reinforcement learning. The course also lays emphasis on various deep learning
techniques and their application to various types of electronic systems/sub-systems (e.g.
control-dominated systems, NLP systems, vision-based systems, communication systems,
embedded systems, IoTs). Additionally, the course covers advance topics in ML such as multi-
modal, multi-task learning as well as transfer learning. The course discusses the challenges in
implementation of ML techniques, complexity analysis of the ML architectures for hardware
implementation, efficient architectures, and various topologies used for implementation.
learning_outcomes: Students should be able to apply ML techniques to model, design, validate, and optimize embedded electronic systems in their area of interest.
Develop the skills and practical exposure in modeling, developing, and debugging ML- based systems.
Develop the foundation required to explore advanced topics of research in ML.

title: Real-Time Embedded Systems
description:
This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing
a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will
also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software
design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation
techniques for these systems.
Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a
job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common
every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and
design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced
concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the
Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management
algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc.
topics: Introduction and Basic Real-Time Concepts
Real-Time Scheduling algorithms
Resource Access Protocols
Real-Time Operating Systems
Inter-task Communication and Synchronization
Memory Management and File systems
Scheduling algorithms for multi-processors
Real-Time specification and Design Technique
Hardware Issues
Software Issues
Fault tolerance and Reliability

title: Signal Theory and Optimization
description:
Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of
random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes;
stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra:
vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition;
matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections
in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and
constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and
numerical optimization techniques.
The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The
first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties,
limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and
random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order
statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical
inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables.
The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as
stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth
module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence
and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for
example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen
value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and
norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an
introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization,
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers,
numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques.
The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random
signals and related theory, ii) linear algebra, matrices iii) optimization techniques and their uses in
communications and signal processing.
learning_outcomes: At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided next generation communication networks.
topics: Preliminaries: classification, definitions, limitations and applications of various signals
Axiomatic probability, various concepts and simple rules/theorems

Random variables: continuous (CRV), discrete (DRV), and mixed (MRV), cumulative distribution function (CDF), probability density function (PDF), probability mass function (PMF), Moment generating function (MGF) &
Characteristic function, properties, Useful inequalities, Central limit theorem, applications, examples
Random variables (Contd.,): transformation of random variables, generation and simulation of random variables, simulation of random variables, multiple random variables
Stochastic processes: Specifying random process, types of random process, wide sense stationarity (WSS), ergodicity, transmission of random process, examples, applications
Linear algebra and matrices
Foundations for optimization (concepts, tools)
Convex and non-convex optimization: key techniques, limitations and few applications
textbooks: A. Papoulis and S. U. Pillai, Probability, Random Variables and Stochastic Processes, 4th ed., McGraw- Hill Education, 2002.
G. Strang, Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 4th ed., Cengage Learning, 2007.
Boyd and L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Cambridge University Press, 2004.
references: Introduction to probability, D. P. Bertsekas, J. N. Tsitsiklis, second edition, Athena scientific, 2008.
Discrete stochastic processes by R. G. Gallager, Springer, 1996.
Random processes for engineers, Bruce Hajek, Illinois, 2014.
Intuitive probability and random processes using MATLAB, S. M. Kay, Springer, 2006.
Todd K. Moon and Wynn C. Stirling, Mathematical Methods and Algorithms for Signal Processing, Prentice Hall, 1999.

title: Modelling and Analysis of Electrical Machines
description:
Review of Rotating Electrical Machines, Element of Generalized Theory of Rotating
Electrical Machines, Linear transformation and Reference-frame Theory, DC Machines, Three-phase
Synchronous Machines, Three-phase Induction Machines, Special Machines, Introduction to motor
parameters estimation and model generation using MATLAB
The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state,
transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to
familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding
on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through
generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and
applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware
setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges
of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for
example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive
maintenance, and advanced control. The prerequisite of this course is, to have a basic understanding
of electrical circuits, electrical machines and control systems; mainly modelling of physical
systems.
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to,
Develop the model of electrical machines using actual machine variables and parameters.
Develop generalized theory (unified approach) based model of electrical machines.
Apply different transformations using reference frame theory to simplify machine modelling.
Develop the block-diagram of electrical machines using their dynamic model.

Develop and visualize machine-model using software such as MATLAB-Simulink, and use the model for analysis and control-loop design for hardware testing and implementation using real-time simulators such as TMS320F28379d.
topics: ● Recap of electrical machines and basic principles of analysis ● Magnetically coupled circuits ● Machine windings and air-gap MMF ● Winding inductance and voltage equations
● Essentials of rotating machines ● Sign-conventions ● Basic two-pole machine ● Per unit system ● Kron’s primitive machine ● Analysis of electrical machines
● Invariance of power ● Transformations in Electrical Machines ● Commonly used reference frame and transformation between them.
● Conventional modelling using system variables, state equations, transfer functions, block-diagram
● Generalized theory based modelling of separately excited dc generator and motor, series and shunt motor ● Linearization techniques

● Machine parameters, voltage/torque equations, and their reference frame variables ● Reactance and time constants ● Steady-state, Short-circuit, transients and dynamic analysis ● Dynamic performance at torque change and three-phase fault
● Equivalent circuit, Voltage and torque equations, ● Transformation, reference frame variables ● Steady-state analysis ● Dynamic performance analysis at torque change and three-phase fault
● Trapezoidal and sinusoidal BLDC ● Basics of VRM and PMSM ● Model of PMSM and BLDC ● Basics of VSI drives steady-state and average values modelling and analysis
references: Krishnan, R., Electric Motor Drives: Modeling, Analysis, and Control. Prentice Hall, 2024
Ong, C. M., Dynamic Simulation of Electric Machinery: Using MATLAB/SIMULINK. Prentice Hall, 1998.
Sang-Hoon Kim, Electric Motor Control: DC, AC, and BLDC Motors, Elsevier Science.

title: Fundamentals of Optoelectronics
description:
This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course
begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p-n junction
configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated
emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic
devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical
amplifiers, and laser diodes. Array detectors, including complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor
(CMOS) and charge-coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic
specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging
with array detectors, and LED displays.
• Understand the fundamental solid-state physics governing light-matter interactions in
semiconductor materials.
• Analyze the operation, design parameters, and performance metrics of modern
optoelectronic emitters (LEDs, Lasers) and detectors (Photodiodes, Solar Cells).
• Evaluate the engineering principles behind advanced display architectures, flexible
electronics, and matrix-based image sensors.
• Apply theoretical knowledge through hands-on computational modeling and simulation of
optoelectronic device behavior.
topics: Review of semiconductor concepts, carrier transport, and energy bands. Direct vs. Indirect bandgap semiconductors E-k diagrams). P-n junction principles, heterojunctions, and energy band diagrams under bias.

Core principles of electroluminescence, efficiencies, and output spectrum. High-intensity quantum well LEDs and modern materials. White LEDs, phosphors, and driver electronics, Organic LEDs (OLEDs), Quantum Dot LEDs (QLEDs)

Laser oscillations: threshold gain coefficient and gain bandwidth. Steady-state semiconductor rate equations. Single-frequency lasers and Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting Lasers (VCSELs). Semiconductor Optical Amplifiers (SOAs).
Flexible silicon and SoI wafers, Techniques for fabricating flexible Si- substrates, Thin Film Transistors (TFTs), TFT-LCD Displays

Principles of the p-n junction, p-i-n, and Avalanche Photodiodes (APDs). Schottky junction and photoconductive detectors. Photovoltaic devices and solar cell efficiencies. Noise parameters in photodetection.
Charge-Coupled Devices (CCDs). Active Matrix Arrays and Complementary Metal-Oxide- Semiconductor (CMOS) image sensors.
Simulation of Optoelectronic devices.
textbooks: Optoelectronics and Photonics: Principles and Practices (2nd Edition) by S.O. Kasap.
references: Solid State Electronic Devices by Ben Streetman & Sanjay Banerjee.
Semiconductor Optoelectronic Devices by Pallab Bhattacharya.

description:
This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters
with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is

title: Power Quality
description:
This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of
prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications
covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics
and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also
covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both
passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active
power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich
students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.
A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically
covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations,
harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries.
The objectives of this course are designed to help students to:
a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact.
b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems.
c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and
load voltage regulation
d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination.
e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable
energy systems.
Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

L6-L9

title: NANO-ELECTRONICS AND NANO-PHOTONICS TECHNOLOGY
description:
Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and
Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain
engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and
non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on
nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and
its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology.
This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast
moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication
systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as
limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover,
integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects
like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors,
quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will
be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic
concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for
engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/
simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

title: Advanced Wireless Communications
description:
Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for
communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless
networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying
and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to
potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in
wireless communications.
a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose
them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next-
generation wireless networks.
b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus
on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks.
c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless
communications.
d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D
communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to
name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the trade-offs in system design parameters (e.g., power, bandwidth, latency, mobility) in the context of modern wireless networks.
Design and evaluate advanced modulation, coding, and diversity techniques for improving link reliability and spectral efficiency in various wireless environments.
Analyze complex wireless channel models (e.g., time-varying fading, spatially correlated MIMO channels) and assess their implications on communication system performance.
topics: Evolution and journey of wireless technologies to 5G and beyond 5G 5G networks: 5G NR characteristics, architecture, performance metrics, key technologies, standardization activities, and introduction to 6G Spectrum and regulations- spectrum challenges in 5G and beyond 5G-mmWave and THz frequency band for wireless communications

Signal Theory- Introduction Characteristic function, PDF, CDF, MGF, Moments of random variables-discrete and continuous random variables Gaussian random variable, complex Gaussian, Rayleigh, Rician, Chi-square, Gamma, exponential, and Nakagami-m distributions Stochastic Processes-White and Gaussian A review of matrix theory for applications to the wireless network design

title: Advanced Digital Communication
description:
Introduction to digital communication systems; signal characterization and
representation of bandpass and low-pass signals; signal space analysis; fundamentals of source coding and entropy;
digital modulation techniques and constellation design; optimum receivers for additive white Gaussian noise
channels; maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection; symbol error probability
analysis; non-coherent detection methods; carrier and symbol synchronization techniques; communication over
band-limited channels; ISI, Nyquist criteria, and signal waveform design, equalization; multicarrier modulation
systems, effects of intercarrier interference (ICI) and carrier frequency offset (CFO); channel capacity limits and
fundamentals of channel coding.
1. To provide fundamental knowledge to model, design, and analyze advanced digital communication
systems, with applications in both industry and R&D.
2. To reinforce theoretical concepts through practical assignments using MATLAB, Python, and USRP.
3. Requires prior knowledge of Linear Systems, Probability Theory, Stochastic Processes, and basic
Communication Systems.
topics: 1-2: Principles of communication, elements of digital communication system, sources of information, communication channels and their characteristics, modulation process, history of digital communication
3-5: Signal spaces, inner product and orthogonal expansion, Gram Schmitt orthogonalization, bandpass/lowpass signal representation
6-9: Coding of analog sources, Memoryless modulation – PAM, phase modulation, quadrature amplitude modulation, FSK, PPM, bi-orthogonal modulation, simplex signal set; Modulation with memory – CPFSK
10-13: Correlation demodulator, matched filter demodulator, optimum detector, ML detector, MAP detector.
14-20: Error probabilities for band limited signaling, power limited signaling, optimal detection in presence of uncertainty – non coherent detection

title: Modern Control Systems
description:
Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even
some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so-
called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course
on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state
variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of
nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and
also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments
drawn from various engineering domains.
topics: L1: Overview of the course and how it takes the previous course forward
L2-3: Review of state space modelling; State space and transfer function inter-conversion
L4-6: Similarity transformation; Controllable, observable, diagonal and Jordan canonical forms (graphical and analytical methods)
L7-8: Solution of state equation; Computation of state transition matrix by Laplace transform and Cayley-Hamilton methods
L9: Discretization of continuous time state space model by step and impulse invariance methods
L10-11: BIBO versus asymptotic stability; Controllability, observability, stabilizability, detectability
L12-13: Introduction to model order reduction techniques: state space/modal/balanced truncation/residualization
L14-15: Introduction to nonlinear systems: representations, examples; Hard nonlinearities
L16-17: Jacobian linearization; Peculiarities of nonlinear systems; Introduction to bifurcation and chaos
L18-19: Analysis of nonlinear systems: describing function method
L20: Analysis of nonlinear systems: phase plane method
L21-22: Stability analysis of nonlinear systems: Lyapunov’s indirect and direct methods and LaSalle’s invariance principle
L23-24: Linear state feedback control and its properties; State feedback with integral action
L25-26: Nonlinear state feedback control: sliding mode control algorithm
L27-29: Basics of calculus of variations
L30-32: Optimal linear state feedback: Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) and its properties
L33-34: Full order state observer; Disturbance observer
L35: Observer based state feedback control; Separation principle
L36: Nonlinear state observer; sliding mode observer
L37: Stochastic processes; Stationarity and ergodicity; White noise
L38-40: Stochastic state estimation – discrete time Kalman filter
L41: Kalman-Bucy filter; Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control
L42: Nonlinear stochastic state observer -Extended Kalman Filter; Concluding comments on the course

title: Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology
description:
The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally
involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the
atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with
emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced
existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course
will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes
occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an
overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic,
and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will
cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution
control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with
environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern
industrialized ecology.
Learning Objectives
The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and
geosphere. Learning objectives for each of the broad topics as discussed in the course plan has been
described along with – what the learner should be able to do by studying these.

title: Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting
description:
Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not
only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also
communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize
transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails
two important and interrelated aspects, i.e.,
a. Recording transactions, and
b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc.
Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing
financial statements.
The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules
of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial
balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership,
credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the
statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold,
recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets.
This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students
and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from
Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and
financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced
courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent
semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance.
Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the
field of finance.
The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by
businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This
reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course
accomplishes enables participants in learning:
a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical
to day-to-day functioning of the company.
b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into
meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement
of income etc.
c. the key components that form part of these financial statements.
d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey
about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
learning_outcomes: Students who complete this course would be able to
Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions.
Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement.
Identify the financial position and performance of the companies.
Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
description:
Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold.
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental,
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy,
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation
forms a major component of this course.
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes:
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.
The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to:
• Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics.
• Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance
management.
• Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation.
• Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques.
• Technical analysis.
• Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio.

Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the assumptions on which each valuation rests.
Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components, and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return.
Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance.
Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff profile and risk of each strategy employed.
Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change.

title: Financial Management
description:
Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as
a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial
decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate
level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic
experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of
Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by
the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm.
In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements,
the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of
firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other
are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available
to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with
uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of
fault lines in the financial markets.
To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress
suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More
importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite
managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm
must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment,
investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing
policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy.
The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital,
investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and
sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.
1
This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance
concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to:
a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations,
b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and
c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices.
Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing,
investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants
to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability.
Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong
foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities,
statistics, and MS-Excel.

title: Financial Risk Analytics and Management
description:
This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market
volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain
crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial
institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry.
The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk
management roles.
Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and
portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory,
Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive
Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at
Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR
weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the
Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering,
Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk
with Derivatives.
The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk
Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and
objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The
three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions
encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a
detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document.
learning_outcomes: Understand and classify financial risks such as interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk, and portfolio risk in modern financial markets.
Analyze and implement risk measurement tools such as Value at Risk (VaR), Responsive VaR, and backtesting techniques.
Interpret and evaluate regulatory frameworks like Basel norms and its guidelines for capital adequacy and systemic risk control.
Develop risk mitigation strategies using derivatives, including hedging techniques and options Greeks, to manage exposure effectively. 1
topics: L1-L5: Introduction to financial risk; Market, Credit, Liquidity, Operational, Interest Rate, Business, Bankruptcy, Default, Settlement and Systemic Risk; Enterprise Risk; Risk–Return Trade-off; Asset Pricing Models (CAPM, Multifactor Models including Fama–French Models).

L6-12 Functions and workings of financial institutions: banks, hedge funds, mutual funds etc. Risk management practices in FIs. Basel Accord (Basel-I, II, III), Basel III capital structure (CET1, AT1 and Tier II Capital), Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR), Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB), Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), leverage ratio, Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Pillar I, Pillar II and Pillar III requirements, Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP), stress testing and scenario analysis, market-risk reforms under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), and the role of Basel regulations in strengthening the resilience and stability of the global financial system.

L13-16 Probability distributions; Statistical concepts for risk modelling; Time-series properties of financial returns; Stochastic Processes; Geometric Brownian Motion; Itô's Lemma; Black–Scholes–Merton Model; Numerical methods and interpolation techniques; L17-27 Risk modeling – Value at risk, C-VaR, Marginal VaR, Component VaR, Options VaR, Fixed income VaR, Credit VaR, scenarios analysis and stress testing, back testing.

L28-35 Risk management using option Greeks, implied volatility, volatility smile, volatility surface, volatility modeling, VIX modeling and application. L36-40 Risk management of fixed income securities. (Optional)

title: Modern Political Concepts
description:
 Concepts of State, Nation, Rights and Duties, Civil Society, Democracy, Citizenship and Justice.
 Ideologies of Modern Politics: Social Contractualism, Liberalism, Socialism, Communism,
Maoism, Anarchism, Secularism.
 Selected Readings from key texts of leading thinkers in the History of Modern Western Political
Philosophy including Machiavelli’s Prince, Hobbes’ Leviathan, Locke’s Second Treatise of
government, Rousseau’s Discourse on the origin of inequality, Marx and Engels’ Communist
Manifesto.
This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/
Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged
through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political
thought.
This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution
emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical
skills, and the understanding of human diversity.
Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the
conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’
knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the
fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the
alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political
discourses.

title: Environment, Development and Climate Change (EDCC)
description:
This course focuses on the concepts of environment, development, and climate
change in the contemporary world. The nature and causes of environmental problems in developing and
developed countries will be explored. Attention is given to both the causes and solutions of environmental
problems and the role of state and non-state actors interacting at local, national and global scales. The goal
of this course is for the learners to appreciate the people-environment relations and to understand the
anthropocentric dynamics of development and climate change.
The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the
debates and issues relating to sustainable development and climate change, so as to sufficiently challenge
them to come up with practical solutions. The course covers theory and practice at the global and local
levels and examines the contemporary policy and practice regarding environment, development and
climate change.

title: Development Theories
description:
This course focuses on the concept of development, development theories and
practices in the modern world. Interplay between theory and practice and the outcome of this relationship are
also explored in the syllabus. The course provides an overview of development thinking from ‘classical’
development ideas to alternative and post development theories. The course then attempts to critically review
contemporary debates about development, including the link between the current world order and the
Development goals of the developing countries.
The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the
debates and issues relating to development and post development. The course covers development theory
and practice at the global and local levels and examines the practice in contemporary times.

title: Effective Public Speaking
description:
Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose
Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases
of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non- Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for
communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering- Effective
Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion
and Job Interviews
The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident,
ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public
speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate
content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids.
The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea
generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent
thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy,
audience suitability, bias, and ethical use.

Critical Thinking
Combating Nervousness
Using Body and Voice to Communicate
Using Wit and Humor

title: Introduction to Conflict Management
description:
Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of
conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different
approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic
class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of
culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and
organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of
communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict
resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques;
mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles.
To develop the knowledge and professional skills necessary to facilitate resolution of conflicts.
Emphasis would be laid on skills and specific techniques to resolve inter-personal,
organizational and community-based conflicts. At the conclusion of the course, the student will
understand the basic dynamics of conflict, most significant interventions used to manage
conflict, benefits and costs of conflict, recognize his or her preferred style of conflict
management and develop an understanding and appreciation of the conflict management styles
of others.
learning_outcomes: Focus and familiarity with the theories and theorists in the conflict school of thought.
Understanding of the basis of conflict in society from the lens of structures like socio- economic class.
Understanding the debates around conflict from the standpoint of gender.
Understanding conflict from the point of view of culture.
Evaluating shaping of conflict from systems of globalization and ethnocentric tensions.
Understanding conformity theories and their association with conflict.
Understanding the power of communication and the development of self.
Evaluating the power of communication with respect to conflict resolution.
Understanding of negotiation strategies and conflict resolution.
topics: Introduction to Conflict Management: An Overview • Nature and dynamics of conflict • Characteristics of conflict • Special focus on theories of Karl Marx and Max Weber • Reasons and sources of conflict • Value of conflict in social change • The different approaches to addressing and managing conflict.

Conflict analysis and socio- economic class • Conflict analysis through socio- economic class perspective • Why does class matter? • Class-based dimensions of conflict • Discuss the various kinds of conflict emerging out of class.
textbooks: Mayer Bernard (2000). The Dynamics of Conflict Resolution, San Francisco: Wiley Company. Additional readings will be uploaded on Nalanda. Class slides/discussions and lectures are important.

title: Marxian Thought
description:
This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After
beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to
the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and
historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory
of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be
applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that
surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.
Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has
limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern
times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on
that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without
fundamentally exploitative structures.
topics: Why Marxism? An introduction to the many theories and narratives that claim to explain inequality in society. Relevance of Karl Marx in the 21st century.

Dialectics and Historical Materialism Brief overview of the history of class society from a Marxist perspective and the marxist method of analysis. Modes and relations of production transition from primitive to feudal society and then to industrial capitalism.
Marx’s Labour Theory of Value What creates value? Use Value – Exchange Value – Surplus Value Cooperation & development of Machinery General law of capitalist accumulation
Fetishism of the Commodity Alienation Marxist Crisis Theories Tendency for Fall in the Rate of Profit Counteracting Factors
Critique of Neoclassical and Neoliberal Ideology 1. Free trade 2. Capitalist Efficiency 3. Self-Interest 4. Say’s Law 5. Invisible Hand of the Market 6. Rational Consumer 7. Marginal Utility
Imperialism Monopoly Capitalism - Why imperialism survives even after decolonization.
What is Socialism and Communism? Discussion on Violence Socialism Now - Case Study on China
Building Alternatives - Reorganizing work and society

title: TECHNIQUES IN SOCIAL RESEARCH
description:
Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance,
dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and
triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and
postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement,
reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field,
historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection
techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data
analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation,
inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software
applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and
thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping
using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics).
This course seeks to provide knowledge and
skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research
process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and
quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address
fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain
methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake
social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data.
learning_outcomes: CLO1: Explain the philosophical foundations, paradigms, and methodological approaches of social research, and distinguish between qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research designs. CLO2: Design ethically sound social research studies by formulating research problems, conducting literature reviews, selecting appropriate research designs, sampling strategies, and data collection methods. CLO3: Apply principles of measurement, reliability, validity, scale development, and sampling to develop rigorous research instruments for social science investigations. CLO4: Analyze quantitative and qualitative data using appropriate statistical and qualitative analysis techniques, including the use of software such as SPSS, Jamovi, and NVivo. CLO5: Evaluate and interpret findings from diverse research methodologies, including experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, content analysis, and secondary data research, to draw evidence-based conclusions. CLO6: Prepare and communicate research reports that demonstrate ethical research practices, critical interpretation of findings, and effective use of research analytics and visualization tools for scholarly dissemination.

title: Readings from Drama
description:
Drama as a distinct genre; History of drama; Performance and stagecraft; Evolution of drama
from a theocentric to a logocentric plane; Distinct characteristics of Western and non-Western
dramas; Aristotle’s Poetics and the genre of tragedy; Bharat Muni’s Natyashastra and the
idea of comedy; Adaptation of myths as Drama; Modern drama.

title: Cross Cultural Skills
description:
1. Providing insights into intercultural communication with powerful and deeply held views
from multiple cultures.
2. Familiarizing the students how to undertake that critical self-reflection which may lead to
better appreciation of the cultural diversity possessed by communities worldwide.
3. Bringing into the discussions, the experiences of intercultural communication, knowledge
of the field of communication studies and mass communication, and perceptions of
intercultural communication as a woman and as men from diverse ethnic, racial and
cultural backgrounds.
4. Using AI to enhance cross-cultural understanding, communication, and adaptation through
interactive learning and real-world simulations.
learning_outcomes: After doing this course the students will be able to

Understand cross-cultural communication and its different dimensions based on national cultures, as propounded by Geert Hofstede and Edward T. Hall, as well as comparative study of various theories developed later, by researchers like Trompenaars & Hampden-Turner.
Gain a comprehensive understanding of how and why cultural groups differ and the nuances of cross-cultural teams.
Develop sensitivity to cultural variations in thinking, feeling, and behaving and adapting the same for cross-cultural communication effectiveness.
Learn management and interpersonal skills to reckon, predict, and leverage cultural differences.
Develop an appreciation for the global mindset vis-à-vis Indian cultural identity.
Know more about diverse national cultures and countries from class projects and presentations.

Theories of Cultural Dimensions – I

CAGE Framework

title: Introductory Philosophy
description:
An overview of major philosophical traditions from the Western and Indian worlds. The course traces the
nature and purpose of philosophy from classical Greek thought through modern rationalism, empiricism,
and existentialism before turning to the classical Indian schools.
A critical survey of major Western and Indian philosophical viewpoints, from antiquity to contemporary
thought. The course aims to equip students with the tools to critically evaluate philosophical arguments
and to appreciate their relevance to questions of knowledge, ethics, and selfhood in human life.
topics: L 1.1 - 1.3 1.1 The subject matter and act of philosophizing.
1.2 The traditional divisions of the discipline - Philosophy 1.3. Relation between philosophy, science, and religion

L 2.1 - 2.4 2.1. The beginning of philosophy in pre-Socratic Greek thinkers and Socrates 2.2 Plato on knowledge and Ideas 2.3 Plato on virtues, self, and society 2.4 Aristotle’s criticisms of Plato’s theory of Ideas
L 3.1 – 3.4 3.1 Continental Rationalism 3.2 – 3.4 Rene Descartes: what do we know with certainty, the self as mind, God, mind-body dualism, external bodies and Spinoza’s metaphysics

L 4.1 – 4.4 4.1- 4.2 Locke’s empiricism, views on knowledge and Berkeley’s subjective idealism and rejection of abstract ideas 4.3 - 4.4 Origin and nature of knowledge, skepticism, problems of substance and cause.
L 5.1 - 5.4 5.1 Nature and scope of Ethics 5.2 Kant on duty 5.3 – 5.4 Bentham and Mill’s
utilitarianism
L 6.1 – 6.4 6.1-6.3 The problems of existence in main existentialist thinkers like Kierkegaard, Sartre and Heidegger 6.4 The idea of ethical self in existentialism
L 7.1 – 7.3 7.1 Various Indian philosophical systems 7.2 Vedas and Upanisadas 7.3 Atman and Brahman
L 8.1 – 8.4 8.1 – 8.2 Samkhya: Prakrti and Purusa; the theory of evolution 8.3 – 8.4 Yoga: chitta and its vritties, Astanga yoga
L 9.1 – 9.3 9.1 Atomism of Vaishesika and Categories 9.2 – 9.3 Nyaya: sources of knowledge and validity and comparison between Aristotle and Nyaya’s inference
L 10.1 – 10.3 10.1 Shankara on the Absolute, self, and world 10.2 Ramanuja’s qualified non- dualism and self 10.3 Comparative analysis of Shankara and Ramanuja’s Vedanta
L 11.1 - 11.4 11.1 To know about the heterodox system of thoughts 11.2 Buddhism: four noble
truths, doctrine of dependent origination and nirvana 11.3 Jainism: jiva, ajiva and anekantavada 11.4 Concluding note on Indian philosophical systems, general aims and relevance
textbooks: Thilly, F., A History of Philosophy, Central Book Depot, Allahabad, revised edition, 2007, reprint: 2014.
Sharma, C.D., A Critical Survey of Indian Philosophy, Motilal Banarsidass, New Delhi, 2009 edition.
references: Puligandla, R., Fundamentals of Indian Philosophy, D.K. Print World (P), New Delhi: 1997.
Hiriyanna, M., The Essentials of Indian Philosophy, Motilal Banarsidass, New Delhi, 2008 edition.

Have basic concepts of South Asia as a region

title: SCIENCE FICTION
description:
Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias,
dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist,
postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal;
and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling.
i) Introduce students to science fiction as a literary mode that critiques technological and social change.
ii) Explore how science fiction engages with questions of environment and the posthuman through
narrative.
iii) Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination.
iv) Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of
science and cultural studies.

title: SRIMAD BHAGAVAD GITA
description:
This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita
and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the
need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices,
viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth),
dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti-
yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these
subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and
the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.
Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself
to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to
understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship
(abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter
isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail.
topics: What is Bhagavad-gita; the five subject matters of Bhagavad-gita

description:

foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management,

title: INTERNATIONALRELATIONS
description:
 Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism;
World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.
 Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11,
China’s entry into WTO.
 Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon
that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.
 Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.
 Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and
Global Governance
 Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of
Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.
 Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR
 India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the
opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and
United States.
International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states
who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the
international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations
between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical
understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted
the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of
international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The
course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary
affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the
international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are
devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.
topics: Why study International Relations? The context of its emergence as a discipline (1-3)
State and International Relations (4-6)
Evolution of the Contemporary State System and Sovereignty; World Wars; League of Nations and United Nations Organizations; Cold War and Fall of USSR (7-11)
The theories of IR (12-26)
Security in IR: Nuclear Deterrence; Terrorism and Counterterrorism; Non- traditional Threats and Wars (27-30)
Human Rights; Climate Change and Pandemic in IR (31-33)
India’s Foreign Policy (33-41)
textbooks: John Baylis, Steve Smith, and Patricia Owen (eds), The Globalization of World Politics 7th ed (OUP: 2017). The soft copy of the book would be made available. 1
references:  Robert Art and Robert Jervis (eds), International Politics: Enduring Concepts and Contemporary Issues 13th ed (Pearson: 2017).  R Jackson & G Sørensen, Introduction to International Relations (OUP, revised edn., 2013).  Mary Kaldor and Iavor Rangelov (eds), The Handbook of Global Security Policy (Wiley-Blackwell: 2014).  Other readings (required): A set of other required readings will be posted online over the course of the semester. Movies pertaining to case studies shall also be discussed/ posted during the course delivery. A few Expert Talks will be scheduled as per the convenience of subject experts.  Suggested Hyperlink: http://www.theory-talks.org/2008/04/theory-talk-1.html.

title: ECOCRITICISM
description:
Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years
or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical
principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective
on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent
ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well-
being of our planet.
1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends.
2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts.
3. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms.
4. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts.
topics: Literature and ecological attention
Umwelt or the subjective world
What is ecocriticism?
Imagining the nonhuman
What makes a text environmental?
Environment as Presence
Beyond the heroic narrative
Reading environment as presence
Environmental tropes and questions
Deep ecology and intrinsic value
Postcolonial critiques of environmentalism
Slow violence: definition, temporality, invisibility
Extinction and biodiversity
Extinction as relational loss
Extinction as Relational loss
Ecocriticism and Human-wildlife conflict
textbooks: Glotfelty, Cheryll and Harold Fromm. Eds. The Ecocriticism Reader: Landmarks in Literary Ecology. Athens and London: U of Georgia Press, 1996. Print. Alex, Rayson K, S. Susan Deborah and Sachindev P.S. Eds. Culture and Media: Ecocritical Explorations. London: Cambridge Scholars Publishing, 2013.
references: Garrard, Greg. Ecocriticism. Routledge, 2004. Buell, Lawrence. The Environmental Imagination: Thoreau, Nature Writing, and the Formation of American Culture. Harvard UP, 1995. Nixon, Rob. Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor. Harvard UP, 2011. Huggan, Graham, and Helen Tiffin. Postcolonial Ecocriticism: Literature, Animals, Environment. Routledge, 2010.

title: Electrical Machines
description:
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion;
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations,
classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors;
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation.
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer,
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better
understanding of the concepts.
learning_outcomes: The students will learn about the operating principles, constructional features, equivalent circuit diagram, efficiency, testing & control and different type of performance characteristics of transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

Introduction to Magnetic circuits

Autotransformer
Transformer: Three- Phase
Transformer

Three-Phase Induction Motors
Fractional Kilowatt Motors(Single-phase Induction Motor)
Synchronous Machine
DC Machine
Special Machines

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description:
Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics
(Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge
carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions,
forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors
(JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor
devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of
semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its
application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later
like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic
diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to
CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.
CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.
CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.
CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.

CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.
topics: Brief history, recent trends and crystal lattices
Semiconductor models Charge carriers, effective mass.
Statistics of donors and acceptors, Space charge neutrality.
Conductivity and mobility, Hall effect
Optical absorption, excess carrier, Quasi- Fermi level
Diffusion of carriers, built-in field, continuity equation
Equilibrium conditions, Fermi levels, Poisson’s Equation, Depletion layer model.
Carrier injection, diode equation, and I-V characteristics, biasing, Reverse-bias breakdown

Junction Field Effect Transistors (JFETs), MESFET, HEMT & MISFET
MOS structure, MOS Transistors, I-V characteristics and secondary effects
BJT operations, terminal current, Gummel plot, small-signal model, charge control model
Photodiodes, Solar cells, and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and their advanced version
Marks (300)

title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
description:
This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using
CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level
building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area-
efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and
fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including
logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.
⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design
of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic.
⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design.
⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential.
⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference
Circuit.
⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs.
⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout.
⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments.
⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels
of design abstraction.

title: Linear Algebra and its Applications
description:
Quick review of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations, Basis and Dimension,
rank-nullity theorem, change of basis; Inner product spaces, Cauchy Schwarz's
inequality, GramSchmidt orthonormalization, QR decomposition, Discrete Fourier
Transform, and their applications, Spectral Theorem, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem,
Decomposition theorem, and Jordan canonical forms, applications of SVD in
Principal Component Analysis, use of SVD in low-rank approximations and to find
least-squares solutions.
Linear algebra has applications in pure and applied mathematics, computer science,
economics, engineering, mathematical biology, operation research, physics, and
statistics. Linear algebra and matrix methods are also important for data analysis.
Linear Algebra and its applications typically aim to equip students with a solid
understanding of fundamental concepts in linear algebra and the ability to apply these
concepts to the above fields.
learning_outcomes: After completion of this course students should be able to CLO1.: Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to construct orthonormal bases in inner product spaces. CLO2. Utilize Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities to prove geometric boundaries and inner product behaviors. CLO3. Factor a matrix into orthogonal and upper triangular components for stable numerical computations. CLO4. Implement the Spectral Theorem and structural decomposition theorems CLO5. Formulate and compute optimal least-squares solutions for linear models using pseudoinverses derived from SVD. CLO6. Apply Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to execute Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on high-dimensional datasets.

L5-L7 : Inner product, Orthogonal vectors, Orthogonal sets
L8-L12 : Orthonormal basis, Orthogonal projection, Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization, Inner product spaces: Cauchy
Schwarz's inequality, Best approximation in inner products
L13-L14 : QR decomposition and Least-square problems
L15-L16 : Applications of QR: Solution of Ax=b, Projections

title: Object Oriented Programming
description:
Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects,
methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of
classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded
programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification,
analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some
object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and
Creational.
a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object-
oriented analysis and design, and design patterns.
b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on
tools like Eclipse.
c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.
learning_outcomes: On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development. CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces, collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading. CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles. CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable. CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability. 1

title: Discrete Mathematics
description:
Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets,
lattices and Boolean algebras;
Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical
inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques;
Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations,
generating function, partitions;
Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and
Hamilton graphs.
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. understand the basic process of mathematical reasoning CLO2. identify valid arguments and fallacies; CLO3. understand the structure of proofs of theorems in Mathematics; 1 CLO4. write valid mathematical proofs; CLO5. use powerful techniques for handling computing problems in Mathematics and Computation; CLO6. understand important structures having wide applications to sciences, computer programming and various classification problems.; CLO7. to create new relations with useful properties from a given relation; CLO8. to learn basic concepts of Graph theory.
