title: Elementary Real Analysis
description:
Countable and uncountable sets, Real numbers and their properties, Sequence of real numbers, Continuous functions of real variable, Metric space, Compact set, Connected set, Completeness, Continuous function on a metric space, Riemann integration, Sequence and series of functions.
This course aims to discuss several properties of real numbers and functions of real variables. The notions of metric spaces will be introduced and a few concepts in analysis, such as continuity, the convergence of sequences, the convergence of sequences and series of functions, will be discussed. We will also discuss the rigorous theory of Riemann integration. Students will also learn to read and write rigorous proofs so that they can communicate mathematical ideas effectively. This course is also a basic course to build background for other advanced courses in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Students will learn about real numbers and their elementary properties, sequences of real numbers, and the generalization of distance to abstract sets.
CLO2. Students will be introduced to the notion of convergence of series and sequence of functions.
CLO3. Students will study the rigorous theory of integration.

Real numbers: construction of real numbers, real numbers as an ordered field, extended real numbers, Infimum and Supremum, Archimedean property
Cardinality of a set: countable and uncountable sets
Sequences and series: sequences, limits of a sequence, monotone and Cauchy sequences, subsequence, limsup and liminf, series, decimal expansion of real numbers

Metric Spaces: metric spaces, compact sets, perfect sets, connected sets, Cantor set; sequences in metric spaces, Cauchy sequence, complete metric space; continuous functions, uniform continuity, continuity and compactness, continuity and connectedness
Sequence and Series of functions: point-wise and uniform convergence of sequence and series of functions and related properties, integrability
Integration: the Riemann integral and its properties

title: Foundations of Data Science
description:
This course introduces the mathematical foundations of data science with emphasis
on probability, Gaussian models, statistical inference, nonparametric methods, optimization,
dimensionality reduction, data preparation, and scalable data analytics. It develops core tools such as
probability bounds, Bayesian inference, PCA and SVD, kernel density estimation, nearest-neighbor
methods, and connects them to practical data-analysis problems.
Pre-requisites: The course is self-contained. However, a basic understanding of probability theory,
calculus, linear algebra, and elementary programming would be helpful.
Students will learn to
 Model data using mathematically grounded ideas from probability, statistics, and linear algebra.
 Bayesian updating, mixture models, nonparametric density and neighborhood methods.
 Deal with high-dimensional data, PCA and SVD, and basic scalable analytics.
 Support data preprocessing, visualization, and interpretation in modern data-science workflows.

title: Multivariable Calculus
description:
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which
are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and
numerous other applications.
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series,
power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
 To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.
 Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.
 To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.
 Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.
 To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to
CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.
CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.
CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.

CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.
CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.
CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.
CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.
CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.
CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems.

L7-L8: Polar coordinates, graphing polar functions of the form a+/-b sin \theta or cos \theta
L9: Limit, continuity, and differentiability of vector functions L10: Arc length, velocity, unit tangent vector L11: Curvature, normal vector
L12: Functions of several variables, level curves L13: Limits, continuity of two/three variable functions

title: OPTIMIZATION
description:
Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality
and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming
nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques.
Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of
making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the
process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems
have become well-established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering,
economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course
is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems.
This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as
Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and
science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses
optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a
brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.

title: Discrete Mathematics
description:
Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets,
lattices and Boolean algebras;
Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical
inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques;
Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations,
generating function, partitions;
Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and
Hamilton graphs.
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to: CLO1. understand the basic process of mathematical reasoning CLO2. identify valid arguments and fallacies; CLO3. understand the structure of proofs of theorems in Mathematics; 1 CLO4. write valid mathematical proofs; CLO5. use powerful techniques for handling computing problems in Mathematics and Computation; CLO6. understand important structures having wide applications to sciences, computer programming and various classification problems.; CLO7. to create new relations with useful properties from a given relation; CLO8. to learn basic concepts of Graph theory.

title: Elementary Real Analysis
description:
Countable and uncountable sets, Real numbers and their properties, Sequence of real numbers, Continuous functions of real variable, Metric space, Compact set, Connected set, Completeness, Continuous function on a metric space, Riemann integration, Sequence and series of functions.
This course aims to discuss several properties of real numbers and functions of real variables. The notions of metric spaces will be introduced and a few concepts in analysis, such as continuity, the convergence of sequences, the convergence of sequences and series of functions, will be discussed. We will also discuss the rigorous theory of Riemann integration. Students will also learn to read and write rigorous proofs so that they can communicate mathematical ideas effectively. This course is also a basic course to build background for other advanced courses in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Students will learn about real numbers and their elementary properties, sequences of real numbers, and the generalization of distance to abstract sets.
CLO2. Students will be introduced to the notion of convergence of series and sequence of functions.
CLO3. Students will study the rigorous theory of integration.

Metric Spaces: metric spaces, compact sets, perfect sets, connected sets, Cantor set; sequences in metric spaces, Cauchy sequence, complete metric space; continuous functions, uniform continuity, continuity and compactness, continuity and connectedness

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
description:
Existence and uniqueness theorems; properties of linear systems; behavior of solutions of nth order
equations; asymptotic behavior of linear systems; stability of linear and weakly nonlinear systems;
conditions for boundedness and the number of zeros of the nontrivial solutions of second order equations;
stability by Lyapunov's direct method; autonomous and non-autonomous systems.
Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science,
engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues
to address and various approaches to choose from:
Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a
unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions?
Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances.
Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of
solutions and do not require solving the differential equation.
Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to
know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we
change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper
understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Existence and uniqueness of ODEs of nth order CLO2. Linear and nonlinear behavior of system of ODEs CLO3. Applications of ODEs in real-world problems

title: Combinatorial Mathematics
description:
Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed
counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about
combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems:
“How many ways can these elements be combined?”
But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the
“best” in some sense.
This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on
combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach.
Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify
Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete.
What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather
than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself.
Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete
Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed
and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage
collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting.
learning_outcomes: The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. At the end of the course, student will be aware of many existing methods used to solve counting problems and when these methods are applicable.

title: TIME SERIES ANALYSIS AND FORECASTING
description:
This 4th level course introduces time series analysis and associated forecasting techniques, in which students
will be equipped with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods for
analyzing time series data. The course reviews extrapolative and decomposition models, introduction to
Box–Jenkins time series analysis, and ARIMA models. The remainder of the course considers various
practical aspects of the principles behind modern forecasting techniques. Students will study and develop
the ability to select appropriate model to carry out forecasting. A one-hour lab will be conducted every
week. Students will learn how to explore and analyze different types of time series data using R
programming.

title: Applied Statistical Methods
description:
Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines
which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis-
tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This
course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing
self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re-
alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter-
pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference,
analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster
analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The
theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R.
This 4th level course is designed with a two-fold purpose. First, it will provide an exposure to various
theoretical univariate/multivariate methods and their practical applications. Second, this course will
improve methodological/analytical maturity to attempt a variety of problems using MS-excel and R.

title: Multivariable Calculus
description:
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which
are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and
numerous other applications.
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series,
power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
 To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.
 Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.
 To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.
 Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.
 To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to
CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.
CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.
CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.

CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear approximation and sensitivity analysis.
CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to model changes in multivariable systems.
CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.
CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.
CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian determinant.
CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems.

L7-L8: Polar coordinates, graphing polar functions of the form a+/-b sin \theta or cos \theta
L9: Limit, continuity, and differentiability of vector functions L10: Arc length, velocity, unit tangent vector L11: Curvature, normal vector
L12: Functions of several variables, level curves L13: Limits, continuity of two/three variable functions

title: Fluid Mechanics
description:
This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on
submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con-
servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of
Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s
Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows.
The objectives of the course are to learn about the following topics:
• Introduction to fluid mechanics and establish its relevance in mechanical engineering.
• Derivation of the equations governing mass, momentum and energy transport.
• Application of the governing equation to solve simple fluid mechanics problems.
• Non-dimensionalization of governing equations and identification of dimensionless
numbers, Modeling and similarity concepts.
• Two dimensional, inviscid, potential flows; Stream function, Velocity potential.
• Analyze laminar and turbulent flows inside pipes, External flow past immersed bodies,
Intro- duction to Boundary layer theory
• One dimensional, compressible flow inside ducts of variable cross-section, normal and
oblique shocks.

description:

title: DESIGN OF MACHINE ELEMENTS
description:
The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes
materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge,

title: Advanced Manufacturing Processes
description:
Unconventional manufacturing processes and analysis, micro-manufacturing technologies,
introduction to computer-aided manufacturing, CNC machines, CNC Part programming,
additive manufacturing, modelling and simulation of manufacturing processes, surface
technologies, related laboratory exercise and fabrication project.
This course introduces students to advanced manufacturing technologies for fabricating
components across multiple length scales. It focuses on the challenges of machining difficult-
to-machine materials and transforming them into high-value products. The course emphasizes
hands-on learning through CNC part programming, CNC machine operation, additive
manufacturing, and digital-to-physical manufacturing workflows. Lectures complement
laboratory sessions by covering the fundamentals, process capabilities, numerical methods, and
optimization techniques required for the analysis and development of advanced manufacturing
processes.

title: Engines, Motors, and Mobility
description:
The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into
mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas
in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck,
locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive
generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course
will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion
engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course
focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as
the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power
electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric
vehicles.
This course has been designed to make the students familiar
with internal combustion engines and electric and hybrid electric power trains.
topics: What is Engine, What is IC engine? Different Types of Engine, Electric and hybrid vehicles Future mobility
Understanding the IC engine components and their working.
• Geometrical parameters of the engine. • Understand the significance of each performance parameter The effect of these parameters on the Engine performance

• Understanding the concept of ideal cycles, performance of a real SI and CI engine through the idealized closed cycle. • Understand effect of fuel-air mixture on the performance, study the factors affecting the performance.

• Comprehend the difference between the Air standard cycle and the Fuel- air Cycle. • Understand the effect of dissociation, specific heat on the higher temperature and pressure of the Otto and Diesel cycle.
Comprehend the difference between actual and air-standard cycle.
Understand the effect of different factors like time loss, heat loss, exhaust blow down etc. on the ideal cycle.
• Study the different types of fuel which are in use and their properties, understand the important qualities of the SI and CI fuel as well as they will understand the rating of the fuel
• Need of alternative fuels and their suitability Different possible alternative fuel like natural gas, hydrogen, alcohols etc.
• What is a Carburettor, and why is it required ,Mixing of fuel and air in the carburetion • Study the mechanism for controlling the air-fuel ratio. How a gasoline fuel injector works
• Understand the importance of fuel injection as it affect the engine performance and the power output. Understand the different element in the fuel injection system
• Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixture, Understand the combustion process in an SI engine, Understand the ignition delay in the SI engine combustion process
• Understand the reason for abnormal combustion and the phenomenon of knocking and detonations. Appropriate design of the combustion chamber for SI engine

• Will comprehend the different stages of the combustion process in the CI engines. • Factor affecting the combustion process, such as ignition delay. How abnormal combustion occur in a CI engine, and how to avoid it.
• Will understand the need of combustion chamber design for proper mixing of the fuel in the air. Study the different flow pattern of the air in order to mix fuel with air.

• Understand the importance of cooling for safe operation of the engine e.g. in order to avoid the chemical and physical changes in the lubricating oil which may cause wear and sticking of the piston rings. • Study the different cooling system and mechanisms.
• What are the important pollutants from the IC engines? What are the emission norms and their importance? What are the emission control techniques used in the IC engine vehicles?
• Study the different performance parameters of the IC engine. • Study the energy management of the IC engine.
• IC engine Vs electric power train • Hybridization of IC engine power train • Performance comparison of IC engine and electric power train

• What are the different energy storage options available for electric vehicles? How a Li-ion battery works? Performance assessment of a battery. How to design a battery pack for electric vehicle? How a battery management system works?
• What are the different types of motor drives used in electric vehicles? How to select a suitable motor for electric vehicle?

title: Data Mining in Mechanical Sciences
description:
Introduction to data mining, clustering, classification & association, sequence analysis, regressions method,
decision trees, machine learning, neural networks, SVM for engineering and manufacturing applications, data
mining for product design, applications of data mining in production, planning and scheduling, data mining for
defect identification, process and quality control, application of data mining in maintenance, data analysis for
machine and manufacturing process monitoring, introduction to cyber physical systems, introduction to big
data handling and big data analytics.
The primary focus of this course is on application of data mining methods in mechanical sciences and
engineering. Following are the details objectives of this course:
• Understanding the fundamental of data mining.
• Building mathematical foundation for data mining.
• Knowledge of data capturing to minimize the information losses.
• Understanding of patterns in data, data classification and clustering.
• Knowledge of application of identified patterns in data in fields like in-processing monitoring, machine
monitoring, defect analysis, machine and maintenance scheduling etc.
• Understanding of different prediction methods based on the data processing.
• Understand the difference between artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning.
• Knowledge of which data mining methods should be used for what type of data.
• Understanding the concept of big data in mechanical and manufacturing domain and how to handle it.
topics: Why data analysis? Importance of data analysis, Data analysis to data mining, Definition of data mining, Objectives of data mining, Analogy of data mining with concept of mechanical science, Steps in data mining/Data mining process, Concept of data warehouses, Why data mining fails?

Data measurement (Sampling method) Structure/ representation of data Temporal and spatial data Different types of data; Numeric and categorical data Dimensionality of data, Mean, variance, data normalization methods, data smoothing methods.
Point estimation, central limit theory, Regression methods, logistical regression, Density and proximity-based outlier detection, clustering based method.

Supervised and unsupervised feature, Architecture for feature subset selection, Principal component analysis for feature selection, relief algorithm, ranking score, entropy method, ChiMerge technique for feature discretization
General approach for classification problem, accuracy and error rate, Decision tree, design of decision tree, algorithm for decision tree, K nearest neighbors, support vector machine algorithm
Objective of clustering, methods for similarity measure, Agglomerative hierarchical clustering, partitional and incremental clustering, DBSCAN algorithm, clustering validity.
Learning machine, types of learning methods; supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, autoencoders
Different case studies for application of machine learning in mechanical system, design and manufacturing.

title: Energy Storage Technologies
description:
This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy
storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and
chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance
characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy
integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems,
supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.
The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage
technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic,
electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations,
performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize
students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of
modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a
simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with
emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.
textbooks: T.B. 1: Robert A. Huggins, Energy Storage: Fundamentals, Materials and Applications, Springer, 2nd Edition, 2016.

title: Introduction to Sport Engineering
description:
The course essentially prepares engineering students to utilize their existing technical knowhow for
sports applications. The specific topics will include, working with human and human movement
patterns, qualitative and quantitative techniques for analysis of human movement. Sports
performance measure and analysis. Anthropomorphy, Ergonomics and Task design. Computer
application in sports, computerized performance measure. Sports surface and its impact on sports
performance, surface testing methods. Sports and training equipment case study, business around
sports
This is an introductory course to impart knowledge and skill set related to working with human in
sports engineering application. Understanding human movement pattern and performance
measurement. Understand, assess and analyze effect of equipment, sports surfaces and environment
on sports performance. Use of ergonomic concepts, image processing, smart sensors and data analysis
in sports engineering. Standard techniques of evaluation and testing of sports equipment and sports
surfaces and appreciation of business around sports industry.
learning_outcomes: Course Learning Outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand the fundamentals of human movement and apply engineering principles to analyze sports performance. Appreciate the role of ethics, human factors, and design considerations in sports technology. Utilize modern computing tools for motion analysis and performance evaluation in sports. Gain insights into sports infrastructure, surface design, and their impact on athlete performance. Explore the business, innovation, and marketing potential within the sports ecosystem from an engineering perspective.

title: Continuum Mechanics
description:
Introduction to tensors, tensor algebra and tensor calculus. Kinematics of deformation (displace-
ment, velocity, deformation gradient, material and spatial field descriptions, description of local
deformation, linearized kinematics, kinematic rates), left & right Cauchy-Green deformation ten-
sor, Cauchy-Lagrangian strain tensor. Traction and stress (first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, second
Piola- Kirchhoff stress, Biot stress etc). Mechanical conservation and balance laws (conservation
of mass, conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, conservation of
energy, work done by stresses and the principle of virtual work, BVP, IVP, calculus of variation).
Constitutive relations (constraints on constitutive relations, frame indifference, objectivity, material
symmetry, constitutive models for linearly elastic, hyperelastic solids and fluid flows).
This course will provide an introduction to continuum mechanics. It aims to develop in students
the foundational mathematical rigor needed to understand advanced topics in solid and fluid me-
chanics.

title: SMART MATERIALS
description:
The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical
mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics
and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological
fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic
modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations
and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural-
health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.
This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus-
responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms,
observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than
advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper
reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended
to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research-
oriented work in smart materials and structures.
learning_outcomes: CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.
textbooks: H. Abramovich, Intelligent Materials and Structures, 2nd Edition, De Gruyter, 2021.
I. Chopra and J. Sirohi, Smart Structures Theory, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
references: M. V. Gandhi and B. S. Thompson, Smart Materials and Structures, Chapman & Hall, 1992.
Class notes, demonstrations, experiments and specified self-study resources announced during the course.

title: Quality Control, Assurance and Reliability
description:

control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of
reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into

title: Mechanism and Robotics
description:
This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and
principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines
capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown
significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in
hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and
established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future.
The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on
the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics,
computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related
to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and
dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into
the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial
applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in
robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future
technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain.
topics: History and evolution of robotics; Difference between mechanisms, machines, and robots; Classification of robots (industrial, service, humanoid, mobile); Applications in manufacturing, healthcare, defense, and space
Basic terminology (links, joints, kinematic pairs); Degrees of freedom (DOF) and mobility; Gruebler’s equation; Planar vs. spatial mechanisms; Four-bar linkages and coupler curves

Forward kinematics and transformation matrices; Denavit–Hartenberg (D-H) parameters (standard & modified); Frame assignment rules; Inverse kinematics (analytical & numerical methods); Workspace analysis and redundancy
Differential motion and velocity propagation; Jacobian matrix derivation for serial robots; Manipulability and velocity ellipsoids; Singularities and their impact on control
Newton-Euler and Lagrangian formulations; Forward and inverse dynamics problems; Dynamic modeling of manipulators; Payload capacity, torque requirements, and force analysis
Fundamentals of robot
control systems; Joint space (PID) control strategies; Task space control (computed torque, adaptive control); Hybrid position- force control
Mobile robot kinematics and navigation; Path and trajectory planning (C- space, PRM, RRT); Robot vision (camera calibration, image processing); AI and machine learning integration in robotics
Industrial robot configurations (SCARA, Cartesian, articulated); Robot programming methods (teach pendant & offline); End-effectors and grippers design; Case studies of robotic automation in industry
Collaborative robots (cobots) and human-robot interaction; Soft robotics and bio-inspired robots; Swarm robotics; Course review and student project presentations
textbooks: (T1) Mittal R. K. & Nagrath, I. J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later).
references: (R1) Groover, M. P., et al., “Industrial Robotics”, McGraw Hill ISE, 1986. (R2) Fu, K. S., et al., Robotic: Control, Sensing, Vision & Intelligence, McGraw Hill ISE, 1987 (R3) Robert J., Schilling, Fundamentals of Robotics: Analysis and Control, Prentice Hall, NJ, 2002.

title: Finite Element Method
description:
Fundamental concepts, matrix algebra and gaussian elimination, one-dimensional problems, trusses,
two-dimensional problems using constant strain triangles, axisymmetric solids subjected to ax-
isymmetric loading, two-dimensional isoparametric elements and numerical integration, beams
and frames, three-dimensional problems in stress analysis, scalar field problems, dynamic con-
siderations, pre-processing and post processing.
The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in
solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural
mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathe-
matical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built.
The objectives of the course are:
CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz
method.
CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value
problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer.
CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid
mechanics and heat transfer.
topics: Introduction to FEM
Variational Methods
Static Analysis of a Bar using 1D bar el- ement
FE modelling of a Truss
textbooks: Introduction to the Finite Element Method, J. N. Reddy, 4th Edition,Tata McGraw-Hill Pub- lishing Company Ltd.,2020
references: Introduction to Finite Elements in Engineering, T. R. Chandrupatla and A. D. Belegundu, 5th Edition, Cambridge University Press, 2021 1

title: Deep Neural Networks
description:
Introduction to neural networks, approximation properties, backpropagation, deep network training,
regularization and optimization, convolution neural networks, recurrent neural networks, attention models,
transformers, neural architecture search, federated learning, meta-learning, applications in time series modeling
and forecasting, online (incremental) learning.
This course is designed to impart the knowledge to understand the basics of deep learning and their applications
in mechanical engineering. The objectives of this course are:
• Understand and explain the architecture, training, and optimization techniques used in deep neural
networks.
• Apply deep learning techniques to solve problems in mechanical engineering domain.
• Analyze the performance and behavior of deep learning models.
• Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different deep learning architectures and techniques for
mechanical engineering specific problems.
• Critically assess the latest advancements in deep learning.

title: Industrial Robotics and Controls
description:
This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics
include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate
transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian
analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and
dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint
control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation
and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell
implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing
environments.
This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control
with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous
foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis,
and operation of industrial robotic manipulators.
Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments
for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems.
Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory
generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using
industrial-grade platforms.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and- place, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.
topics: Robot Terminology (M1) | Lectures 1 to 8 – Introduction to Industrial Robotics, Mechanisms and Machines, Types of Joints and Degree of Freedoms, Pose of a Rigid Body, Rotation Matrices, Euler Angles, Quaternions, Homogenous Transformations, Denavit Hartenberg Convention and Parameters.

Robot Kinematics and Trajectory Planning (M2) | Lectures 9 to 20 – Forward and Inverse Kinematics, Jacobian, Workspace Analysis, Singularity in a Robot, Trajectory Planning, Manipulability, Velocity Ellipses.
Robot Statics and Dynamics (M3) | Lectures 21 to 28 – Statics and Force/Torque Ellipses, Dynamics using Euler- Lagrange equations and Newton-Euler Formulation.
Robot Control (M4) | Lectures 29 – 36 – Open and Closed Loop System, Independent Joint Control, Computed Joint Torque/Multivariate Control, Force Control.
Robot End-Effector Design (M5) | Lectures 36 – 42 – Robot Pick and Place operations with end-effector design using the concepts learnt.
textbooks: (T1) Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control — John J. Craig For: Fundamental concepts of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control. (T2) Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control — Bruno Siciliano et al. For: Advanced mathematical treatment of robotics modeling and planning.

J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later) (R3) Mark W. Spong and M. Vidyasagar, “Robot, Dynamics, and Control”, John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

title: Moulding Methods for Electronic Components
description:
This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in
the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic
components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module
provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety
considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic-
moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects
related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components.
Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into
advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry.
This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry,
as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced
casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the
principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the
parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical
exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies.

CO2 Selection of appropriate materials for the electronic industry. CO3 Design and fabricate different plastic components using moulding processes. CO4 Acquire basic design skills related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould. CO5 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical electronic component fabrication problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.

L (3-5): Material selection and properties: different metallic, polymeric, ceramic, and composite materials used in the electronics industry. Material Selection Criteria: material properties, including electrical properties, thermal stability, mechanical properties, and environmental resistance. Polymer material characterization and testing.

L (6-20): Plastic Moulding Techniques: Principles, process fundamentals, tooling involved, material selection, and process parameters for different processes, including injection moulding, compression moulding, transfer moulding, blow moulding, pressure casting, and die casting. Case study.

title: Computer Aided Design & Additive Manufacturing
description:
This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design
(CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and
manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform
Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation,
and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro-
duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on
training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on
the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the
fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and
the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative,
lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.
The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric mod-
elling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques. It enables students to
apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering
software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products.
The course is intended to enable students to:
learning_outcomes: At the end of the course, students will be able to: CLO1. Understand the mathematical and computational foundations of parametric geo- metric modelling; CLO2. Construct and interpret curves, surfaces, solids, assemblies, and product-data rep- resentations; CLO3. Apply ASME Y14.5 concepts to communicate functional dimensional and geomet- ric requirements; CLO4. Formulate and interpret generative-design and topology-optimization problems; 1 CLO5. Understand additive-manufacturing processes, materials, preprocessing, process parameters, post-processing, and safety; and CLO6. Integrate CAD, GD&T, optimization, and additive manufacturing in a coherent digital product-development workflow.

L4: Synthetic curves and continuity; L5: Bézier curves; L6: B-spline curves

description:
The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool
structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and
displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The
course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow,
Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes.

title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
description:
This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics.
This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations
and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices.
The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world
applications at the micro- and nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of
microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives
are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces,
to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand
the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains.

title: SMART MATERIALS
description:
The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical
mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics
and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological
fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic
modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations
and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural-
health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.
This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus-
responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms,
observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than
advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper
reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended
to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research-
oriented work in smart materials and structures.
learning_outcomes: CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of major smart-material families and smart structural systems. CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials. CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements. CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.
textbooks: H. Abramovich, Intelligent Materials and Structures, 2nd Edition, De Gruyter, 2021.
I. Chopra and J. Sirohi, Smart Structures Theory, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
references: M. V. Gandhi and B. S. Thompson, Smart Materials and Structures, Chapman & Hall, 1992.
Class notes, demonstrations, experiments and specified self-study resources announced during the course.

title: Quality Control, Assurance and Reliability
description:
Basic concepts of probability and probability distribution, Standard probability distribution, Sampling and
Sampling Distributions, Confidence intervals, testing significance, Statistical tolerance, Various types of
control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of
reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into
production process.
This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles
and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are
covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and
methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students
to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their
never-ending quest for quality.

title: ADVANCED VLSI DESIGN
description:
The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone
through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621
VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of
advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design
of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will
focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground
noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking
overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI
design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed
analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.
The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has
revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and
entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices.
Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power
with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital
techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in
an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages
of the design of a modern digital system.
learning_outcomes: Students will develop an understanding of common design and timing issues/challenges in digital systems. They will be introduced to high-speed/low-power circuit logic/ power minimization techniques, as well as wiring models used in digital systems. Additionally, they will learn about the clock system design and various noise sources that can interfere with these systems.
topics: General Introduction- digital system, data rate, pin count, serial/ parallel communication, eye diagram
Signal encoding, and signaling modes, voltage/ current Input/output drivers (with low power constraint) for C, and LRC loads
Timing issues in synchronous VLSI systems. Asynchronous system design
Wire design models in the nanometer region- lumped, distributed, transmission line, termination
High-performance / low-power circuit logic, delay/ power minimization using logical effort
Clock signals distribution and clock generation, clock drivers, Digital phase locked loop, digital delay locked loop, synchronizer - design and meta-stability issues
Noise management, power supply distribution
Memory design (self-reading)

title: Advanced VLSI Architectures
description:
The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their
implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and
their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various
techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels.
Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism)
data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be
exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors,
SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and
Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy
organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research
directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures.
The objective of the course is to understand and gain an
in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor
architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have
evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The
scope of the course covers the following in detail:
a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation
techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques
b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific
architectures and implementations
c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism
and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors)
d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and
application domain-specific processors
learning_outcomes: Explain the advantages of CORDIC in hardware implementation, especially in terms of multiplier-less architecture, low power, and area efficiency.
Analyze the design principles of advanced VLSI processor architectures and their microarchitectural implementation strategies for high-performance computing systems.
Evaluate various memory hierarchy designs and optimizations, including their microarchitectural aspects, in the context of different processor types.
Apply concepts of parallelism—such as instruction-level, data-level, thread-level, and task-level parallelism—to optimize system performance.
Design architectural solutions using specialized processing units such as SIMD processors, vector processors, multimedia processors, GPUs, multi-core systems, and domain-specific accelerators.
Explore contemporary research trends and emerging technologies in VLSI processor and memory system architecture to identify potential areas for innovation.
topics: CORDIC algorithm
Fundamentals of Quantitative Design and Analysis
Memory Hierarchy Design
Pipeline architectures
Introduction to Parallel Processing, ILP
Data-Level Parallelism in Vector, SIMD
GPU Architectures
TLP & multicores
Multiprocessor interconnects
Application / Domain Specific Processor design

title: Advance Analog and Mixed Signal Design
description:
Mixed signal blocks design issues,, design of high resolution,
speed Comparators,, design of Active Mixers-balanced/ unbalanced,, Data
Converters Architectures, CMOS multipliers , dividers and modulators , filters-
active/ passive/ switched capacitor, Signal Conditioning and sensor associated
circuits, Frequency Synthesizers, Phase Locked Loop, Power Management Circuits,
Integrated Voltage Regulators, Energy Harvesting Circuits, Analog Testing, Analog
layouts, noise issues, emerging trendshigh
This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and
hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits
with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap
between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks
such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters
(ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal
blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging
trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted
analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial
innovation.
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will be able to
Analyse and Design high-resolution, high-speed comparators, mixers, and signal conditioning blocks for mixed-signal interfaces.
Architect and Evaluate various ADC and DAC topologies based on speed, resolution, power, and area metrics.
Design and Simulate PLLs and oscillator-based clock generation systems with attention to phase noise, jitter, and loop stability.
Implement of Biasing Circuits and Optical/Wireline Receiver Transmitter circuits.
Understand and Apply analog layout methodologies, matching principles, and noise-aware design techniques.
Demonstrate Proficiency in using industry-grade tools (e.g., Cadence) to model, simulate, and layout mixed-signal circuits.
topics: Mixed-Signal Design Foundations
Basics of Amplifier stability and Mismatc
stability and Mismatc
Biasing Circuits
Fundamentals of Phase Noise and Jitter, Oscillators Fundamentals

Analog-to-Digital Conversion, 4th Edition Marcel J.M Pelgrom.

title: VLSI Fabrication Technology
description:
Historical perspective; Processing overview; Crystallography of semiconductors; Defects in semiconductors;
Clean room; Wafer- growth; cleaning; oxidation; epitaxy; wet and dry etching; lithographic process; diffusion;
ion implantation; deposition of films using CVD, and PVD techniques; device and circuit fabrication; Process
Integration: Passive components, Bipolar Technology and MOSFET Technology, Fabrication of advanced
VLSI devices; System on chip; Future trends and Challenges:
Laboratory components: Simulation of key fabrication processes using CAD tools; Demonstration of basic
FEOL/BEOL fabrication processes; Fabrication and testing of electronic devices.
The objective of the course is not only to introduce the basic principles involved in IC fabrication, but
also, to discuss processing technology. Fabrication of integrated circuits is a joint venture by electrical
engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges
across various disciplines.
textbooks: S. M. Sze, VLSI Technology, TATA McGraw-Hill.
references: Plummer, Deal, and Griffin, Silicon VLSI Technology, Pearson.
May and Sze, Fundamentals of Semiconductor Fabrication, Wiley.
William D. Callister and Jr. David G. Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction, Wiley.
S.A. Campbell, The Science and Engineering of Microelectronic Fabrication, Oxford.

title: Digital VLSI Design
description:
We will study the fundamental structures of VLSI Systems at the lowest levels of system abstraction,
namely those associated with the direct application of VLSI devices to particular problems of interest.
The broad topics of coverage includes Principles of operations of CMOS transistors used as a digital
switch and various other topologies used in Digital VLSI Design, Logic implementation strategies and
performance characterization of the VLSI circuits, Low Power Design, different clocking strategies,
symbolic layout systems, CMOS subsystems design and Memory modules.
The objective of this course is to understand the need and importance of digital VLSI design in CMOS
integrated circuits. To understand different design principles used in the design of Digital VLSI
Circuits & Systems using CMOS with emphasis on low power and high performance.
topics: Introduction to VLSI Design
Introduction to MOS Physics
Device Characteristics
Static NMOS/CMOS inverter: voltage- transfer characteristics
MOS Capacitances, Dynamic Behavior of CMOS Inverters
CMOS Process Technology , Layout and Design Rules
Scaling of MOS Devices
Combinational CMOS logic circuit
InterConnect Parasitics
CMOS Sequential logic Design
Dynamic & Domino Logic Design
Clocking Strategies
Aspects of Memory design
Adder architectures
Introduction to Finfet based circuit design
textbooks: a).(T1) Essentials of VLSI Circuits and Systems, Kamran Eshraghian, Douglas A. Pucknell and Sholeh Eshraghian, PHI, 2005/2009. b).(T2) CMOS Digital Integrated Circuit, Analysis and Design, Sung-Mo Kang and Yusuf Leblebici, Publisher: McGraw- Hill Companies, Inc.2003
references: a).(R1) Digital Integrated Circuits, A Design Perspective, Jan M Rabaey, Anantha Chandrakasan, Borivoje Nikolic, 2nd edition, Prentice Hall, 2005. 1

title: Physics and Modeling of Microelectronic Devices
description:
Physics and properties of semiconductor - a review; Semiconductor transport model,
modeling of metal-semiconductor junctions, pn homojunction and heterojunctions, bipolar transistor, JFET,
MESFET, HEMT and; MOS capacitor, modeling of MOSFET, scaling issues, and recent trends in advanced
MOSFETs
Laboratory Components: Modeling and simulation of silicon-based devices with TCAD software. I-V, C-V
measurement of MS and MOS junctions.
This course is designed to provide the basic physical concepts behind microelectronic devices and imparts
information on modeling of these devices for their use as circuit elements in integrated circuits. It will provide
the ability to deal with advanced concepts of microelectronic devices along with non-ideal effects in devices
with an attempt to establish an introduction to research methodology.
topics: Basics of Semiconductors, Band and Bond model of solids
Thermal-equilibrium statistics, photogeneration & Quasi-Fermi levels
Free Carriers in semiconductors, scattering, velocity saturation
textbooks: R. S. Muller and T. I. Kamins, Device Electronics for Integrated Circuits, 3rd ed. Wiley, New York
references: Chenming Calvin Hu, “Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits”, Pearson Education.
Donald A. Neaman and D. Biswas, “Semiconductor Physics and Devices”, 4th ed., Tata Mc Graw Hill

title: Verification, Test, and Testability of VLSI Circuits
description:
VLSI design flow, Simulation based verification, Test bench
tools and languages, System Verilog, Formal verification, Impact of scaling, wafer
sort or probe test, DC and AC parametric test, Test economics and product quality,
Fault models and types; Fault equivalence, Fault dominance, Automated test
generation for combinational logic (fault simulation, ATPG, D-algorithm, PODEM,
FAN); Test generation for sequential logic; Testability measures, Design for
testability (Full-scan and partial scan, BIST, Boundary scan), Delay fault; Analog
and mixed signal circuit testing, Memory test, IDDQ test
The objective of this course is to deal with the study of VLSI
design flow, Functional verification, verification flow, need of electronic testing,
fault modeling, test generation for combinational circuits, test generation for
sequential circuits, fault simulation, Built-In Self-Test (BIST), Memory testing,
Design for Testability (DFT), SoC test, fault diagnosis, Analog/RF test.
learning_outcomes: Students will learn the VLSI design flow, understand the importance of design verification during design flow and also understand the importance of post fabrication testing in VLSI design flow with exposure to the design tools.

L 1.2-L1.5 Low power VLSI design flow and verification
L2.1. Functional verification and verification challenges , Verification Methodology Evolution
L2.2. Verification Environment Basics , Assertions, Testbench and tester, Layered Testbench
L2.3. Verification example: CALC 1, Deterministic Verification of Calc1
L2.4 CALC2 Overview, Calc2 Verification Plan

Michael. L. Bushnell, and Vishwani. D. Agrawal, “Essentials of Electronic Testing For Digital, Memory and Mixed Signal VLSI Circuits” Kluwer Academic Publishers, Third Edition, 2004

Stuart Sutherland, Simon Davidmann, Peter Flake” System Verilog for Design,” Springer Publications, Second Edition 2006.

H. Fujiwara, “Logic Testing and Design for testability” MIT Press, 1985.

title: Materials Science and Engineering
description:
Introduction, Structure of Materials (Metal and Ceramics), Dislocations, heat treatment of steel and
strengthening Mechanisms of Metals, Phase diagrams, Iron-carbide phase diagram, Phase transformation
in Metals, Mechanical and thermal properties of Metals, Polymers (Structure, processes and properties),
powder metallurgy.
CO1. Develop familiarity with the different levels of structure (atomic, crystal, microscopic) in
engineering materials and deviations from “perfect” structure (structural defects).
CO2. Introduction to characterization method like optical microscope, XRD, SEM, TEM
CO3. Understand the effects of microstructure on the mechanical properties of materials.
CO4. Understand the basis for microstructure development in materials.
CO5. Understand how materials are processed.
CO6. Selection of Materials for specific application
topics: L1.1.Introduction of Engineering materials, classification into metals, polymers and ceramics and their properties.
L 1.2. Atomic structure, crystal structure, micro structure and macro structure of materials.
T1.1. Exercise problems on structure property correlations.
L2.1 Bravice lattice, unit cell, arrangement of atoms in common crystal structure

L2.2. Miller indices for planes and directions, identification of miller plan and directions. Determination of close packed plan, close packed directions, slip system and influence of crystal structure on properties of materials
T2. Exercise problems on crystal structure and its influence on properties.
L3.1 Classification of crystal defects, point defects, vacancies, interstitials, vacancy concentration and influence of point defect on properties of materials.
L3.2. Line defects-edge dislocation, screw dislocation, Burger vector. Influence of line defects on plastic deformation of
materials and deformation by slip and Planer defects- tilt boundaries, twin boundaries, grain boundaries and surfaces. Influence of planer defect, strengthening mechanisms twinning,
T3. Exercise problems on crystal imperfections and its effect.
L4.1 Cooling curve of pure metal and alloys, method of arriving at phase diagram from cooling curves, Gibb’s phase rule and phase equilibrium.

L4.2. Isomorphous system of phase diagram with Cu-Ni system as example, liquidus, solidus line, lever rule and determination of phases. Eutectic system with Pb-Sn system as example, eutectic, hypo eutectic, hyper eutectic phase transformations, microstructure and properties
T4. Exercise problems on phase diagrams.
L5.1 .Cooling curve of pure iron, allotropic transformations, effect of carbon. Three invariant reactions and regions

L5.2. Steel region of Fe-Fe C phase 3 diagram, eutectoid reaction, phase transformation. Effect of Carbon on properties of steel, Plain carbon and alloy steels, their influence on microstructure and properties.
L 5.3 Cast iron region of Fe-Fe C phase 3 diagram, white cast iron and it’s properties, Grey, ductile and Malleable cast iron and their applications
T5. Exercise problems on Iron- carbon system
L6.1. Brief introduction to solidification of pure metals, critical nucleation sites and growth, transformation rate and temperature. Analogy between liquid to solid transformation and solid to solid
transformation, S curves and formation of isothermal transformation diagram, Metallic glasses.
L6.2. Formation of TTT diagram for eutectoid steel, different phases and regions, influence of cooling rate and phase transformation, critical cooling rate and martensitic transformation.
L 6.3 Size effect, hardenability, effect of alloying elements, Austempering and martempering .
T6. Exercise problems on TTT and CCT diagram.
L7.1. Stress-strain diagram of metals, polymers and ceramics. Engineering stress, engineering strain, elastic modulus, True stress, true strain, and relationship.
L7.2.Ductile and Brittle fracture, fractography, impact testing, ductile to brittle transition temperature and failure of materials.
L 7.3 Fatigue and creep, SN Curve, endurance limit, Types of fatigue cycle and fatigue life estimate..
L 7.4 Creep, typical creep curve, effect of temperature and stress on creep curve, stress rupture test and determination of creep life. LMP approach.
T9 and T10- Tutorial problems on fatigue, creep and fracture.
L 8.1Determination of coordination number AX,AmXp and AmBnXp structures of Ceramics.
L8.2. Density Calculation, silicates and polymorphs of Carbon and their structure.Types and application of ceramics.
T 11. Tutorial Problems on Ceramics.
L 9.1Determination of coordination number AX,AmXp and AmBnXp structures of Ceramics.

L9.2 Polymeric structure, crystallinity, polymeric molecules and chemistry, determination of molecular weight. Glass transition temperature, Properties and application of polymers. Advances polymeric materials
T 12. Tutorial Problems on polymeric materials
L10.1Types of composite materials, rule of mixtures and it’s applications.
L10.2.Control of composite properties, different types and applications, Manufacture and testing of composites
T13. Tutorial problems on Composite materials.
L11.1.Materials chart with properties.
L11.2Determination of materials performance index and it’s use in materials selection decision. Application of materials selection with case study.
T14. Tutorial problems on selection of Materials.

title: Transport phenomena in Manufacturing
description:
The course contents include: Introduction to Transport
phenomena and its importance in manufacturing engineering, Fundamental
concepts in Fluid statics and in motion, Heat and mass transfer theories,
Conservation laws for Transport phenomena and solution methodologies, Important
solutions and correlations in Transport phenomena, Radiation heat transfer and
Special topics relevant to manufacturing such as Heat transfer with phase change,
Simultaneous heat and mass transfer etc.
This is a first level course aimed for imparting the fundamentals of fluid mechanics
and heat transfer to students for solving transport phenomena problems pertaining
to manufacturing processes.

title: DESIGN OF MACHINE ELEMENTS
description:
The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes
materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge,
and imaginative skills to be developed in a student. The machine elements covered are Shafts, Screw fasteners,
Welded joints, Springs, Brakes & Clutches, Bearings and Gears.
To prepare a student of mechanical engineering to apply theory and practice of Design of Mechanical Elements.
It is an introductory course laying foundation on design ground rules, application of strength of material principles,
selection of components, and selection of materials for a given application.
topics: Mechanical Engineering Design Principles, Preferred Number, Concept of Safety Factor, Engineering Units.
textbooks: Budynas, R. G. and Nisbett, K. J., “Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design" Tata Mc-Grow Hill, 10th Edition, 2017 or a later ed.
references: Robert L Norton, Machine Design an integrated approach, fifth edition, Pearson Education Asia, 2018
V B Bhandari, Design of Machine Elements, 5th edition Tata Mc-Grow Hill publishing Co, 2020
