title: AUTOMATION AND CONTROL
description:
This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The
necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt,
due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems.
Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies,
combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as
simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied
to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such
as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly
enhanced by the application of mechatronics.
This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad
introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation
systems.

Basic control concepts: open, close, proportional derivative, integral, multivariable, digital, adaptive control systems

title: Machining and Machine Tools
description:
Significance of metal machining and machine tools, Geometry of cutting tools, Mechanics of
machining processes and analysis, Role of cutting fluids and properties, Abrasive machining
processes and analysis, Economics of machining, Regulation of speed and feed rates in machine
tools, Design of machine tool structures, Guideways, Spindles, Design of cutting tools for various

machine tools.

title: Lean Manufacturing
description:
Fundamentals of continuous improvement, value-added and waste elimination, elements of lean production:
small lot production, setup time reduction, maintaining and improving equipment, pull production systems,
focused factories and group technologies, work cells and cellular manufacturing, standard operations, quality
of design, systems for eliminating defects, simplified production planning and control systems: scheduling for
smooth flow, synchronizing and balancing process, planning and control in pull production, beyond the
production systems: managing the supply chain, activity based costing, performance measurement.
In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and
process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price-
cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business
leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler
combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean
manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent
decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain
competitive advantage. But are they?
The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and
efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any
business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of long-
term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning
enterprise – the Toyota way.
At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The
Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the
Toyota way
textbooks: Pascal Dennis, "Lean Production Simplified", 2nd Edition, Productivity Press, 2007.
Jeffrey K. Liker, “The Toyota Way”, MaGraw-Hill Edition, New Delhi, 2004.
references: James P. Womack and Daniel T. Jones, “Lean Thinking: Banish Waste & Create Wealth in Your Corporation, Revised Edition, Simon & Shuster, 2001. 1
Nicholas, John M., “Competitive Man ufacturing Management”, Tata McGraw Hill Education Pvt. Ltd. New Delhi, 2012.

title: Supply Chain Modelling and Empirical Analysis
description:
The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insight into the
application of various supply chain modelling approaches and empirical analysis for
evidence driven decision making in supply chain. The objectives of the course are:
• To introduce concept of decision making on the basis of multiple experts’ opinion on
various different supply chain problems, practices and strategies.
• To develop skill sets to analyze the qualitative data with a focus on empirical modelling
for data driven decisions in supply chain.
• To develop model for life cycle analysis for measuring environmental sustainability in
supply chain.
• To understand and analyse the various aspects of digital supply chain, cultural
implications and their impact on supply chain performance.
learning_outcomes: No Course Outcomes CO1 To understand the importance of various modelling approaches and empirical analysis in supply chain. CO2 To become familiar with various decision making processes considering multiple experts’ opinion CO3 To learn various aspects of conducting survey for empirical analysis such as questionnaire development, data collection and data cleaning. CO4 To understand and apply computer-based statistical packages for empirical analysis in supply chain. CO5 To develop and analyze the supply chain model using Structural Equation Modeling approach and heterogeneous data concept. CO6 To understand, develop and analyze the LCA model for environmental sustainability assessment in supply chain. CO7 To become familiar with various aspects of digital supply chain, cultural implications and their impact on supply chain performance.
topics: Overview of supply chain modelling and empirical analysis
Data Collection
Structural Equation Modeling
Modelling Heterogeneous Data
Life Cycle Modelling
Digital supply chain and Performance modelling

title: INNOVATION AND DESIGN THINKING
description:
Human-centered innovation, Design thinking (DT), consumer needs, creativity for new ideas/products (or re-
design products) for solving problems, DT process’ stages– inspiration, ideation & implementation, DT tools
– stakeholder map, user persona, Hook’s canvas, empathy map, AEIOU model, PoV, problem statement,
stakeholder wish list, SCAMPER, prototyping & testing, MVP or minimum viable product, business
model/canvas & business ecosystem. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning.
The objective is to develop knowhow and skills that promote human-centered approach to innovation through
design thinking (DT). It will aim to develop understanding of consumer needs & using creativity for new
ideas/products (or re-design products) for solving problems. Course will also help understand prototyping,
testing of new ideas & see the context of the larger ecosystem. Focus will be on understanding design
thinking concept and tools for effective innovations that can solve consumers’ needs holistically. Design
Thinking process is laid across 3 stages- inspiration, ideation and implementation for new product
development or re-design & concepts like MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas &
business ecosystem will be also covered. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning.
topics: Basic innovation concepts & HBR article - Brown, T. (2008). Design thinking
HBR article ‘Why Design Thinking’ by J M Liedtka, examples of innovations around us
Introduction, groups, item & problem statement
Inspiration stage: Part 1
Inspiration stage: Part 2
Ideation stage: Part 1
Ideation stage: Part 2
Implementation stage: Part 1

title: Marketing
description:
This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic
and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating,
communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market
drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be
on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions.
On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to
critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an
intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing
plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate
planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course.
Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to
the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing
literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles
will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis
on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a
group marketing project assignment.

Strategic Marketing and marketing Plan
The Marketing Environment
Market research
Building Customer satisfaction, Value and retention

title: Managing People & Organization
description:
The course studies human behavior in organizations at three levels:
individual, group, and organizational systems. It examines variables and key concepts related
to individual attitudes, motivation, and leadership, along with group dynamics, organizational
structure, and change management, while also covering the strategic role of HRM in attracting,
developing, motivating, and retaining talent through recruitment and selection, training and
development, performance management, employee engagement, compensation, and talent
management.
In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing
economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such
scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover,
management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies
on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic
and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its
employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As
people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in
the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and
relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and
managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the
necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this
course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the
organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against
which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and
developed.
learning_outcomes: By the end of the course the students are expected to
CLO1. Comprehend the fundamental concepts in organizational behavior and human resource management and the tight coupling between them
CLO2. Apply concepts of organization behavior to their everyday workplace context
CLO3. Apply frameworks for managing talent at their workplace
CLO4.Comprehend the pros and cons of different organizational structures and apply them, as needed at their workplace. 1
CLO5.Comprehend the importance of organizational culture and change management strategies
textbooks: TB1. Organizational Behavior by Stephen P. Robbins & Timothy A. Judge. Pearson Education, Updated 18th Edition, 2022
TB2. Dessler Gary & Varkkey, Biju. Human Resource Management, 16th edition. Pearson Education, 2020.
RB1. Aswathapa, Human Resource Management- Text and Cases Tata McGraw Hill, 10th Edition, 2017
RB2. Understanding Organizational Behavior by Udai Pareek. Oxford University Press, 2nd Edition, 2007.

title: Statistics & Basic Econometrics
description:
Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important
Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA,
MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy
variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity,
heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in
this course.
This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics,
wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine
business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference,
estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance
(ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical
technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical
considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative
functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in
the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core
concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting
statistical inference.
A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and
analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency
in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students should be able to: CLO1:Apply statistical and econometric models to estimate relevant business parameters, predict economic outcomes, and test hypotheses using quantitative data. CLO2:Understand the fundamental assumptions underlying the classical linear regression model and identify and address potential violations, such as autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity. CLO3:Develop and sustain a foundational knowledge of econometrics that will serve as a basis for further study in business analytics and advanced statistical methodologies.
topics: analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency
in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R

Gujarati, D. N., Porter, D. C., & Gunasekar, S. (2012). Basic econometrics. Tata McGraw-Hill Education.
references: Heiss, F. (2016). Using R for introductory econometrics. Florian Heiss.
Verzani, J. (2018). Using R for introductory statistics. CRC press.
Hatekar, N. R. (2010). Principles of Econometrics: An Introduction (using R). SAGE Publications India.
Madnani, G. M. K. (2015). Introduction to Econometrics: Principles and Applications. Oxford and IBH Publishing.

title: Data Management & Warehousing (DMW)
description:
This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems
become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful
completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data
requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER)
diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and
write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights
from databases through data analytics powered by SQL.
The course covers various Database Management and Data Warehousing concepts and enhances learning
effectiveness through developing scripting skills. It aims to provide students with the necessary knowledge and
skills to understand the data infrastructure underpinning business intelligence and analytics. Students
undertaking this course should be able to appreciate the complexities involved in Database management and be
prepared to solve the issues a business analyst faces.
learning_outcomes: Understand the database environment and the complete development process, including requirements gathering, design, and implementation.
Model data using Entity-Relationship diagrams and design logical and physical relational databases.
Write effective SQL queries to manage and manipulate data within relational databases.
Explain the architecture of database applications, foundations of data warehousing, and principles of data quality and integration.
Explore the role of databases in Big Data analytics and understand essential tasks in database administration.

Relational Model
Database Design Using the E-R Model
Relational Database Design
Structured Query Language
Complex Data Types
Data and database administration

Serializability
Concurrency Control

Data Warehousing and Analytics

Data Mining

title: Programming for Analytics
description:
Variables & data types, operators, conditional statements, iteration statements, functions,
Objects, and classes for Python; Data structures – vectors, matrices, lists, tuples, dictionaries, data
frames, Packages: using existing packages and creating new packages, Data loading: from CSV, MS
Excel, JSON & SQL databases Data wrangling: describing, summarizing, manipulating, and handling
missing values of data in data frames; perform an operation such as delete values, find unique
values, drop duplicate values, grouping, and performing loop operations over columns or rows;
merging data frames; handling categorical data; handling time-series data, handling text data, web
scraping, and handling images. Basics of version control using Github. Primary languages are R and
Python.
1. To develop proficiency in programming to automate analytical workflows, including data
cleaning, transformation, and report generation, reducing manual effort and increasing accuracy.
2. To gain hands-on experience with programming tools and libraries (e.g., Python’s pandas, R’s
tidyverse) to efficiently process, manipulate, and analyze large and complex datasets beyond the
capabilities of traditional tools.
3. To apply programming best practices to ensure reproducibility, and transparency, for analytical
processes, enabling consistent validation and collaboration across teams.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. To be able to understand different types of data structures and implement them using R and Python. CLO2. To be able to load datasets using R and Python language. CLO3. To be able to transform and manipulate datasets using R and Python language.
topics: • Installing R and RStudio • Arithmetic and Logical Operations • Using Functions • Creating Variables • Numeric, Character and Logical Data • Vectors, Data Frames, Factors, Sorting Numeric, Character, and Factor Vectors
• Installing and loading packages • Setting up your working directory • Downloading and importing data • Working with missing data • Writing R scripts • Adding comments and
documentation
• Measures of central Tendency, variability, Skewness and kurtosis, Summary functions, describe functions, and descriptive statistics by group • Correlations • Scatter Plots, Box Plots • Histograms
• Messy Data • Renaming Columns • Attaching / Detaching • Tabulating Data: Constructing Simple Frequency Tables
• while loops • for loops • If / else • Boolean logical operators
• Writing SQL statements in R • Using the Select, From, Where, Is, Like, Order By, Limit, Max, Min SQL functions
• RMarkdown basics • Text formatting • Code chunks • YAML header • Preview of notebooks, presentations, websites, and dashboards

title: Deep Learning for Business
description:
This course offers an introduction to deep learning and its practical relevance in
business contexts. It covers foundational concepts such as neural networks, linear and logistic
regression using neural architectures, deep neural networks, hyperparameter tuning, and advanced
models like CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs, GANs, and deep reinforcement learning. The course blends
theoretical understanding with hands-on applications to solve real-world business problems. It also
highlights the challenges and limitations of deep learning methods in practice.
The course aims to equip students with foundational and practical
knowledge of deep learning algorithms and their applications in solving business challenges. The
course emphasizes:
a. Understanding core deep learning architectures and techniques
b. Translating business problems into machine learning tasks
c. Developing, training, and tuning deep learning models using appropriate tools
d. Applying deep learning to solve business challenges
e. Utilizing TensorFlow and Keras libraries on Google Colab to implement and explore deep learning
algorithms
f. Recognizing the limitations, ethical concerns, and interpretability issues of deep models in
business decision-making
g. Engaging in a group-based project, where students apply deep learning techniques to some real-
world business problems
learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to
Understand the fundamental principles of neural networks and deep learning algorithms, including their relevance to solving business problems.

Develop and train deep neural networks, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), using TensorFlow and Keras on Google Colab.
Implement and fine-tune models through effective hyperparameter optimization strategies.
Use deep learning techniques to address business use cases.
Conduct group projects that involve problem formulation, data preparation, model development, and presentation of results for real-world business problems.
Assess the challenges, limitations, and ethical implications of deploying deep learning models in business problems.
Communicate technical outcomes and business insights from deep learning models to both technical and non-technical stakeholders. 1

title: PRESCRIPTIVE ANALYTICS WITH MATHEMATICAL
description:
Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive
and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics
entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for
how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases.
The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all
business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that
performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most
management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post-
mortem analysis.
The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to
happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally
external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will
occur.
The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest
actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option.
While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based
company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of
Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data
analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance
improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things
(IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics
and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making.
Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given
the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and
prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution)
based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints.
Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era.
Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and
solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo
from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling
Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved.
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to formulate prescriptive analytics real-life problems and use their applications.
Students will learn the basics of Linear Programming, Transportation and Assignment problems, Integer Programming, Waiting Line Problems, Simulation modeling, and Goal Programming

Students will be able to formulate real-life large-sized problems in Lingo software and solve them. They will also learn how to interpret Lingo results and apply them to real-world decision- making for prescriptive analytics problems.
topics: (I) (i) Operations Research Approach to Problem Solving
Linear Programming (LP): Model Formulation and Graphical Solution
(ii) Linear Programming: Computer Solution and Sensitivity Analysis
Solving Linear Programming (OR) Problems in Lingo
(iii)Linear Programming: Modelling and Applications
(iv) Linear Programming: The Simplex Method
(II) (i)Transportation and Assignment Problem
(ii) Integer Programming (IP) and Goal Programming (GP)
(III) (i) Waiting Lines and Queuing Theory Models
(ii) Simulation Modelling
Some Advanced Applications of Prescriptive Analytics

TB2. Render, B., Stair, Jr., R.M., Hanna, M.E., and Badri, T.N.; Quantitative Analysis for Management, Pearson Education, India, 10th Edition or above.
RB1. Frederick S. Hillier and Mark S. Hillier; Introduction to Management Science: modelling and case studies approach with spreadsheets, McGraw-Hill Irwin, 5th Edition or above.
RB2. Taha, H. A. (2003). Operations research: an introduction. Pearson Education. Some Reference links

title: MARKETING ANALYTICS
description:
This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods,
and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role
of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence,
analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling.
Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and
positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience,
retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as
cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and
diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks,
and optimization.
The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics,
recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on
practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX,
and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights,
evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels,
and brands.
topics: Introduction to Marketing Analytics
Segmentation
Positioning
Product Analytics
Pricing
Marketing Mix
Customer Journey
Nurturing Customers
Customer Analytics
Digital Analytics: Metrics and Measurement
Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
Data Visualization

title: Pricing Analytics
description:
This course provides an introduction to both the theory and the practice of revenue management and pricing,
Fundamentals of price theory, Segmentation and price differentiation, Break- even analysis, Price sensitivity

optimization, The hedonic pricing model, Revenue Management, Monte Carlo simulation for pricing decisions,

primarily through lectures, class discussions and assigned readings.

title: Marketing Research & Metrics
description:
All organizations need to research their markets periodically and employ various elements of
marketing research process viz. problem definition, development of an approach to the problem,
research design formulation, fieldwork & data collection, data preparation & analysis and finally
report preparation and presentation.
The emphasis of the course is proportionately focused on foundational concepts, methodology &
techniques, and marketing research applications. A number of cases will be assigned for discussion
in the class. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” and a project
assignment in this course characterizes this orientation.
To impart necessary foundational concepts, methodologies and tools/techniques for role of
a market researcher. That role envisages generation of actionable, reliable and accurate
information to identify various marketing problems viz. demand forecasting,
segmentation, targeting, positioning, new product development etc. and find their
effective solutions.
topics: Definition of marketing research, marketing research process.
Defining the market research problem and developing an approach to the problem.
Research designs, classification of various research designs, ethical and special considerations in international M.R
Distinction between primary and secondary data, criteria for evaluating secondary data, use of internet in identifying and analyzing secondary data
Classification of qualitative research; focus group, depth interviews and projective techniques.
Classification and comparative evaluation of survey methods. Description of major observation methods.
Conditions of causality, role of validity in experimentation, classification of experimental designs, test marketing
Measurement and scaling procedures, nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio. description of comparative and non- comparative scaling tech
Non-comparative techniques; continuous and itemized rating scales; Likert, semantic differential and staple scale
Purpose, objectives and steps involved in designing

title: FINANCIAL DERIVATIVES AND ANALYSIS
description:
This course introduces students to the fundamentals of financial derivatives and their applications in
managing financial risk. It covers the basic concepts of forwards, futures, options, and swaps, along with
their trading mechanisms, pricing principles, and hedging strategies. Students will also gain an introductory
understanding of option pricing models, including the Binomial and Black–Scholes models, and explore the
use of derivative instruments in equity, currency, interest rate, and fixed-income markets.
topics:  Basics of Derivatives  Derivatives market – Evolution  Derivatives market – Instruments  Derivatives market – Participants

 Short Selling  Repurchase Agreements  Risk & Return: Risk Preferences  Market Efficiency & Theoretical Fair Value  Risk Management: Case Study “Does The Use of Derivatives Impact Bank Performance? A Case Study of Relative Performance during 2002-2009”
 The structure of Forward and Futures Market  Futures Arbitrage Strategies  Forward and Futures Hedging, Spread and Target Strategies  Swaps: Credit Defaults
 Carry Trades and Foreign Currency Arbitrage  Currency Futures  Forward Contracts  Currency Swaps  Hedging Concepts  Hedging Contingent Foreign Currency Risk
 Understanding Index  Attributes of an Index  Index Construction, Maintenance and Revision: Case of BSE Indices  Target Beta with Stock Index Futures
 Treasury Bond Futures  Intermediate- and Long-Term Interest Rate Arbitrage  Target Duration with Bond Futures  Tactical Asset Allocation Using Bond Futures
 Structure & Development of Options Market  Call & Put Options  Over-the-Counter Options  Options Terminology

 Spot, Strike, Time Decay  Volatility  Option Greeks  Analysis of Call Option Trading from Buyer’s versus Seller’s Perspective  Analysis of Put Option Trading from Buyer’s versus Seller’s Perspective
 The Binomial Pricing Model  The Black & Scholes Model  Using Black-Scholes-Merton Model to understand volatility
 Terminology & Notations  Stock Transactions  Synthetic Puts and Calls  Option Spreads

title: Financial Modelling and Valuation
description:
A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's
value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by
increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise
acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every
significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is
to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed
to make thoughtful decisions on company value.
This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a
company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial
valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial
statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality
because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies.
We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company.
This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment
banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who
would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their
knowledge of financial analysis and discover how companies produce and quantify value for
their investors.

title: People Analytics
description:
There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises,
questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that
will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases
and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this
course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through
Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test
comprehension of the theory and readings.
People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of
Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding
of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging
discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations.
However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all
people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key
driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data
driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory,
Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data
analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip
students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve,
analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation
information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating
the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in
students’ value addition and employability.
The learning objectives of the course are as under:
 This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of
human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting.
 The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and
the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision
making.
 The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR
related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.
 Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources
information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).
 Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human
resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.
 Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make
data driven decision making.
 Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results.
textbooks: HR Analytics: Understanding Theories and Applications (2017), by Dipak Kumar Bhattacharyya, Sage Publications, 2017.
Making Human Capital Analytics Work: Measuring the ROI of Human Capital Processes and Outcomes, by Jack Philips and Patricia Philips, McGraw-Hill Education, 2019.
references: The HR Scorecard: Linking People, Strategy, and Performance, by Brian E. Becker, Mark A. Huselid, Mark A Huselid, David Ulrich, 2001.
Predictive Analytics for Human Resources by Fitz-enz Jac and Mattox II John, Wiley, 2nd Edition, 2014.

and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this
course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through
Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test
comprehension of the theory and readings.
People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of
Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding
of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging
discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations.
However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all
people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key
driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data
driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory,
Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data
analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip
students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve,
analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation
information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating
the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in
students’ value addition and employability.
The learning objectives of the course are as under:
 This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of
human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting.
 The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and
the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision
making.
 The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR
related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.
 Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources
information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).
 Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human
resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.
 Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make
data driven decision making.
 Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results.

title: Supply Chain Modelling and Empirical Analysis
description:
The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insight into the
application of various supply chain modelling approaches and empirical analysis for
evidence driven decision making in supply chain. The objectives of the course are:
• To introduce concept of decision making on the basis of multiple experts’
opinion on various different supply chain problems, practices and strategies.
• To develop skill sets to analyze the qualitative data with a focus on empirical
modelling for data driven decisions in supply chain.
• To develop model for life cycle analysis for measuring environmental
sustainability in supply chain.
• To understand and analyse the various aspects of digital supply chain,
cultural implications and their impact on supply chain performance.

title: Pharmaceutical Analysis
description:
Basic techniques of pharmaceutical analysis, data handling and analysis, sources of
error in analysis. The analytical methods would comprise various titrimetric methods, such as acid-base,
complexometric, non-aqueous, oxidation-reduction, precipitation, conductometric; physical and instrumental
analysis such as gravimetric, polarography, nephelometry, amperometry, turbidometry, potentiometry;
chromatographic separations such as TLC, column, ion-exchange, extraction methods such as gel-filtration,
fractionation processes, analysis of metallic and non-metallic elements; water content, as well as evaluation
of drug constituents in various pharmaceutical preparation.
The objective of this course is to provide students with knowledge
of basic principles of quantitative analytical chemistry necessary for use and interpretation of pharmaceutical
methods of analysis especially those methods official in the Indian, United States and British
Pharmacopoeias.

title: PHARMACEUTICAL FORMULATIONS II
description:
Physical, chemical, and biopharmaceutical considerations in formulations, absorption,
distribution, and elimination of drugs; pharmaceutical additives; formulation, manufacturing, packaging,
quality control, and stability of solid dosage forms, semi-solid dosage forms, liquids dosage forms, and
sterile preparations including parenteral suspensions, emulsions, depot formulations; microencapsulation
and controlled release formulations; targeted drug delivery systems; multi-unit particulate systems;
transdermal, gastroretentive, and nasopulmonary drug delivery systems; aerosol products and packaging.
It is a course intended to give students insight into the problems
involved in making drug dosage forms. It brings together the various sciences involved in developing
pharmaceutical product formulations and evaluating their quality. The laboratory component involves some
fundamental exercises in the evolution of products such as tablets, ointments, solutions, parenteral products,
sustained-action medications, etc. It also imparts knowledge of newer dosage forms.
learning_outcomes: CLO1. Explain the principles of preformulation, formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of conventional pharmaceutical dosage forms, including solid, liquid, semi-solid, and sterile preparations. CLO2. Apply pharmaceutical formulation principles and standard manufacturing techniques to prepare and evaluate conventional and modified-release dosage forms, while adhering to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and quality requirements. CLO3. Compare and evaluate the design, advantages, limitations, and pharmaceutical applications of novel drug delivery systems, including controlled-release, targeted, transdermal, gastroretentive, multiparticulate, nasopulmonary, and aerosol dosage forms.

good manufacturing practices and international certification. This course also deals with

title: Herbal Drug Technology
description:
Operations in the herbal drug industry, the quality of raw material, guidelines for
quality of herbal drugs, classical ayurvedic and conventional formulations, nutraceuticals, herbal
cosmetics, herbal excipients, etc. Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), patenting, and regulatory issues
of herbal drugs.
This course will give a basic understanding of the herbal drug industry, the quality
of raw material, and knowledge of the WHO and ICH guidelines for evaluation of herbal drugs, herbal
cosmetics, natural sweeteners etc.

Students will understand Patenting & Regulatory requirements of natural products CLO3. Students will learn about Indian Systems of Medicine

title: QUALITY ASSURANCE & REGULATORY AFFAIRS
description:
Quality control, assurance and management, various parameters for achieving quality
pharmaceutical products, application of statistics in quality assurance, reliability, cGMP for
pharmaceutical manufacturing , pharmaceutical process validation, drug regulatory affairs, clinical
research protocols, new drug applications.
This course deals with the basic need of quality in the manufacturing of Pharmaceutical products
and it's build up with the help of quality control and quality assurance management. Various
current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP) to be followed in a pharmaceutical organization and
its validation procedure are part of the course. This course also covers the regulatory procedures
applicable in clinical trials and approval of new drug products.

title: PARENTERAL PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT
description:
B Introduction to parenteral product & their types, products characteristics;
Vehicles requirement for Parenteral Products manufacturing; Formulation & process consideration
for development of parenteral products; Introduction & understanding of various aspects of unit
operation in parenteral product manufacturing; Critical Quality attributes of Parenteral Product;
Various Sterilization techniques for parenteral products; Understanding of key requirements for
aseptic processing; Understanding of Lyophilization techniques of stable product development;
Regulatory consideration for safety assessment of Parenteral Products; Packaging requirement for
Parenteral Drug Products; Regulatory perspective for Complex Injectable products development and
filing.
This course will provide overview on parenteral product development &
designed for students to understand critical aspect of parenteral product development and
manufacturing. This course covers basic information, understanding and application of key
operations followed during parenteral product manufacturing like lyophilization, aseptic processing,
& filtration along with Quality Assurance, control & packaging requirement. This course also covers
regulatory consideration for parenteral product assessment with respect to safety for intended
application.
learning_outcomes: Complete understanding of formulation, process, manufacturing and packaging aspect of parenteral drug product
Complete understanding, importance & application of lyophilization process.
Knowledge of critical quality attributes in parenteral product development.
Knowledge of regulatory expectation for safety assessment of parenteral products
topics: Introduction, Historical Perspective, Characteristics & Types
• Aqueous - Key requirement for High Quality water system (WFI) for parenteral product • Non-aqueous solvents

• Formulation development - Selection & optimization of various excipients like Buffers, antioxidants, surfactants, pH adjusting agents, tonicity modiViers, etc. to obtain desired quality attributes • Process development – Key consideration for process development and control of parameters like temperature, light, oxygen, hydrolysis, etc.

(cid:0) Introduction & understanding of various aspects of parenteral product manufacturing unit operations like dispensing, compounding, Villing, stoppering, sealing, inspection, labelling & packaging

• Introduction, understanding & compendial requirement for various quality attributes like • Physical – Surface Tension, Viscosity, Particulate Matter, Color, Clarity, etc. • Chemical – Assay, Impurities, content of functional excipients, etc. • Microbiological – Bioburden, BET, Sterility, CCIT, etc.

• Selection of sterilization method – Decision Tree • Terminal Sterilization – Dry Heat and moist heat Sterilization, Cycle development, D-value determination, validation, Indicator, Minimum Maximum load Filtration – Types of Vilters like Cartridge, Capsule, Depth, Membrane Vilters, etc.; Filter Material of Construction like PES, PVDF, Nylon, PTFE, etc.; Modes of Viltration – Series Viltration, Parallel Viltration, etc.; Filter validation studies. Basic understanding and application of other techniques like Ethylene oxid sterilization, Gamma Sterilization, E- beam sterilization, X-ray sterilization, etc.

(cid:0) Understanding of key requirements for aseptic processing like (cid:0) Personnel, Equipment and building requirement (cid:0) Cleaning, disinfection & sterilization requirement – CIP, SIP, VHP, etc. (cid:0) Media Vill trials – overview and Approaches

title: Immunopharmacology
description:
This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated,
organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and
immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its
components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and
mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological
disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic
disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help
the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong
learning and career development.
topics: Introduction to Immunology
Humoral Immunity
Cell-mediated Immunity
Infection and Immunity
Vaccinology
Transplantation immunology
Tumor immunology
Autoimmunity
Immunodeficiency diseases, allergy and hypersensitivity reactions
Immunodiagnostics
textbooks: Kuby Immunology by Owen et al., 7th Ed. Freeman press. 2013.

title: Modern Pharmaceutical Analytical Techniques
description:
This course is a laboratory oriented course and covers various analytical aspects like principles of sample
preparation, method development for analysis and characterization of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API)
and formulations, using techniques such as High Performance Liquid chromatography (HPLC), bio-
chromatography, size exclusion, affinity, chiral, fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC). Characterization of
nanopharmaceutcials using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM),
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) techniques. 1H and 13C Nuclear
Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in structural characterization, Mass Spectrometry and its applications,
Elemental analysis, Optical, chiro-optical techniques in structure elucidation.
The course is aimed at exposing the students to modern analytical techniques in relevance to pharmaceutical
industries. Training with respect to the handling and operation of sophisticated instruments, interpretation of
results obtained for the characterization of molecules, their qualitative and quantitative evaluation are emphasized.
learning_outcomes: Handling of analytical instruments for performing qualitative and quantitative analyses of drugs. Design and development of suitable analytical methods for drugs based on their physico-chemical characters meeting the standard requirements. Ability to interpret the analytical graphs and spectra for drug identification, characterization, evaluation and decision making.

title: Computer Aided Drug Design
description:
3D structure and function of bio-molecules; targets of drugs and design principles; molecular modeling
methodologies; quantitative structure-activity relationships; chemical compound databases and search tools;
interactive graphics in drug design; molecular surfaces and algorithm of automated docking of drugs into
receptor sites; receptor mapping; introduction to molecular modeling and docking software.
To develop an appreciation of inter- and intra- molecular energies and forces. To introduce the techniques of
computational chemistry and to demonstrate their application to the design of drugs. To demonstrate the use
of simulation as an alternative to experimental work. On completion the student should be aware of the scope
and limitations of the various theoretical and computational tools available to the pharmaceutical scientist and
of the application of these techniques in the design of novel drugs. The student will also have gained insight
into the practical implementation of the methods of molecular and bio-molecular modeling.
topics: Drug design overview, reason for failures of drugs, stages where computational methods can be used
Drug likeliness criteria, lead likeliness, hurdles in drug discovery
textbooks: Manfred E Wolff- "Burger's Medicinal Chemistry and Drug Discovery", Wiley-Interscience, Seventh Edition, N.Y., 2010, Vol. I - VIII.
references: P.K.Larson, T.Liljefors & U.Madsen- “Textbook of Drug Design and Discovery”, 1st edition, Indian edition, Chennai, 2004.
Cramer, C. J. Essentials of Computational Chemistry: Theories and Models; Second Edition, Wiley, 2004. Besides the above relevant information on the topics are also available in the following
Annual Reports in Medicinal Chemistry - Academic Press Inc, Various volumes.
Journal of Medicinal Chemistry-ACS-Different Volumes.

title: Computer Aided Drug Design
description:
3D structure and function of bio-molecules; targets of drugs and design principles; molecular modeling
methodologies; quantitative structure-activity relationships; chemical compound databases and search tools;
interactive graphics in drug design; molecular surfaces and algorithm of automated docking of drugs into
receptor sites; receptor mapping; introduction to molecular modeling and docking software.
To develop an appreciation of inter- and intra- molecular energies and forces. To introduce the techniques of
computational chemistry and to demonstrate their application to the design of drugs. To demonstrate the use
of simulation as an alternative to experimental work. On completion the student should be aware of the scope
and limitations of the various theoretical and computational tools available to the pharmaceutical scientist and
of the application of these techniques in the design of novel drugs. The student will also have gained insight
into the practical implementation of the methods of molecular and bio-molecular modeling.
topics: Drug design overview, reason for failures of drugs, stages where computational methods can be used
Drug likeliness criteria, lead likeliness, hurdles in drug discovery

title: Advanced Physical Pharmaceutics
description:
Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like,
pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and
solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study,
specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed
details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in-vitro in-vivo correlation
(IVIVC), polymer science, etc.
Prior to the development of any dosage form with a new or old drug candidate, it is essential that certain
fundamental physical and chemical properties of the drug molecule and other derived properties of the drug
are determined. This information dictates possible approaches in formulation development. The aim of this
course is to make the students understand those physicochemical principles which must be applied in the
formulation and development of an efficacious dosage form, so that required duration and intensity of effect
can be ensured at the intended site of action.
topics: 1. Introduction to physical pharmaceutics
2. Overview of pharmaceutical product development.
1. Overview of preformulation studies carried out during/ prior to formulation development
2. Rational approach to development and validation of stability-indicating analytical method
3. Study and impact of polymorphism, hydrates, hygroscopicity; vapour pressure
4. Determination of solubility. Factors/ parameters affecting solubility
5. Impact of powder densities, particle size, particle size distribution on process and product performance
6. Compatibility test for solid and liquid dosage forms.
1. Important physicochemical/ mechanical aspects to be considered during design and formulation of good quality pharmaceutical preparations
1. Stability studies of drug substances and drug products with special reference to ICH guidelines,
2. Specifications and impurity limits
3. Physical stability testing of pharmaceutical preparations
1. Concept and parameters of optimization, optimization techniques in pharmaceutical formulation and processing.
1. Principles and applications of adsorption; Factors affecting surface tension and Pharmaceutical applications of surfactants
2. Newtonian and Non- Newtonian flow characteristics and application
1. Various types of polymers employed in dosage forms and approach for choosing the right ones; Mechanism of release with respect to polymers
1. Principles of diffusion and dissolution, Release characterization
2. In-vitro drug release (dissolution) test design. Similarity factors – f2 and f1
3. In vitro - in vivo correlations (IVIVC) with respect to BCS classification
4. Linearity Concept of significance, Standard deviation, students T-test , ANOVA test.
1. Recent journal articles for discussion
textbooks: Carstensen, J. T, Pharmaceutical Preformulation. Technomic Publishing comp. USA.
references: Carstensen, J. T., Rhodes, C.T., 2000. Drug Stability: Principles and Practices, Drugs and Pharm. Sci. Series, Vol. 43, 3rd edn, Marcel Dekker Inc., New York.
Martin’s Physical Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences.
ICH Q guidelines -http://www.ich.org/fileadmin/Public_Web_Site/ICH_Products/ Guidelines/Quality
Sanford Bolton, Charles Bon, Pharmaceutical Statistics, Informa Healthcare, 5th Edition, 2010.

title: CLINICAL RESEARCH
description:
Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board;
regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP);
related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study
design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial
management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology,
implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data
interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report
preparation for various submissions.
There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical,
biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the
development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in
conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to
the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills
required to design, monitor, and manage clinical trials. Courses include the drug
development process; regulations, guidelines, and standards; research methodology and
biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring, and documentation; and project
management.
topics: I ntroduction to clinical research
Regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA applications
Decision on goals; primary questions to be answered; decision on response variables, population, and patient selection
Designs for clinical trials, classification of clinical trials, blinding, randomization techniques, baseline assessment
Clinical trial protocol, recruitment, case report form, and data management
Data quality and its control, problems in data collection, and methods to minimize poor data, participant compliance, monitoring response variables, and study termination methods
textbooks: Lawrence M Friedman, Curt D Furberg and David L DeMets, "Fundamentals of Clinical Trials”, Spring Verlag, New York, 5th Ed., 2015.
Shein-Chung Chow, Jen-Pei Liu, “Design and Analysis of Clinical Trials”, Wiley-IEEE, 2013.
references: Steven Piantadosi, “Clinical Trials-A Methodologic Perspective”, John Wiley & Sons, 2005.
R A Guarino, "New Drug Approval Process" Marcel Dekker, New York, 2nd Edn., Vol. 56, 1993. 1

title: Pharmacokinetics & Clinical Pharmacy
description:
Introduction to pharmacokinetic modeling of drugs; Compartmental modeling including one
compartmental and two compartmental models; Non-compartmental analysis (NCA); Bioequivalence and
comparative bioavailability studies; Pharmacokinetic Pharmacodynamic modeling techniques,
determination of order of absorption and absorption rate constant by Wagner-Nelson method; non-linear
pharmacokinetics; Pharmacokinetic drug interactions; multi-dose pharmacokinetics of drugs following one
compartmental model; Design of multi-dose regimen; Dosage regimen adjustment in renal impairment;
Application of the pharmacokinetic principles for better therapeutic outcomes
The course imparts knowledge of pharmacokinetics, its application, pharmacokinetic studies, mathematical
modeling, and experimental design. This will help students to gain knowledge in a very important area of
pharmacy. Practicals are designed to expose students to pharmacokinetic studies.

title: Pharmaceutical Biotechnology
description:
The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the
field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular biology,
molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bio-
informatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. The
applications of genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, hybridoma technology,
transgenic animals, gene therapy, drug delivery aspects of biotechnology products and their clinical
evaluation are also dealt with in this course.

title: Pharmaceutical Administration & Management (PAM)
description:
This course introduces students to various organizational aspects, focusing on pharmaceutical
management. Topics include technology innovation, drug planning, strategy, project execution, product
development, production, scale-up, marketing, IPR, HR, industrial relations, documentation, R&D, and ethics.
The objective of the course is to help students understand new drug and
product considerations and planning; strategic considerations; project implementation; product development;
production management & scale-up; marketing strategy; human resources development; ethical issues; and R&D
management.
learning_outcomes: CLO1: Explain the principles of pharmaceutical product innovation, new drug and product planning, strategic decision-making, project implementation, and product development processes in the pharmaceutical industry. CLO2: Apply the concepts of production management, scale-up, documentation, intellectual property rights (IPR), and marketing strategies to evaluate pharmaceutical product development and commercialization. CLO3: Analyze the roles of research and development (R&D) management, human resource development, industrial relations, and ethical practices in achieving sustainable and compliant pharmaceutical operations.

Mickey C. Smith, Principles of Pharmaceutical Marketing, Lea & Febiger, 3rd Edition.

title: Advanced Drug Delivery Systems
description:
A study of physicochemical and biopharmaceutical factors involved in the design of novel drug delivery systems like
mucosal, particulate systems for systemic delivery of bioactive molecules. Special considerations for delivery of protein,
peptide and other biological products. In vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel drug delivery systems
The prime objective of this course is to impart knowledge of design, development and evaluation of novel drug delivery
systems (NDDS). The primary focus would be on integrating the biopharmaceutical, physiochemical and physiological
properties for design and development of (NDDS) with due consideration of pharmacological action. Excipients used
in design and development of NDDS would be covered exhaustively.

title: Retrosynthetic Analysis
description:
This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic
molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically
to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and
understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course.
Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to
develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This
course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic
Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug
molecules with appropriate justification.
topics: Introduction & basic concepts of retrosynthetic analysis
Retrosynthesis of Aromatic compounds
One group C-X disconnections
Chemoselectivity as strategy
Two group C-X disconnections
Umpolung strategy
Amine synthesis
One Group and Two Group C-C Disconnections
Regioselectivity as strategy
Alkenes and alkynes
Carbonyl condensation as strategy
Two Group C-C Disconnections: 1,3-, 1,5-, 1,2- 1,4-, and 1,6 difunctionalized compounds
Reconnection as strategy

description:
This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in

title: Classical Mechanics
description:
This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical
perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles,
central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies
in inertial, and rotating reference frames.
To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the
mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with
elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics,
including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity.
learning_outcomes: Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.

Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.
Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.

Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects.
topics: Vector Algebra: Basic Operations, Differential Operators (Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian) in curvilinear coordinate systems, Multivariable Calculus (total derivatives and chain rule)
Newtonian mechanics for a particle/system of particles: Conservation principles, etc.
Constrained Motions: Classification of constraints. Degree of freedom (DOF), generalized coordinates.
Systematic methods to eliminate/bypass constraints, Principle of virtual work, d’Alembert’s principle (may shock you at first and certainly test your patience!), Euler- Lagrange’s (E-L) equation
Setting up the problem through Lagrangian approach: Reduction of two-body problem to an equivalent one-body problem.
Two first integrals of motion, classification of orbits based on bounded/unbounded motion, stability criteria, closure property, etc.
Orbits under inverse-square law of force, any deviation from inverse square law? Qualitative understanding of precession of orbits via phenomenological model.
Principle of least action : Fermat’s principle in optics, Geodesics for material bodies, Material bodies in conservative force fields (Brachistochrone, Tautochrone, etc.)
Derivation of the Euler– Lagrange Equations from Hamilton’s principle
Derivation of conserved quantities from the symmetries of the Lagrangian
Construction of the Hamiltonian from Lagrangian (the Lagrangian's twin sibling!) through duality transformation.
Four basic CTs and the corresponding generating functions (GF)
Poisson bracket and other canonical invariants (where you start sensing quantum mechanics lurking in the background!)
Independent Coordinates, Orthogonal Transformations, Formal properties of transformation matrix
Euler Angles, Finite and Infinitesimal Rotations
Rate of Change of a vector, Coriolis Effects (hard to avoid when you're sitting in a lecture room on the rotating Earth!)
textbooks: H. Goldstein, C. Poole, and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, Third Edition, Pearson Edu. Inc., 2002.
N. C. Rana and P. S. Joag, Classical Mechanics, McGraw Hill, First Edition, 2008.
references: L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, Mechanics, Third Edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2000.
L. N. Hand and J. D. Finch, Analytical Mechanics, Cambridge Univ. Press, 1998. 1

title: STATISTICAL MECHANICS
description:
This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics,
quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of
equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems.
Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant
interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth
century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the
subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that
scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of
matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required
classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in
bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves.
In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of
basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course
aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging
the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions.
❖ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics.
❖ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic
descriptions of thermodynamic systems
❖ Learn key methods of ensemble theory
❖ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of
ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems.

learn to use scientific programming and visualization tools, including Monte Carlo and Markov Chain
