title: Particle Physics
description:
(Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the
course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it
addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a
fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of
paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in
place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the
course.)
Bright blue sky:
What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics?
1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the
Universe?
2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural
hierarchy we see at different levels?
3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above
questions?
4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental
particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the
answers we know?
Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our
present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle
Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle
Physics.
Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory:
Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle
physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of
fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and
their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and
smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely
high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths).
Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and
1
baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures
relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the
momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons
are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily
large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your
underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily
large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system
of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic
interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is
demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can
survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle
physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and
classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative
calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow
an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle
physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle
physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them.
From relativistic quantum mechanics to scattering cross-sections and decay rate:
Answers to questions 1 and 2 have been the content of the latter half of your Nuclear and Particle Physics
course. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot
about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on
calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of
relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also
discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will
introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations
in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman
diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that
is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure.
Indiscreet fall of the discrete symmetries:
Symmetry transformations can be continuous or discrete. Discrete symmetries are essentially invariances
under a discrete transformation and will be the subject of module-4. Their examples are parity (P) (inversion
about origin, i.e., changing x,y,z to -x,-y,-z), time reversal (T) (changing t to -t), and charge conjugation (C)
(changing particles to antiparticles and vice versa). Naively, Physics was expected to be invariant under
each of these discrete transformations separately. However, it turns out that individually, each of them is
violated. In fact, the so-called CPT theorem states that any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with
a Hermitian Hamiltonian must be invariant under the combined transformation of Charge conjugation (C),
Parity (P), and Time reversal (T). It turns out that the weak interactions violate all three (C, P, and T) and
also the combination CP. However, the combined CPT transformation is so far known to be an exact
symmetry and any violation of CPT would signal a fundamental trouble either in quantum mechanics or
relativity or local interactions. The Story of the separate violations of C, P, and T is intricately tied to the
story of weak interaction and will be covered in module 5.
Building the Universe from scratch - the blocks and the glue:
2
Module-6 would be the last module of the course and will answer question number 4 in the affirmative and
offer a convincing discourse on the same. Until the advent of Particle Physics in the 20th century,
symmetries and conservation laws largely served a utilitarian purpose of bookkeeping. Conservation laws
offer our first shot at dynamics without having to confront the dynamics head-on. Just look at the stuff
before and after a dynamical event, and if conservation laws are applicable, we can pull out the unknown
energy or momentum by a straightforward bookkeeping of conserved quantum numbers. However, during
the latter half of the 20th century, we learnt that the symmetries aren’t just utilitarian. They are the rhyme
and the reason behind why things are the way they are.
What do you need to build the Universe from scratch? The bricks (fundamental particles), the cement (glue
to bind them to form bound states), and a blueprint (the Lagrangian). All of these and much more are a
consequence of some symmetry principles which can be broadly divided into two categories -- spacetime
symmetries (Lorentz or, strictly speaking, Poincaré symmetries), and internal or local gauge symmetries. So
the question of kinematics, or why the fundamental particles of different mass and spin exist at all, is
answered by the spacetime symmetries. Particles of different mass and spin exist as representations of
Poincare group. On the other hand, the question of the existence of three different fundamental interactions
(excluding gravity for the moment) is answered by the "internal" local gauge symmetries. They are
"internal" in the sense that they operate in an abstract internal space different from the "external" spacetime.
All the fundamental interactions are explained within the overarching theme of gauge theories.
How to break a symmetry without actually breaking it? A massive question:
If you think the question is an oxymoron and with a blatant misuse of adjectives, please bear with me until
the mist clears. We now have the basic building blocks (particles) and the glue (interactions) which bind
them in place as a consequence of spacetime (Poincaré) and internal (Gauge) symmetries. But what is the
origin of the mass of the particles? It turns out that you cannot just put a mass term in your fundamental
Lagrangian by hand and get on with the business. The question of mass is intricately tied to the question of
Lorentz invariance and gauge invariance, and will be covered in the latter half of module 6. In a jigsaw
puzzle, each piece is constrained by the shape of the neighbouring pieces. We cannot accommodate mass
without fundamentally tweaking the particle content and introducing a "subtle breaking" of the gauge
symmetries. There are three different ways in which a symmetry can be broken: explicit, spontaneous, and
anomalous (beyond the scope of the course). It turns out that putting a mass term by hand explicitly breaks
the local gauge symmetry, and that is nothing short of a sacrilege in particle physics. We can nevertheless
break it through the "back door", that is, break it spontaneously! Our Lagrangian, equations of motion,
commutation relations, and Feynman rules all respect gauge symmetry, and yet, the choice of a ground state
violates the symmetry. Spontaneous symmetry breaking may appear mysterious, but it is rather common.
The most famous example is that of a ferromagnet. Its Hamiltonian is invariant under rotational symmetry.
This is why, above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature, thanks to thermal agitation, all the
spin dipoles are randomly oriented and hence the net magnetization averages out to zero. However, below
the Curie temperature, all dipoles spontaneously align in a specific direction, giving non-zero net
magnetization. The Hamiltonian is still rotationally invariant, and yet magnetic dipoles select a specific
direction and align. It turns out that to realize such spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics, we
need to add a spin-0 field and its accompanying dynamics. How exactly the machinery of the Higgs
mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking end up endowing fundamental particles with mass cannot
be elaborated here. It is said that the proof of the pudding is in eating. We hope to get this far and discuss
these issues.
3
Dark Clouds:
We started with bright blue skies and end with dark clouds. I wish I could end this preface on a positive
note. However, truth be told, all of our knowledge about fundamental particles and their interactions is like a
small lamp in a largely dark room. I am collecting here a laundry list of questions about which we have only
speculations to offer without any hint of empirical verification.
The above description conveys the scope and objective in great
detail.

title: SOFT CONDENSED MATTER PHYSICS
description:
Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems
that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations.
They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These
materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale
comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant.
In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter.
What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter?
• Develop familiarity with the basics of soft condensed matter.
• To develop an understanding about the forces and order of thermal fluctuations in soft matter.
• Why some part of matter is classified as soft matter?

title: Group Theory and Applications
description:
This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with
an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a
simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these
symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual
group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain
a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as
‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups.
We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical
mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.
• Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational
concepts of group theory.
• Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible
components and interpret their physical significance.
• Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry
structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies.
• Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such
as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups.
• Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie
groups and Lie algebras.
topics: L1: Introduction of the course in view of its necessity in the context of fundamental physics; the course structure will be briefed
L2—L3: Importance of symmetry in nature and in natural law, groups as the language of symmetry, definition and introduction.

L4—L7: Subgroups, cosets, invariant and normal subgroups, quotient groups and product groups, Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms. L8—L12: Group representation: unitary representation, reducible and irreducible representation, direct sum and tensor products, character table, Schur’s lemmas.

L13—L17: Lie groups, infinitesimal transformation, Jacobi identity, structure constants, killing forms, subalgebras; Real and Complex Lie algebra, Irreducible representations of Lie groups and Lie algebras; Adjoint Representations.

L18—L20: Rotations and Angular Momentum, SO(3) and SU(2), Infinitesimal rotations and generators, covering groups, applications, introduction to Spinor representations, Clifford algebra, Dirac matrices, Majorana and Weyl fermions, Representations of SU(3), Pauli vs Gell-Mann matrices
L21—L24: Relativistic symmetries, Lorentz and Poincaré groups, introduction to particle representations, Casimir operators.

L25—L38: Introduction to Cartan-Weyl basis, Classification of simple Lie algebras, Roots and weights, Dynkin diagrams, SU(3) representations revisited, Eightfold way, Isospin, Meson and Baryon masses, symmetry breaking, color, introduction to Abelian and Non-Abelian gauge groups

Lie Algebras in Particle Physics, H. Georgi, (Westview Press)
Group Theory a Physicist’s Survey, Pierre Ramond, (Cambridge University)
Group Theory in a Nutshell for Physicists, A. Zee, (Princeton).

title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices
description:
This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays
an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum
theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the
devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed.
The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of the basic phenomenon of the semiconductor devices.
The main content of the course is having theoretical description of these devices which is an essential requirement in
order to understand the operational details of any device.
topics:  Crystal Structures  Miller Indices  Imperfections and Impurities in Solids  Growth of Semiconducting Materials
 Energy bands and band gap.  Energy Band theory of semiconductors  Electrical Conduction in solids
 Fermi Dirac Distribution  Charge carriers in Semiconductors

references: Physics of Semiconductor Devices, S.M. Sze, K.K. Ng, Wiley India, 3e, 2007. Introduction to Solid State Physics – Charles Kittel, Wiley, 8th Edition.

title: Classical and Quantum Waves
description:
This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics,
tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics.
We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced
oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and
frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of
a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall
study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction.
Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle
duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg
uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a
particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce
scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.
● Understand oscillatory motion: Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the
effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor
● Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes,
and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling
waves, and energy transport
● Analyze wave behavior and propagation: Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how
waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference
● Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and
the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and
1
energy quantization in simple systems
● Apply quantum tunneling to real-world technology: Calculate transmission coefficients for barrier
tunneling and connect this phenomenon to practical applications such as scanning tunneling microscopy
learning_outcomes: Develop the ability to analyze and understand oscillatory mechanical systems that are coupled
Ability to solve the wave equation for certain boundary conditions
To understand Interference and diffraction phenomena
To describe wave-particle duality and the photon concept, derive the de Broglie wavelength for matter waves, and articulate the physical meaning of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle
Solve the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a one-dimensional box, interpret the resulting wavefunctions, and calculate the quantized energy levels of the system
Calculate the transmission coefficient for a particle tunneling through a potential barrier, and explain how this phenomenon underlies the operation of a scanning tunneling microscope

Potential Energy Minima, and
Departure from stability
Effect of Viscous Damping, Decay of Free Vibrations, Quality Parameter, Light Damping, Critical Damping, Heavy Damping
of Free Vibrations, Quality
Parameter, Light Damping,
Critical Damping, Heavy Damping

Concepts of Modern Physics by Arthur Beiser, Shobit Mahajan, and S. Rai Choudhury, Tata McGraw-Hill Companies, 2006

title: Introduction to Classical and Quantum Waves
description:
Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic
oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal
waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave
equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves,
introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle
duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications;
Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers.
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and
quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and
progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition
from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in
an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and
lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes
physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical
formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and
quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced
courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines.
learning_outcomes: (i) Explain the principles of simple harmonic motion and analyze damped and forced oscillations, resonance, and the superposition of oscillatory motion as the foundation of wave phenomena. 1 (ii) Describe the behavior of classical waves, including wave propagation, wave equations, energy transport, sound waves, and the formation of standing waves in one-dimensional systems. (iii) Explain the wave nature of light through interference and diffraction and discuss the experimental observations that established the quantum nature of light, including the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. (iv) Describe the concept of matter waves by explaining wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the extension of wave concepts from light to material particles. (v) Interpret the physical meaning of quantum wave functions in one dimension and explain their role in describing quantum systems, including an introductory understanding of multi-electron atoms through Pauli's exclusion principle and the principles of X-rays and lasers.

Crawford Jr, Special Indian Edition, McGraw-Hill, 2011. (iii) Fundamentals of Optics, Fourth International Edition, Jenkins & White, McGraw-Hill, 1981. (iv) Concepts of Modern Physics, 7th Edition, Arthur Beiser, McGraw-Hill, 2017

title: Fundamentals of Supply Chain – Concepts
description:
The fundamentals of supply chain – concepts course is aimed at providing a solid grounding
and understanding of what constitutes a supply chain, setting the stage for more advanced
topics. The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insights into the
various key components and concepts of the supply chain. This course will assist in
understanding Supply Chain Management (SCM) not as a technology but rather a business
strategy tool for the companies trying to create competitive advantage in the market.
The objectives of the course are mentioned below:
• Attain familiarity with the fundamental concepts of the SCM and its use in organizations.
• Understand the key components of the Supply Chain and the interrelationships.
• Importance of supply chain in today’s business environment and the impact of
Globalization.
• Supply Chain emerging trends

Identify and analyze the key components, entities, processes, and CO2 interrelationships within a supply chain ecosystem. CO3 Apply supply chain concepts and models to understand and evaluate sourcing, procurement, manufacturing, inventory, warehousing, transportation, and order-fulfilment processes. CO4 Analyze the impact of globalization, e-commerce, digitalization, AI, automation, and emerging technologies on supply chain performance and competitiveness. CO5 Evaluate supply chain strategies, drivers, performance metrics, risks, and resilience mechanisms to achieve strategic fit and competitive advantage. CO6 Discuss emerging supply chain practices, including supply chain analytics, Generative AI, sustainability, and circular economy approaches, for improving supply chain efficiency and creating business value.

title: Advanced Operations Management
description:
Types of Manufacturing, Manufacturing, maintenance, quality and service operations management concepts.
Manufacturing Management measures, Factory/plant performance, Operations Improvement framework.
Maintenance management, optimising maintenance costs; Improving asset lifecycle; Preventive maintenance;
Total productive maintenance (TPM); Quality management - practices and processes; Total quality
management (TQM); Service Operations Management definition; Customer loyalty and satisfaction.
This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the
manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view
of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply
chain. The objectives of the course are mentioned below:
• This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and
maintenance management as practised on the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing
operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure
operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed. This will
help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are
critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain.
• This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various
quality management tools and techniques used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and
services are produced.
• This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design,
service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed.
topics: Course introduction. Definition and scope of operations management. Role of operations management in organisations. Functions and challenges of operations management. Types of manufacturing (job, batch, mass, continuous). Product-process matrix: linking volume- variety with process choice. Breakeven Analysis.

Productivity measures (labour, capital, multi- factor productivity). Numerical: productivity index calculation. Cycle time, throughput, takt time. Numerical: takt time and throughput calculation for a given demand/production scenario. Capacity utilisation and efficiency measures. Numerical: capacity utilisation and efficiency exercise from plant output data.
Role of maintenance in operations management. Maintenance definition, need, objectives, functions, benefits, and impact. Standards in maintenance management.

Evolution of maintenance. Types of strategies: reactive, preventive, predictive, and prescriptive maintenance. The bathtub curve and product failure behaviour; predicting failures with condition monitoring; understanding the P-F interval and the P-F curve; selecting a maintenance strategy based on machine asset type; functional blocks of digital maintenance; and sustainability aspects.

Measuring failures and KPIs: failure rate, MTTF, MTBF, MTTR, downtime, availability, maintainability. Maintenance trade-offs: preventive cost vs. breakdown cost, optimal maintenance interval. Preventive Maintenance (PM) modelling. Hands-on exercise for designing PM schedules.

Predictive maintenance workflow: acquire data, pre-process data, identify health indicators, train the model using machine learning, deploy, and integrate. Remaining useful life, hyperparameter tuning, performance assessment. Industrial use cases and success stories. Hands-on: building a predictive maintenance model with a linear regression algorithm.

TPM philosophy, objective of TPM, TPM vs traditional planned maintenance, 5S foundation, TPM pillars (autonomous maintenance, planned maintenance, quality maintenance, focused improvement, early equipment management, training and education, safety, health, environment, TPM in administration), benefits of TPM. Factory/plant performance: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE), productivity loss: understanding the six big losses, world- class OEE. Case-based calculation and discussion.
Asset lifecycle stages: acquisition, operation, maintenance, disposal/replacement. Life- cycle costing: total cost of ownership across the asset's life and replacement problems.
Definition, need. Quality management system. Quality in service. Cost of quality: prevention costs, appraisal costs, internal failure costs, external failure costs. Core

title: Logistics and Procurement
description:
Supply chain network design; Supply chain Relationships; Freight modes; Logistics planning; Shipment
execution; Transportation sourcing and procurement; Freight Billing and Payments; Omni-Channel
Distribution; Global Trade Management (GTM); Warehousing; RFID in supply chain; Warehouse Picking;
Yard Management; Strategic Sourcing; Agreements, Supplier Management; Supplier Risk Management,
Spend Analysis and Optimization; AI and use cases in procurement; Inventory management-Concepts and
classifications; Types of Inventory Transactions; Managing Uncertainty; cost management; inventory control
techniques; Product genealogy traceability and recall management; Replenishment; Material movements
across facilities; CPFR concept; Project Based Supply Chain; Digital Technologies in SCM; Integration with
other SCM systems.
This course will give students a broad overview of the fundamental theories regarding various logistics
functions and their overall management. With this course, students will be able to approach logistics
management with a holistic view and understand, analyse, and coordinate various functions within a coherent
supply chain framework.
• This will help students understand the various components of procurement – sourcing, contracting,
supplier management, qualification management, purchasing of direct and indirect materials, spend
analysis, and its integration with other management systems/applications.
• This will help explore the importance of inventory management, the key components involved, and
the best practices that businesses can implement to improve their inventory management processes.
topics: Course introduction. Introduction to logistics: definition, scope, objectives, components, and importance of logistics. Types of logistics (procurement, production, distribution, reverse, after-sales, global, domestic). Role of logistics in manufacturing and the economy. Difference between logistics and supply chain management. Supply chain relationships. Case study.

Mathematical formulation of transportation and distribution models. Quantitative techniques to obtain an initial basic feasible solution for balanced and unbalanced transportation problems. Northwest Corner Method (NWCM). Least Cost Method. Hands-on numerical examples.

Quantitative Techniques to determine optimal movement of goods between plants, warehouses, and customers. Vogel's Approximation Method (VAM) for obtaining high-quality initial solutions. Comparison of

different initial solution methods and their efficiencies. Optimal transportation plans. MODI method. Degeneracy. Solving maximisation transportation problems. Spreadsheet implementation. Interpreting results for managerial decision-making.
Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP). Vehicle Routing Problems (VRP). Distribution routing strategies. Logistics routing applications. Case studies and optimisation exercises.

Transportation network planning. Integration of transportation with distribution planning. Carrier selection. Transportation performance measures. Strategic transportation decisions and industry applications.

Introduction to inventory management and its role in supply chains. Objectives and functions of inventory. Types and classifications of inventory (raw materials, WIP, finished goods, MRO). Inventory transactions, including receipts, issues, transfers, returns, adjustments, and stock verification. Inventory cost components include ordering, holding, shortage, and purchasing costs. Hands- on exercises on inventory classification and inventory transaction scenarios with practical numerical examples.

Continuous demand, instantaneous replenishment model. Inventory replenishment concepts and assumptions of the EOQ model. Development and mathematical derivation of the EOQ model. Analysis of total inventory cost, reorder point, and inventory cycle. Sensitivity analysis and managerial interpretation of EOQ. Step-by-step solution of a variety of numerical problems and hands-on implementation.
Economic Production Quantity (EPQ) model and its applications. Quantity

title: Management Accounting
description:
Success in any organization—from the smallest corner store to the largest
multinational corporation—requires the use of cost accounting concepts and practices. Cost accounting
provides key data to managers for planning and controlling, as well as costing products, services, even
customers. Cost accounting is one of very important managerial tool for business strategy and
implementation.
This course focuses on how cost accounting helps managers make better decisions, as cost accountants
are increasingly becoming integral members of their company’s decision-making teams.
The objectives of the course are mentioned below:
i. This course will equip students with the knowledge and analytical skills required to apply
management accounting tools and techniques for planning, decision making, cost control,
and performance evaluation in organizations.

title: Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology
description:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address
critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This
course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and
nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this
rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials,
their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical,
electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics,
medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed.
The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale
systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future
directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview
of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis
of nanoparticles and nanostructures.
Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials
and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights
real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological
domains.
This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical
exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into
advanced study or research in the field.
learning_outcomes: After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1 ◦ Explain the fundamental principles of nanoscience, including size-dependent properties and quantum effects at the nanoscale. ◦ Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials. ◦ Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.
topics: L1-L10: Course introduction, what is nanoscience and nanotechnology? Difference between micro and nano, classification of nanostructured materials, unique properties of nanomaterials: structural, electronic, magnetic, optical, mechanical.
L11-L14: Bottom-up: physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), sol- gel, spray conversion, wet chemical synthesis, self- assembly
L15-L17: Top-Down: Mechanical alloying, equal channel angular pressing, high-pressure torsion (HPT), accumulative roll bonding (ARB), Nanolithography
L18-L20: Basics of quantum physics, wave mechanics, Schrödinger wave equation, concepts of quantum well, wire and dots, tunneling, applications of quantum mechanics in nanotechnology.
L21-L23: Synthesis, properties, and applications of carbon nanostructures: fullerenes, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, nanodiamonds, and diamond-like carbon (DLC).

title: Fundamentals of Solid-State Physics
description:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of
solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers
crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the
origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course
further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before
discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying
physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors,
and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials
science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology.
This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics
that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal
structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the
thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary
electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the
relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum
mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in
semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of
semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses.
learning_outcomes: (i) Describe crystal structures, Bravais lattices, crystal systems, common crystal structures, and Miller indices, and explain their significance in determining the physical properties of crystalline solids. (ii) Apply the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to explain wave-particle duality, quantized energy levels, and the origin of electronic states in solids. (iii) Differentiate between Maxwell–Boltzmann, Bose–Einstein, and Fermi–Dirac statistics, and explain the statistical behavior of electrons and other particles in solids. (iv) Explain electrical conduction in solids using the Drude model and band theory, and relate density of states and effective mass to the electronic properties of materials. (v) Analyze the electrical properties of intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors and explain carrier transport through drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect. 1 (vi) Explain the thermal and magnetic properties of solids in terms of lattice vibrations, phonons, heat capacity, and magnetic ordering. (vii) Explain the optical properties of semiconductors and relate them to the operation of optoelectronic devices, including LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and semiconductor sensors.
topics: § Introduction to solids, Basics of crystal structure, Basis, Unit cell § Bravais lattices: Primitive and conventional cells § Fundamental types of lattices: 2D, 3D § Simple crystals: NaCl, Hexagonal closed pack, ZnS § Crystals of inert gases, Ionic crystals, Covalent crystals
§ Wave equation, Schrödinger equation, Superposition, Expectation values § Solution of Schrödinger equation: Particle in a box, Finite potential well, tunneling

§ Basics of statistical physics: Microstates, macrostates § Maxwell-Boltzmann (classical) statistics: Distinguishable particles § Quantum statistics: Bose-Einstein, Fermi-Dirac, and their applications

§ Classical free electron model; Electrical conduction: Drift velocity, mobility, conductivity; Need for quantum description § Band theory: Valence and Conduction bands, Kronig-Penney model § Classification of solids: Metals, Semiconductors, and Insulators § Conceptual introduction of density of states, Idea of effective mass

§ Intrinsic semiconductors: Electron-hole pairs, carrier density, temperature effect § Extrinsic semiconductors: Donor impurities (n-type) and Acceptor impurities (p-type) § Carrier transport: Drift, diffusion; Hall effect
§ Thermal properties: Lattice vibrations § Magnetic properties: Diamagnetism, Paramagnetism, and Ferromagnetism
§ Optical properties and applications: Photoconductivity, Solar cells, Photodetectors, LEDs
textbooks: (i) Charles Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th Ed., Wiley (2012) [TB1]. (ii) Arthur Beiser, Concepts of Modern Physics, 8th Ed., McGraw-Hill (2026) [TB2] (iii) Donald A. Neamen, Semiconductor Physics and Devices, 4th Ed. (2007) [TB3]
references: (i) Neil W. Ashcroft and N. David Mermin, Solid State Physics, Harcourt College Pub. (1976). (ii) Kenneth S. Krane, Modern Physics, 4th Ed., Wiley (2021).

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
description:
Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics
(Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge
carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions,
forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors
(JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).
The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor
devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of
semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its
application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later
like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic
diodes will also be discussed in this course.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students will be able to
CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction, quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.
CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.
CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.
CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.

CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and electronic systems.
topics: Brief history, recent trends and crystal lattices
Semiconductor models Charge carriers, effective mass.
Statistics of donors and acceptors, Space charge neutrality.
Conductivity and mobility, Hall effect
Optical absorption, excess carrier, Quasi- Fermi level
Diffusion of carriers, built-in field, continuity equation
Equilibrium conditions, Fermi levels, Poisson’s Equation, Depletion layer model.
Carrier injection, diode equation, and I-V characteristics, biasing, Reverse-bias breakdown
Capacitance of p-n junctions, Transient Analysis, non-ideal behavior.
Band-diagram of MS junction, Schottky diodes, & Ohmic contacts
Junction Field Effect Transistors (JFETs), MESFET, HEMT & MISFET
MOS structure, MOS Transistors, I-V characteristics and secondary effects
BJT operations, terminal current, Gummel plot, small-signal model, charge control model
Photodiodes, Solar cells, and Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and their advanced version

title: Object Oriented Analysis and Design
description:
The course covers the object oriented analysis and design methodology, requirements-analysis using
a use case model, use interaction models to capture the requirements and the design of the solution,
in sufficient detail. The course will also cover topics like design patterns, implementation, testing,
and architecture with respect to object oriented systems. After completion of the course the students
will have good understanding of object oriented analysis and design using the unified process and
will be able to apply the methodology to typical cases. The course aims at imparting a good
understanding of the main UML models used in the use case driven unified process and their
application to given problems.

title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
description:
Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con-
cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There
are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de-
sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside
of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger
and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of
knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in
parallel with the software development life cycle.
This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by
applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to
function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative
and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this
course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and
interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions
learning_outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to
Understand and apply fundamental software engineering principles throughout the software development life cycle.
Identify, formulate, and solve complex software engineering problems using appropriate en- gineering, scientific, and mathematical principles.
Elicit, specify, and analyze software requirements for real-world systems.
Design structured, modular, and maintainable software systems.
Develop, test, and maintain software using modern tools and best practices. 1
Function effectively as a member or leader of a diverse team, demonstrating collaboration and project management skills.
Plan and manage software projects, including task estimation, scheduling, and risk analysis.
Demonstrate awareness of ethical, legal, and societal issues in software engineering.
topics: Background and Introduction (2 Lectures)
Software Development Life- cycle Models (3 Lectures)
Requirements Analysis and Specifications (6 Lectures)
Software Project Manage- ment (10 Lectures)
textbooks: Software Engineering, Sommerville I., 10th, Pearson Education, 2010.
Software Engineering: A Practitioner’s Approach, Pressman, R.S., McGraw Hill Inter- national Edition, 2010.
references: Ref1. An Integrated Approach to Software Engineering, Jalote, P., 2nd Edition, Narosa, 1998. Ref2. Software Engineering, Schach, S., Tata MCgraw Hill, 7th Ed., 2007. Ref3. Software Engineering Fundamentals, Behforooz, A. & F.J. Hudson, OUP, 2006. Ref4. Foundations of Software Engineering, Ahmed A, CRC Press, 2016. Additional Readings as assigned and/or made available online by the I/C.

title: Social Conduct 1
description:
Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and
Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity &
Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety.
This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all
students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core
emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes
conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries
and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior
and building awareness against substance abuse.
learning_outcomes: At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to CLO1.Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being, including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness. CLO2. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures. CLO3. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics. CLO4. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital contexts. CLO5. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct. CLO6. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment. CLO7. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and promote openness around mental well-being. CLO8. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and accountable student community.
topics: Belonging, Life Skills & Neurodivergence-Inclusive Norm
Emotional Expression & Empathy
Self-Talk, Self-Awareness & Managing Transitions
Emotional Regulation & Resilience
Conflict Resolution
Healthy Habits & Grooming
Mental Health Literacy, Myth-Busting & Help-Seeking
Parent, Teacher and Peer Dynamics and High- Achievement Stress
Breaking Myths: Masculinity and Gender Roles
Sex, Sexuality, Gender and Gender Identity
Boundary-Setting, Saying No, Self-Worth and Healthy Relationships
Setting boundaries and learning to say “No”
Know Your Campus Policy: Substance Abuse and Sexual Harassment
